(p-349) Sūrat Āl ʿImrān.

The people of tafsir (exegesis) mention that it is Madinan, and that the beginning of it was revealed concerning the delegation of Najran. They came to the Prophet ﷺ with sixty riders, among them al-ʿĀqib and al-Sayyid, and they disputed with him about ʿĪsā. They said: "If he is not the son of God, then who is his father?" So the beginning of (Āl ʿImrān), up to about eighty-odd verses of it, was revealed concerning them.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He has sent down to you the Book﴾, meaning: the Qur'an, ﴿with the truth﴾, meaning: with justice. ﴿Confirming what was before it﴾ of the scriptures. It has been said: the reason He said of the Qur'an "nazzala" (with the doubled letter) and of the Torah and the Gospel "anzala" is that each of those two was sent down at one time, whereas the Qur'an was sent down on many occasions. As for the Torah, Ibn Qutayba related from al-Farrāʾ that it is derived from "wara al-zand yarā," meaning when its fire comes out, and "awraytuhu," intending that it is a light. Ibn Qutayba said: there is also another dialect: "wara yarī," and it is said: "waraytu bika zandī" (I struck my fire-stick by you). As for the Gospel (al-Injīl), it is from "najaltu al-shayʾa," meaning when I extracted it; and a man's offspring is his "najl," as if he himself extracted it. It is said: "qabbaha Allāh nājilayhi," meaning his two parents. It is also said of water that drips from a well: "najl," and it is said: "istanjala al-wādī," [when its outflow appeared]. "Injīl" is on the pattern "iflīl" from this, as if God brought forth through it the effaced remnant of the truth that had been obliterated. Our shaykh Abū Manṣūr al-Lughawī said: "al-Injīl" is a non-Arabic word that has been Arabized. He said: some of them said: if it is Arabic, its derivation is from "al-najl," which is the appearance of water on the face of the earth and its spreading; and "najaltu al-shayʾa" means I extracted it and made it manifest, so the Gospel is that through which sciences and wisdoms are extracted. It has been said: it is "iflīl" from "al-najl," which is the origin; so the Gospel is the source of sciences and wisdoms. And concerning "al-Furqān" (p-350) here there are two views. The first: that it is the Qur'an, said by Qatada and the majority. Abū ʿUbayda said: the Qur'an was named "al-Furqān" because it distinguishes between truth and falsehood, and between the believer and the disbeliever. The second: that it is the decisive distinction between truth and falsehood concerning the matter of ʿĪsā when they differed about him, said by Abū Sulaymān al-Dimashqī. Al-Suddī said: in the verse there is inversion (taqdīm wa-taʾkhīr); its meaning is: "And He sent down the Torah, and the Gospel, and the Furqān, wherein is guidance for mankind."

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 3, verse 7:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿It is He who has sent down to you the Book, in which are verses that are decisive (muhkamat)﴾. The *muhkam* is that which is perfected and clear. Regarding what is meant by it here, there are eight opinions. The first: it is the *nasikh* (the abrogating verse, the abrogating ruling, i.e., *naskh*, abrogation). This was said by Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, al-Suddi, and others. The second: it is the lawful and the unlawful (*halal* and *haram*). This is related from Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid. The third: it is that whose interpretation the scholars know. This is related from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah. The fourth: it is that which has not been abrogated. This was said by al-Dahhak. The fifth: it is that whose wording is not repeated. This was said by Ibn Zayd. The sixth: it is that which stands on its own and does not need explanation. Qadi Abu Ya'la mentioned this from Imam Ahmad. al-Shafi'i and Ibn al-Anbari said: it is that which admits of only one interpretation. The seventh: it is the whole Qur'an apart from the disjointed letters (*al-huruf al-muqatta'a*). The eighth: it is the command and the prohibition, the promise and the threat, and the lawful and the unlawful. Qadi Abu Ya'la mentioned this and the preceding one. "The Mother of the Book" (*Umm al-Kitab*) is its origin. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Jubayr. So it is as if He said: they are the origin of the Book, the verses by which rulings are acted upon, and the gathering point of the lawful and the unlawful.

Regarding the *mutashabih* (ambiguous verses), there are seven opinions. The first: it is the abrogated (*mansukh*). This was said by Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, al-Suddi, and others. The second: it is that for which the scholars have no way of knowing its meaning, such as the establishment of the Hour. This is related from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah. The third: it is the disjointed letters, such as His saying *Alif Lam Mim*, and the like. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas. The fourth: it is that whose meanings are unclear. This was said by Mujahid. The fifth: it is that whose wording is repeated. This was said by Ibn Zayd. The sixth: it is that which admits of several interpretations. Ibn al-Anbari said: the *muhkam* is that which does not admit of interpretations and is not hidden from one who discerns, and the *mutashabih* is that which is subject to various interpretations. The seventh: it is the narratives and the parables. Qadi Abu Ya'la mentioned this.

If it is said: what is the benefit of sending down the *mutashabih*, when the purpose of the Qur'an is clarification and guidance? Then there are four answers to this.

The first: since the speech of the Arabs is of two kinds. One is the concise, which is not hidden from its hearer and admits of no meaning other than its apparent one. The second is the metaphorical, the allusive, the indirect, and the suggestive. This second kind is the most pleasing to the Arabs and the most original in their speech. God, exalted is He, sent down the Qur'an in these two kinds, so that their inability to produce its like might be established. It is as if He said: challenge it with whichever of the two kinds you wish. Had it all been sent down as decisive and clear, they would have said: "Why was it not sent down in the style we find pleasing?" And whenever there occurs in speech an allusion, an indirect expression, an oblique reference, or a simile, it becomes more eloquent and more striking.

Imru' al-Qays said:

*"Your two eyes only wept so that you might strike with your two arrows at the sections of a slain heart."*

Here he made the glance like an arrow by way of simile. This pleases every listener and reciter and adds to its eloquence. Imru' al-Qays also said:

*"She shot me with an arrow that struck the heart, on the morning of departure, and I was not avenged."*

And he also said:

*"When it stretched out its back, and drew up its rear and sank down upon its breast, I said to it..."*

Here he gave the night a back and a chest by way of simile, and his poetry is made beautiful by this. Another said:

*"From a bay horse whose cooks made it excellent; not every death of it was in the cooking pots."*

By "the cooks" he meant the night and the day, by way of simile. Another said:

*"She weeps for Hashim every dawn, as the dove weeps upon the branch."*

Another said:

*"I marvel at how her singing could be eloquent, when she has not opened her mouth with speech."*

Here he gave her singing and a mouth by way of metaphor.

The second answer: God, exalted is He, sent it down to test His servants by it, so that the believer would stop at it and return it to its knowledge, thereby greatly increasing his reward, and so that the hypocrite would doubt it, and deviation would enter him, and he would thereby deserve punishment, just as He tested them with the river of Talut.

The third: God, exalted is He, willed to occupy the people of knowledge with referring the *mutashabih* back to the *muhkam*, so that their thinking would be prolonged by this, and their concern with investigating it would continue. Thus they are rewarded for their toil, just as they are rewarded for all their other acts of worship. Had He made the whole Qur'an *muhkam*, the knowledgeable and the ignorant would be equal in it, the scholar would not excel others, and thoughts would die out. Reflection and resourcefulness arise only with the need for understanding. The wise have said: the defect of wealth is that it produces dullness, and the merit of poverty is that it spurs resourcefulness, for when one is in need, one devises.

The fourth: the people of every craft place obscure meanings and subtle questions in their sciences, in order to test those whom they teach and train them in extracting the answer. For when they are able to handle the obscure, they are even more able to handle the clear. Since this is considered good among the scholars, it is permissible that what God, exalted is He, has sent down of the *mutashabih* should be of this kind. These answers convey the sense of what Ibn Qutayba and Ibn al-Anbari mentioned.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿As for those in whose hearts is deviation﴾. Regarding *zaygh* (deviation) there are two opinions. The first: it is doubt. This was said by Mujahid and al-Suddi. The second: it is inclination. This was said by Abu Malik. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas as in both opinions. It was also said: it is inclination away from guidance. Regarding these people there are four opinions. The first: they are the Kharijites (*al-Khawarij*). This was said by al-Hasan. The second: they are the hypocrites. This was said by Ibn Jurayj. The third: they are the delegation of Najran from the Christians. This was said by al-Rabi'. The fourth: they are the Jews, who sought to know the duration of this community from the reckoning of the *Jumal* (the numerical value of letters). This was said by Ibn al-Sa'ib.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿so they follow what is ambiguous of it﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: they refer the *muhkam* to the *mutashabih* and the *mutashabih* to the *muhkam*, and they confuse matters. al-Suddi said: they say, "What is the matter with this verse? It was acted upon thus-and-so, and then it was abrogated?!"

Regarding the meaning of *fitna* (discord) here, there are three opinions. The first: it is disbelief. This was said by al-Suddi, al-Rabi', Muqatil, and Ibn Qutayba. The second: it is doubts. This was said by Mujahid. The third: it is the corruption of mutual relations. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

Regarding *ta'wil* (interpretation) there are two views. The first: it is *tafsir* (exegesis). The second: it is the expected outcome.

*Al-Rasikh* means the firm, the established. It is said: *rasakha yarsukhu rusukhan*. Do those firmly rooted in knowledge know its interpretation or not? Regarding this there are two opinions. The first: they do not know it, and they begin a new clause. Tawus related from Ibn 'Abbas that he recited "and those firmly rooted in knowledge say: We believe in it." This is the view of Ibn Mas'ud, Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Ibn 'Abbas, 'Urwa, Qatada, 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-Aziz, al-Farra', Abu 'Ubayda, Tha'lab, Ibn al-Anbari, and the majority. Ibn al-Anbari said: in the reading of 'Abd Allah (ibn Mas'ud), "Its interpretation is not known except to God, and those firmly rooted in knowledge..." and in the reading of Ubayy and Ibn 'Abbas, "and those firmly rooted say..." God, exalted is He, has sent down in His Book things whose knowledge He has kept to Himself, such as His saying: ﴿Say: Its knowledge is only with my Lord﴾ [al-A'raf 7:187], and His saying: ﴿and generations between that, many﴾ [al-Furqan 25:38]. God sent down the general (*mujmal*) so that the believer would believe in it and be blessed, and the disbeliever would disbelieve in it and be wretched.

The second opinion: they do know it, and so they are included in the exception. Mujahid related from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "I am among those who know its interpretation." This is the view of Mujahid and al-Rabi', and Ibn Qutayba and Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi preferred it. Ibn al-Anbari said: the one who related this view from Mujahid is Ibn Abi Najih, and his transmission of the exegesis from Mujahid is not sound.

"His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Our Lord, do not let our hearts deviate after You have guided us﴾, meaning: they say, "Our Lord, do not incline our hearts away from guidance after You have guided us." Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami, Ibn Ya'mur, and al-Jahdari read "lā tuzigh" with a fatḥah on the tā' and "qulūbunā" with a ḍammah on the bā' (i.e., "lā tazigh" with the subject "qulūbunā" in the nominative, making the hearts the subject that deviates).

"Ladunka" means "ʿindaka" (from You, in Your presence).

"Al-Wahhāb" (the Bestower) is the One who gives generously without being asked in return (istithābah), whereas created beings cannot grant a cure to the sick or a child to the barren, while Allah, Exalted is He, is able to grant all things."

"His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Our Lord, do not let our hearts deviate after You have guided us﴾, meaning: they say, "Our Lord, do not incline our hearts away from guidance after You have guided us." Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami, Ibn Ya'mur, and al-Jahdari read "lā tuzigh" with a fatḥah on the tā' and "qulūbunā" with a ḍammah on the bā' (i.e., "lā tazigh" with the subject "qulūbunā" in the nominative, making the hearts the subject that deviates).

"Ladunka" means "ʿindaka" (from You, in Your presence).

"Al-Wahhāb" (the Bestower) is the One who gives generously without being asked in return (istithābah), whereas created beings cannot grant a cure to the sick or a child to the barren, while Allah, Exalted is He, is able to grant all things."

Allah's words: ﴿Their wealth will not avail them at all against Allah﴾ means: it will not repel (anything). For wealth does repel (harm) from its owner in this world, and so do children. But in the Hereafter, a disbeliever's wealth will not benefit him, nor will his children. And Allah's words ﴿from Allah﴾ mean: from His punishment.

Allah's words: ﴿Like the custom of the people of Pharaoh﴾. Regarding "da'b" (custom, habit) there are two opinions.

The first: it means habit, so the meaning is: "like the habit of the people of Pharaoh," meaning the disbelief of the Jews is like the disbelief of those before them. This was said by Ibn Qutaybah. Ibn al-Anbari said: the "kaf" in "ka-da'bi" (like the custom of) is connected to a hidden verb, as if he said: "The Jews disbelieved, like the disbelief of the people of Pharaoh."

The second: it means striving (ijtihad, exertion), so the meaning is: the da'b of these people, which is their striving in their disbelief and their collaboration against the Prophet (ﷺ), is like the collaboration of the people of Pharaoh against Moses (peace be upon him). This was said by al-Zajjaj.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 3, verse 12:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say to those who disbelieve: "You will be overcome and gathered to Hell."﴾ Ibn Kathir, 'Asim, Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir read (سَتُغْلَبُونَ وتُحْشَرُونَ) with the ta' (ت, the feminine/second-person prefix), and (يَرَوْنَهُمْ) with the ya' (ي, the third-person prefix). Nafi' read all three with the ta'. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read all three with the ya'. (p-356) Regarding the occasion of its revelation (sabab al-nuzul), there are three opinions. The first: when the Jews of Madinah saw the battle of Badr, they were inclined to accept Islam and said, "This is the Prophet whom we find in our Book; his banner will not be turned back." Then some of them said to others, "Do not hasten until you see him in another battle." When Uhud came, they doubted and said, "He is not that one." They broke a covenant that had been between them and the Prophet, and Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf set out with sixty riders to the people of Makkah. They said, "Let our word be one," and this verse was revealed. Abu Salih narrated this from Ibn 'Abbas. The second: it was revealed concerning Quraysh before the battle of Badr, and Allah fulfilled His promise on the day of Badr. This is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak. The third: Abu Sufyan, with a group of his people, gathered against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) after the battle of Badr, and this verse was revealed. This was said by Ibn al-Sa'ib.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 3, verse 13:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿There has already been a sign for you in two armies which met.﴾ Regarding those addressed by this, there are three opinions. The first: they are the believers; this is narrated from Ibn Mas'ud and al-Hasan. The second: they are the disbelievers, in which case it is coordinated with the one before it (i.e., the previous verse), and this follows the view of Ibn 'Abbas which we mentioned just now. The third: they are the Jews; this was mentioned by al-Farra' (grammarian), Ibn al-Anbari, and Ibn Jarir (al-Tabari). If it is said: Why did He say ﴿qad kana lakum﴾ (masculine verb "kana") and not "qad kanat lakum" (feminine)? The answer is in two respects. The first: that which is not truly feminine may have its verb made masculine. The second: that He returned the meaning to "bayan" (clear evidence), so the meaning is: "there has already been clear evidence for you." He went with the meaning and left the wording, and they recited:

"Whoever among you women is deceived by one woman after me and after you in this world, he is indeed deceived."

The meanings of "ayah" (sign) and "fi'ah" (group) have already been explained, and any difficult point whose explanation I have left out, you will find it in what has preceded. The intended "two armies" are the Prophet ﷺ and his companions, and the polytheists of Quraysh on the day of Badr. This is said by Qatadah (p-357) and the majority.

Regarding His saying, the Exalted: ﴿They saw them as twice their number﴾ there are two views. The first: they saw them as three times their number; this is said by al-Farra', who argued that when you say, "I have a thousand dinars, and I need twice that," you need three thousand. The second: its meaning is that they saw them and an equal number to them; al-Zajjaj said: this is the correct view.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿with the sight of the eye﴾ means: in the sight of the eye. Ibn Jarir said: this is on the verbal noun of "ra'aytuhu" (I saw him); it is said: "ra'aytuhu ra'yan" and "ru'yah." They differed about the seeing group on three views, which are those we mentioned in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿There has already been a sign for you﴾. If we say the seeing group are the Muslims, its reasoning is that the polytheists were prone to overestimate the number of the Muslims, so they saw them as they were, and then Allah gave them victory. Likewise if we say they are the Jews. If we say they are the polytheists, then the Muslims appearing few in their eyes was among the causes of victory. Nafi' recited "tarawnahum" with a ta' (second person). Ibn al-Anbari said: he took the address to be to the Jews. Al-Farra' said: whoever recites "yarawnahum" with a ya' may make the verb refer to the Jews, even though He had addressed them in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿There has already been a sign for you﴾, because the Arabs shift from address to third person and from third person to address. We have explained this in al-Fatihah and elsewhere. If it is said: how can it be said that the polytheists overestimated the Muslims, and the Muslims overestimated the polytheists, when His saying, the Exalted, clarifies: ﴿And when He showed them to you when you met, few in your eyes, and He made you few in their eyes﴾ [al-Anfal: 44], that the two groups were equal in each one considering the other small? The answer: they overestimated them in one state and considered them few in another state. If we say the seeing group are the Muslims, then they saw the number of the polytheists at the beginning of the fighting as it was, then Allah made the polytheists few in their eyes until they became bold against them, and Allah gave them victory by that cause. Ibn Mas'ud said: "We looked at the polytheists and saw them doubling us, then we looked at them and we did not see them exceed us by even one man." And in another narration he said: "They were made few in our eyes until I said to a man beside me: Do you see them as seventy? He said: I see them as a hundred. Then we captured a man from them, and I said: How many were you? He said: A thousand." If we say the seeing group are the polytheists, then they considered the Muslims few in one state, so they became bold against them, and they overestimated them in another state, and that was the cause of their being forsaken. It is reported that when the polytheists were captured that day, they said to the Muslims: "How many were you?" They said: "We were three hundred and thirteen." They said: "We did not see you except as doubling us."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And Allah strengthens﴾ means: He strengthens ﴿with His help whom He wills﴾... ﴿Indeed in that is a lesson﴾: regarding the demonstrative there are two views. The first: it refers to the victory. The second: it refers to the sight of the army as twice their number. "Al-'ibrah" (lesson) is the evidence that leads to certainty and results in knowledge; it is from "al-'ubur" (crossing over), as if it were a path by which one crosses and reaches the intended goal. It was said: "al-'ibrah" is the sign by which one crosses from the station of ignorance to the station of knowledge. "Al-absar" (the insights) means: the intellects and perceptions.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 3, verse 14:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Beautified for people is the love of desires﴾. Abu Razin al-Uqayli, Abu Raja al-Utaridi, Mujahid, and Ibn Muhaysin recited "zayyana" with a fatha on the zay and "hubba" with a nasb on the ba'. The explanation of beautification (tazyin) has already been given in al-Baqarah. Al-qanatir is the plural of qintar. Ibn Duraid said: the nun in it is not original, and I think it is arabicized (mu'arrab). The scholars differed over whether it is a defined (mahdud) quantity or not, and there are two views.

The first: it is defined, and on this there are eleven views. The first: it is one thousand and two hundred uqiyya (ounces), narrated by Ubayy ibn Ka'b from the Prophet (ﷺ), and Mu'adh ibn Jabal, Ibn Umar, Asim ibn Abi al-Najud, and al-Hasan in one narration also said so. The second: it is twelve thousand uqiyya, narrated by Abu Hurayrah from the Prophet (ﷺ). And from Abu Hurayrah there is a view like the two views (above), and in another narration from Abu Hurayrah also: twelve uqiyya. The third: it is one thousand and two hundred dinars, mentioned by al-Hasan, and al-Awfi narrated it from Ibn Abbas. The fourth: it is twelve thousand dirhams, or one thousand dinars, narrated by Ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn Abbas, and it is reported from al-Hasan and al-Dahhak like this view and the one before it. The fifth: it is seventy thousand dinars, reported from Ibn Umar and Mujahid. The sixth: it is eighty thousand dirhams, or one hundred ratls of gold, reported from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab and Qatadah. The seventh: it is seven thousand dinars, said by Ata. The eighth: it is eight thousand mithqals, said by al-Suddi. The ninth: it is one thousand mithqals of gold or silver, said by al-Kalbi. The tenth: it is a bull's hide filled with gold, said by Abu Nadrah and Abu Ubaydah. The eleventh: the qintar is a ratl of gold or silver, related by Ibn al-Anbari.

The second view: the qintar is not defined. Al-Rabi ibn Anas said: the qintar is abundant wealth, piled one upon another. It is reported from Abu Ubaydah that he mentioned from the Arabs that the qintar is a weight that has no limit, and this is the choice of Ibn Jarir al-Tabari. Ibn al-Anbari said: some linguists said: the qintar is a firm, strong bundle of wealth.

Regarding the meaning of al-muqantara (the heaped-up), there are three views. The first: it is the multiplied, Ibn Abbas said: the qanatir are three, and the muqantara is nine; this is the view of al-Farra. The second: it is the completed, as you say: "badra mubadhdhara" and "alf mu'allafa"; this is the view of Ibn Qutaybah. The third: it is that which has been minted until it became dinars and dirhams, said by al-Suddi.

Regarding al-musawwama (the marked), there are three views. The first: they are the grazing (horses), narrated by al-Awfi from Ibn Abbas, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid in one narration, al-Dahhak, al-Suddi, al-Rabi, and Muqatil also said so. Ibn Qutaybah said: it is said "sامت الخيل" (the horses grazed), and they are sa'ima; and "asmatha" (he pastured them), and they are musamma; and "sawwamtuha," so it is musawwama, when you pasture them. The musawwama in other than this sense is the one marked in war with a sawma and with a sima, i.e., with a sign. The second: they are the branded, narrated by Ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn Abbas, and Qatadah said so, and al-Zajjaj chose it, and from al-Hasan there are views like the two. Regarding the meaning of "al-mu'allama" there are three views. The first: it is marked with a shiyya, which is the color that differs from the rest of its coloring, narrated from Qatadah. The second: with a brand (kayy), narrated from al-Mu'arrij. The third: that they are piebald (balq), said by Ibn Kaysan. The third (view overall): that they are the fine ones (hisan), said by Ibn Ikrimah and Mujahid.

As for al-an'am, Ibn Qutaybah said: they are the camels, the cattle, and the sheep; its singular is na'am, and it is a plural that has no singular from its own form. Al-ma'ab is the return.

These mentioned things may be good, in that the servant's intention in engaging with them is rewarded, and he is recompensed for them; blame is directed only at bad intention regarding them and in them.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 3, verse 15:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say, "Shall I inform you of something better than that?"﴾ 'Ata' ibn al-Sa'ib narrated from Abu Bakr ibn Hafs, who said: When the saying of the Exalted was revealed, ﴿Adorned for people is the love of desires﴾, 'Umar said: "O Lord, now, when You have adorned them?!" Then the verse was revealed: ﴿Say, "Shall I inform you of something better than that?"﴾ The meaning of the verse is that He informed that what is with Him is better than what is in this world, even if the latter is loved, so that they would abandon what they love for what they hope for.

As for ﴿al-Ridwan﴾ (approval), 'Asim read it with a raised ra' (ri') throughout the Qur'an, except Hafs and Aban ibn Yazid from him (i.e., from 'Asim), and Yahya and al-'Ulaymi (al-Ulaymi) are excepted: they read the ra' with a kasra in al-Ma'ida in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿whoever follows His approval﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 16]. The rest read it with a kasra on the ra', and the kasra is the dialect of the Quraysh. Al-Zajjaj said: It is said: "radiytu al-shay'a arda'hu ridan wa mardatan wa ridwanan wa rudwanan" (I was pleased with the thing; I am pleased with it; approval, a pleasing state, and approval in two forms).

﴿And Allah is Seeing of the servants﴾ — He knows who prefers what is with Him over those who prefer the desires of this world, and so He will recompense them for their deeds.

(p-361) His saying, the Exalted: ﴿the patient﴾, meaning: patient in obedience to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and in refraining from what He has forbidden; ﴿the truthful﴾ in their beliefs and their statements; ﴿the obedient﴾, meaning those who are obedient to Allah; ﴿the spenders﴾ in His obedience. Ibn Qutayba said: it means by spending, charity (sadaqa). Regarding the meaning of their seeking forgiveness (istighfar), there are two views. The first: it is the seeking of forgiveness known by the tongue, said by Ibn Mas'ud and al-Hasan, among others. The second: it is the prayer (salat), said by Mujahid, Qatada, al-Dahhak, and Muqatil, among others. According to this view, prayer was called istighfar because they sought forgiveness through it. As for al-sahar (the pre-dawn hours), Ibrahim ibn al-Sari said: al-sahar is the time before the break of dawn, which is the first receding of the night until the break of dawn. Thus Allah described them with these acts of obedience, then described them as seeking forgiveness because of the intensity of their fear.

(p-361) His saying, the Exalted: ﴿the patient﴾, meaning: patient in obedience to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and in refraining from what He has forbidden; ﴿the truthful﴾ in their beliefs and their statements; ﴿the obedient﴾, meaning those who are obedient to Allah; ﴿the spenders﴾ in His obedience. Ibn Qutayba said: it means by spending, charity (sadaqa). Regarding the meaning of their seeking forgiveness (istighfar), there are two views. The first: it is the seeking of forgiveness known by the tongue, said by Ibn Mas'ud and al-Hasan, among others. The second: it is the prayer (salat), said by Mujahid, Qatada, al-Dahhak, and Muqatil, among others. According to this view, prayer was called istighfar because they sought forgiveness through it. As for al-sahar (the pre-dawn hours), Ibrahim ibn al-Sari said: al-sahar is the time before the break of dawn, which is the first receding of the night until the break of dawn. Thus Allah described them with these acts of obedience, then described them as seeking forgiveness because of the intensity of their fear.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 3, verse 18:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿God bears witness that there is no god but He﴾. The occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul) of this verse: "Two rabbis from the rabbis of Syria came to the Prophet ﷺ. When they saw Medina, one of them said to his companion: 'This city resembles the description of the city of the Prophet who will emerge at the end of time.' When they entered upon the Prophet ﷺ, they recognized him by the description and said: 'Are you Muhammad?' He said: 'Yes.' They said: 'And Ahmad?' He said: 'Yes.' They said: 'We want to ask you about a testimony. If you inform us of it, we will believe in you and affirm you.' He said: 'Ask me.' They said: 'Inform us about the greatest testimony in the Book of God.' Then this verse was revealed, and they embraced Islam." This is related by Ibn al-Sa'ib. Others said: this verse is a refutation of the Christians of Najran concerning what they claimed about 'Isa, peace be upon him, and their report has already been mentioned at the beginning of the surah. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: around the Ka'bah there were three hundred and sixty idols, and every tribe of the Arabs had one or two idols; when this verse was revealed, the idols fell down prostrate.

Regarding the meaning of ﴿God bears witness﴾ there are two views. One: it means "decreed and judged," related by Mujahid, al-Farra' and Abu 'Ubaydah. The second: it means "made clear" (bayyana), related by Tha'lab and al-Zajjaj. Ibn Kaysan said: God bears witness, through His wondrous governance and His firmly established affairs in His creation, that there is no god but He.

Some of the Bedouin were asked: "What is the proof of the existence of the Creator?" He said: "A dropping indicates the camel, and the traces of a footprint indicate the passage. So a lofty structure of such subtlety, and a lowly center of such density — do these not both indicate the All-Knowing Creator?"

Ibn Mas'ud, Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Ibn al-Sumayfa' and 'Asim al-Jahdari read (shuhada'a lillah) with a damma on the "shin," a fatha on the "ha'" and "dal," a raised hamza after the lengthening, and a kasra on the "ha'" of the name of God, Exalted is He. ﴿standing in justice﴾, i.e., with equity (bi'l-'adl).

Ja'far al-Sadiq said: He repeated "there is no god but He" because the first is a description and declaration of divine unity (tawhid), and the second is a directive and teaching, i.e., say: "There is no god but He."

The Quranic phrase ﴿Indeed, the religion with Allah is Islam﴾. The majority of readers recite "inna" with a kasra, except al-Kisa'i (al-Kisa'i), who recited the alif with a fatha. This reading (qira'ah, a recognized variant recitation) is also attributed to Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Abbas, Abu Razin, Abu al-Aliyah, and Qatada.

Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi said: When the Jews claimed that there is no religion better than Judaism, and the Christians claimed that there is no religion better than Christianity, this verse was revealed.

al-Zajjaj said: "Din" (religion) is a term for everything that Allah has made His creatures worship Him by, and has commanded them to adhere to, and that becomes their custom, and by which He will reward them.

Our shaykh Ali ibn Ubayd Allah said: "Din" is what the servant commits himself to for the sake of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

Ibn Qutayba said: "Islam" means entering into peace (al-silm), that is, into submission and obedience. Its equivalent is "istislam." It is said: "Fulan submitted (sallama) to your command," "istaslama," and "aslama," just as you say: "ashta al-rajul," meaning he entered the winter, and "arba'a," meaning he entered the spring.

Regarding "those who were given the Book" there are three opinions. The first is that they are the Jews, as reported by al-Rabi'. The second is that they are the Christians, as reported by Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr. The third is that they are both the Jews and the Christians, as reported by Ibn al-Sa'ib. It has also been said that "the Book" here is an ism jins (a collective noun used in the sense of "the books").

Regarding "those who differed concerning it," there are four opinions. The first is that it refers to their religion. The second is the matter of Jesus. The third is the religion of Islam, though they knew its truth. The fourth is the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ), though they knew his description.

﴿Except after knowledge had come to them﴾: that is, the clarification of what they differed about. ﴿out of jealous animosity among themselves﴾. al-Zajjaj said: Its meaning is that they differed out of rebellion, not out of a desire for proof. We have already mentioned in al-Baqarah the meaning of "swift in reckoning."

**Ibn al-Jawzi, *Zad al-Masir*, on Surah 3, verse 20:**

God's words: ﴿Then if they argue with you﴾, meaning they dispute with you and contend with you. Muqatil said: "It means the Jews." Ibn Jarir said: "It means the Christians of Najran concerning the matter of ʿIsa." Others said: "The Jews and the Christians." God's words: ﴿Say: I have submitted my face to God﴾. Al-Farra' said: "Its meaning is: I have made my deeds sincere." Al-Zajjaj said: "I have directed my worship to God."

God's words: ﴿And whoever follows me﴾. The people of Madina and Basra kept the *ya'* (the final long vowel "ī") when connecting (*wasl*, continuous recitation) but not when pausing (*waqf*, stopping). Ibn Shanabudh transmitted this from Qunbul, and Ibn Shanabudh and Ya'qub paused with the *ya'*. Al-Zajjaj said: "The more preferred reading, to me, is following the *muṣḥaf* (the written codex)."

As for the *ya'* elided in cases like God's words ﴿and whoever follows me﴾ (*wa-man ittabaʿna*), ﴿if You delay me﴾ (*la-in akhkhartani*), ﴿my Lord has honored me﴾ (*rabbī akramanī*), and ﴿my Lord has humiliated me﴾ (*rabbī ahānanī*), it falls into two categories:

The first is where it occurs with the *nūn*. If it is at the end of a verse, the grammarians permit eliding the *ya'*, and they call the final words of verses *al-fawāṣil* (the rhyme-endings). They permitted this in poetry as well. Al-A'sha said:

*"And from a hater, hostile in his thoughts, who, when you claim lineage to him, denies it [ankarana]."*

*"Will my venturing into the wastelands, fearing that death will come upon me [yaʾtiyanna], prevent me?"*

If it is not the last word of a verse or a rhyme-ending, then the more common practice is to keep the *ya'*, though eliding it is also good, especially with the *nūn* forms. The original form of *ittabaʿanī* was *ittabiʿī*, but the *nūn* was added to preserve the fatḥah on the *ʿayn*. So the kasrah accompanying the *nūn* takes the place of the *ya'*. When there is no *nūn*, as in *ghulāmī* (my boy) and *ṣāḥibī* (my companion), keeping the *ya'* is the better practice. Eliding it without the *nūn* is permitted, though rare. You say: *hādhā ghulāmun, qad jāʾa ghulāmī*, and *ghulāmī* may be read with a fatḥah or with sukūn on the *ya'*. Elision is permitted here because the kasrah indicates it.

God's words: ﴿And say to those who were given the Book﴾, meaning the Jews and the Christians, ﴿and to the unlettered﴾, meaning the idolaters of the Arabs. The explanation of this term has already been given in *al-Baqara*.

God's words: ﴿Have you submitted?﴾ Al-Farra' said: "It is an interrogative in form, but its meaning is a command, like God's words: ﴿So will you not desist?﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 91]."

**Section**

The scholars of *al-nāsikh wa-l-mansūkh* (abrogating and abrogated verses, i.e., the doctrine that some Qur'anic rulings were superseded by later ones) differed concerning this verse. One group held that it is *muḥkam* (not abrogated), and that its purpose is to comfort the Prophet ﷺ when those who did not respond to him refused, because he was eager for their faith and was pained when they abandoned acceptance. Another group held that its purpose is limiting the duty to conveying the message, and that this is abrogated by the verse of the sword.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 3, verse 21–22:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in the signs of Allah﴾. Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi said: By this He means the Jews and the Christians. Ibn ʿAbbas said: By "the signs of Allah" is meant Muhammad and the Qur'an. The explanation of their killing of the prophets, and of the (qist) justice and the (adl) justice, has already been given in (Al-Baqarah). The majority of readers recite ﴿and kill those who enjoin justice﴾, while Hamzah recites "wa yuqatilun" with an alif. Abu ʿUbaydah ibn al-Jarrah related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "The Children of Israel killed forty-three prophets at the beginning of the day, in a single hour. Then a hundred and twelve men from among the worshippers of the Children of Israel stood up, and they enjoined upon those who were killing them what is right and forbade them what is wrong, so they were all killed at the end of the day. They are the ones whom Allah mentioned in His Book, and He revealed the verse concerning them." It was only with this that He rebuked the Jews who were in the time of the Prophet (ﷺ), because they supported those people and were pleased with their deed. ﴿So give them good tidings﴾: here "tabshir" means "inform them." Its explanation has already been given in (Al-Baqarah). And the meaning of ﴿have become void﴾ (habitat) is: became null and invalid.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 3, verse 21–22:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in the signs of Allah﴾. Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi said: By this He means the Jews and the Christians. Ibn ʿAbbas said: By "the signs of Allah" is meant Muhammad and the Qur'an.
