Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 3, verse 23:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Scripture?﴾ Regarding the occasion of its revelation there are four opinions.

The first: "The Prophet (ﷺ) entered the bayt al-midras (the house of study) upon a group of Jews, and he called them to Allah. Two men among them said: 'Upon which religion are you?' He said: 'Upon the millah (religion) of Ibrahim.' They said: 'But he was a Jew.' He said: 'Come to the Torah.' They refused him, and this verse was revealed." Narrated by Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: "A man and a woman from the Jews committed adultery. They disliked stoning them because of their rank, so they referred their case to the Prophet (ﷺ), hoping he would have a concession. He ruled that she be stoned. They said: 'You have acted unjustly toward us, O Muhammad; stoning is not incumbent upon us.' He said: 'Between me and you is the Torah.' Ibn Suriya came and read from the Torah, but when he reached the verse of stoning he placed his palm upon it and read what came after it. Ibn Salam said: 'He has passed it over.' Then he stood up, read it, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) ordered the two Jews to be stoned, and the Jews became angry. Then this verse was revealed." Narrated by Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas.

The third: "The Prophet (ﷺ) invited the Jews to Islam. Nu'man ibn Abi Awfa said: 'Come, let us have you judged by the rabbis.' He said: 'Rather, by the Book of Allah.' He said: 'Rather, by the rabbis.' So this verse was revealed." This was said by al-Suddi.

The fourth: "It was revealed concerning a group of Jews whom the Prophet (ﷺ) invited to Islam. They said: 'We have more right to guidance than you, and Allah has sent no prophet except from the Children of Israel.' He said: 'Bring out the Torah, for in it is written that I am a prophet.' They refused, and this verse was revealed." This was said by Muqatil ibn Sulayman.

As for the tafsir: the portion they were given is the knowledge that they were taught from the Torah. Regarding the Book to which they were called there are two opinions. The first: it is the Torah, narrated by 'Ikrimah from Ibn 'Abbas, and it is the saying of the majority. The second: it is the Qur'an, narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas, and it is the saying of al-Hasan and Qatadah. Regarding that which the Book is intended to judge between them concerning, there are four opinions. The first: the millah of Ibrahim. The second: the hadd (prescribed punishment) for adultery; both were related from Ibn 'Abbas. The third: the soundness of the religion of Islam, said by al-Suddi. The fourth: the soundness of the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ), said by Muqatil.

If it is said: "Tawalli" means "turning away" (i'rad), so what is the benefit of repeating it? The answer has four aspects. The first: emphasis (ta'kid). The second: the meaning is that they turn away from the one calling them, and turn away from what he called to. The third: they turn away with their bodies while turning away from the truth with their hearts. The fourth: that "those who turned away" refers to their scholars, and "those who turned away" refers to their followers; this was said by Ibn al-Anbari.

(p-368) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That is because they said﴾. That is, what led them to turn away and be averse was that they said: ﴿The Fire will not touch us except for a number of days, counted﴾, and we have mentioned it in al-Baqarah. And (yaftaruna) means they fabricate (yakhtaliqun). Regarding what they fabricated there are two opinions. The first: it is their saying, "The Fire will not touch us except for a number of days, counted," as said by Mujahid and al-Zajjaj. The second: their saying, "We are the sons of Allah and His beloved ones," as said by Qatadah and Muqatil.

Allah's words, ﴿So how will it be when We gather them﴾: its meaning is, "How will their state be when We gather them (for a Day)," that is, for the recompense of a Day, or for the reckoning of a Day. It has been said that the "lam" (اللام) in "لِيَوْمٍ" carries the meaning of "fi" (فِي), "in."

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 3, verse 26:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say: O Allah, Owner of sovereignty﴾. Concerning the occasion of its revelation there are three reports. The first: when the Prophet (ﷺ) conquered Makkah and promised his community the dominion of Persia and Rome, the hypocrites and the Jews said, "Far-fetched!" So this verse was revealed. This was related by Ibn ʿAbbas and Anas ibn Malik. The second: the Prophet (ﷺ) asked his Lord that the dominion of Persia and Rome be given to his community, and so this verse was revealed. This was reported by Qatadah. The third: the Jews said, "By Allah, we will not obey a man who came to transfer prophethood from the Children of Israel to others." So this verse was revealed. This was stated by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi.

As for the explanation of the words, al-Zajjaj said: al-Khalil, Sibawayh, and all the trustworthy grammarians said: "Allahumma" means "Ya Allah," and the doubled "mim" was added as a substitute for the "ya," because they did not find "ya" together with this "mim" in one word, while they found the name of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, used with "ya" when the "mim" is not mentioned. Thus they knew that the "mim" at the end of the word has the same position as the "ya" at its beginning. The "damma" on the "ha" is the damma of the single vocative noun (al-ism al-munada al-mufrad, the addressed noun in the singular). Abu Sulayman al-Khattabi said: The meaning of "Owner of sovereignty" is that it is in His hand; He gives it to whom He wills. He said: Its meaning may also be "Owner of kings," and it may be understood as: "Inheritor of sovereignty on the Day when no claimant will claim it," like His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿The sovereignty on that Day belongs truly to the Most Merciful﴾ [al-Furqan: 26].

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿You give sovereignty to whom You will﴾. Regarding this "sovereignty" there are two views. One: it is prophethood, said by Ibn Jubayr and Mujahid. The second: it is wealth, slaves, and grandchildren (al-hafadah, descendants and servants), mentioned by al-Zajjaj. Muqatil said: ﴿You give sovereignty to whom You will﴾ means Muhammad and his community, ﴿and You strip sovereignty from whom You will﴾ means Persia and Rome. ﴿And You honor whom You will﴾ means Muhammad and his community, ﴿and You humble whom You will﴾ means Persia and Rome. By what does this honor and humiliation come about? There are three views. One: honor by victory and humiliation by subjugation. The second: honor by wealth and humiliation by poverty. The third: honor by obedience and humiliation by disobedience.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿In Your hand is all good﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: That means victory and spoils of war. It was also said: Its meaning is "In Your hand is the good and the evil," but He mentioned only one of them, because it is the one sought.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿You cause the night to enter into the day﴾, meaning: You make what is lost from this enter into that. Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid said: what decreases from one of them enters into the other. Al-Zajjaj said: it is said *walaja al-shay'a yaliju wulujan wa-walajan wa-waljatan* (he entered the thing).

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And You bring forth the living from the dead and You bring forth the dead from the living﴾. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, and Abu Bakr, on the authority of 'Asim, read *wa-tukhriju al-hayya mina al-mayyiti wa-tukhriju al-mayyita mina al-hayyi* (with *al-mayyita* and *al-hayyi* in the second clause). And (*li-baladin mayyitin*) [Al-A'raf: 57], and (*awa man kana maytan*) [Al-An'am: 122], and (*wa-in yakun maytatan*) (p-370) [Al-An'am: 139], and (*al-ardu al-maytatu*) [Ya-Sin: 33]: all of these with light (unstressed) *mayt*. Nafi', Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i read: (*wa-tukhriju al-hayya mina al-mayyiti wa-tukhriju al-mayyita mina al-hayyi*), (*li-baladin mayyitin*), and (*ila baladin mayyitin*), and Hamzah and al-Kisa'i lightened other than these letters. Nafi' read (*awa man kana maytan*), (*al-ardu al-maytatu*), and (*lahma akhihi maytan*) [Al-Hujurat: 12], and lightened in the rest of the Qur'an what did not die (*lam yamut*). Abu 'Ali said: the original is the heavy form, and the light form is derived from it; *mata* (he died) and *lam yamut* (he has not died) are equivalent in usage in this category. They cited:

"A watering place in which the crow is dead; I gave drink from it to the people and I drew water for myself."

So this one has died. Another said:

"He who died and rested is not a dead one; the dead one is the dead of the living."

So he lightened what died and stressed what did not die. Similarly His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed you are dying and indeed they are dying﴾ [Az-Zumar: 39:30].

Then there are three opinions regarding the meaning of the verse. The first: it is the bringing forth of a living human from a sperm-drop, which is dead, and the bringing forth of the sperm-drop from a human; likewise the bringing forth of the chick from the egg and the bringing forth of the egg from the bird. This is the saying of Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Ibn Jubayr, and the majority. The second: it is the bringing forth of the living believer by faith from the dead disbeliever by disbelief, and the bringing forth of the dead disbeliever by disbelief from the living believer by faith. Al-Dahhak related something similar from Ibn 'Abbas, and this is the saying of al-Hasan and 'Ata'. The third: it is the bringing forth of the living ear of grain from the dead grain, and the living palm tree from the dead date-stone, and the dead date-stone from the living palm tree; this was said by al-Suddi. Al-Zajjaj said: He brings forth the tender plant from the dry seed, and the dry seed from the living, growing plant.

(p-371) His saying, the Exalted: ﴿without reckoning﴾, meaning: without restriction. Al-Zajjaj said: it is said of one who spends lavishly: "So-and-so spends without reckoning," as if he does not count what he has spent.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 3, verse 28:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Let not the believers take the disbelievers as allies﴾. Regarding the occasion of its revelation there are four opinions. The first: ʿUbadah ibn al-Samit had allies among the Jews, and on the day of the Confederates (al-Ahzab) he said: "O Messenger of Allah, I have five hundred Jews with me, and I have decided to seek their support against the enemy." So this verse was revealed. Related by al-Dahhak from Ibn ʿAbbas. The second: it was revealed concerning ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy and his companions among the hypocrites, who used to befriend the Jews and bring them news, hoping for them to gain victory over the Prophet (ﷺ). So Allah forbade the believers from acts like theirs. Related by Abu Salih from Ibn ʿAbbas. The third: a group of Jews used to secretly associate with some of the Ansar in order to seduce them from their religion, so a group of Muslims forbade that and said: "Avoid these Jews." But they refused, and so this verse was revealed. This is also related from Ibn ʿAbbas. The fourth: it was revealed concerning Hatib ibn Abi Balta'ah and others, who used to show affection to the disbelievers of Makkah, so Allah, Mighty and Majestic, forbade them from that. This is the saying of the commentators al-Muqatil, Ibn Sulayman and Ibn Hayyan.

As for the interpretation, al-Zajjaj said: The meaning of His saying ﴿rather than the believers﴾ is: the believer should not make his allegiance to one who is not a believer; that is, he should not take allegiance from a place other than the place of the believers. This is a speech following the figurative use of place, as you say: "Zayd is beneath you," and you do not mean physical place, but you have made nobility like elevation in place and baseness like being low in place. And the meaning of ﴿then there is nothing of Allah in him﴾ is: then Allah is free of him.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Except that you fear a danger from them, a fear﴾. Ya'qub and al-Mufaddal from ʿAsim read "taqiyyah" with a fatha on the ta' without an alif. Mujahid said: "Except in outward courtesy in worldly affairs." Abu al-ʿAliyah said: "The taqiyyah is with the tongue, not with action."

Section

Taqiyyah is a concession (rukhsah), not an obligation (ʿazimah). Imam Ahmad said: "It has been said: if you are presented with the sword, would you respond (with disavowal)?" He said: "No." And he said: "When a scholar answers out of taqiyyah and the ignorant out of ignorance, then when will the truth become clear?" We will explain this matter in (Surah) al-Nahl, at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿except one who is compelled﴾ [al-Nahl: 106], if Allah wills.
His words, exalted is He: ﴿Say: Whether you conceal what is in your breasts or reveal it﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: it means the taking of the disbelievers as allies (awliya').

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 3, verse 30:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿On the Day every soul will find what it has done of good present﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: He put "the Day" in the accusative by His saying: ﴿and Allah warns you of Himself﴾, [meaning] on that Day. Ibn al-Anbari said: It is permissible for it to be connected to "al-masir" (the return), and the implied meaning is: "And to Allah is the return, on the Day when you find." It is also permissible for it to be connected to a hidden verb, and the implied meaning is: "Remember the Day when you find." Regarding how the deed is "found," there are two views. One: its existence as written in the Record. The second: the existence of the recompense for it. And al-Amad means the limit (al-ghayah).

(p-373) Al-Tirimmah said:

"Every living thing completes the span of its lifetime, and it is one who departs when its term (amad) has ended."

He means the limit of its appointed term.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 3, verse 31:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: If you should love Allah, then follow me; Allah will love you﴾. Regarding the occasion of its revelation there are four reports.

The first: "That the Prophet ﷺ stood over the Quraysh while they had set up their idols and were prostrating to them, and he said: O assembly of Quraysh, 'You have indeed opposed the religion of your father Ibrahim (Abraham).' They said: O Muhammad, we only worship these out of love for Allah, so that they may bring us near to Allah in closeness. Then this verse was revealed." Reported by al-Dahhak from Ibn Abbas.

The second: "That the Jews said: We are the sons of Allah and His beloved ones. So this verse was revealed, and the Prophet ﷺ presented it to them, but they did not accept it." Reported by Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas.

The third: That some people said: "Indeed we love our Lord with an intense love." So Allah, desiring to make a sign for their love, revealed this verse. This was said by al-Hasan and Ibn Jurayj.

The fourth: That the Christians of Najran said: "You only say this about Isa (Jesus) out of love for Allah and in exaltation of Him." So this verse was revealed. This was mentioned by Ibn Ishaq, from Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr, and it was chosen by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 3, verse 32:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Say: Obey Allah and the Messenger﴾. Regarding the occasion of its revelation there are three opinions. The first: that ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy (the leader of the hypocrites in Medina) said to his companions: "Muhammad makes his obedience like the obedience to Allah, and he commands us to love him as the Christians loved ʿIsa ibn Maryam (Jesus, son of Mary)." So this verse was revealed. This is the saying of Ibn ʿAbbas. The second: "The Prophet (ﷺ) invited the Jews to Islam, and they said: 'We are the sons of Allah and His beloved, and we love Allah more intensely than what you invite us to.' So ﴿Say: If you should love Allah﴾ was revealed, and this verse was revealed." This is the saying of Muqatil. The third: that it was revealed concerning the Christians of Najran; this was said by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 3, verse 33:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah chose Adam﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: The Jews said: "We are the sons of Ibrahim, Ishaq, and Ya'qub, and we are upon their religion." So this verse was revealed. Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning of "isṭafāhum" (chose them) in the language is: he selected them, making them the elite (ṣafwah) of His creation. This is an illustration through what is seen, because the Arabs illustrate a known matter by a visible thing. When the listener hears that, the known matter is for him like something witnessed directly. We see that the pure thing is clear, meaning free of turbidity, and likewise the elite of Allah's creation. The word has three forms: ṣafwah, ṣifwah, and ṣufwah. As for Adam, he is Arabic, and we have mentioned his derivation in "al-Baqarah." As for Nuh, he is non-Arabic, Arabicized (mu'arrab). Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi said: The name of Nuh is al-Sakan, and he was named Nuh because of his much lamenting (nawh). Concerning the cause of his lamentation there are five opinions. The first: that he used to lament over himself; this was said by Yazid al-Raqashi. The second: that he used to lament over the disobedience of his family and people. The third: because of his petitioning his Lord concerning his son. The fourth: because of his supplication against his people for destruction. The fifth: that he passed by a mangy dog and said, "Begone, ugly one!" Then Allah revealed to him: "Do you blame Me, O Nuh, or do you blame the dog?"

Concerning "the family of Ibrahim" there are three opinions. The first: that it refers to those who were upon his religion; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan. The second: that they are Isma'il, Ishaq, Ya'qub, and the tribes (al-asbat); this was said by Muqatil. The third: that the intended meaning of "the family of Ibrahim" is himself, as in His saying: ﴿And a remnant of what the family of Musa and the family of Harun left behind﴾ [al-Baqarah: 248]; this was mentioned by some of the exegetes.

Concerning "'Imran" there are two opinions. One: that he is the father of Maryam; this was said by al-Hasan and Wahb. The other: that he is the father of Musa and Harun; this was said by Muqatil.

Concerning "his family" there are three opinions. The first: that it refers to 'Isa (peace be upon him); this was said by al-Hasan. The second: that his family are Musa and Harun; this was said by Muqatil. The third: that the intended meaning of "his family" is himself; this was mentioned by some of the exegetes. He singled out these persons for mention because all the prophets are from their offspring.

Concerning the meaning of the choosing of these mentioned persons there are three opinions. The first: that the intended meaning is that He chose their religion over all other religions; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas, and preferred by al-Farra' and al-Dimashqi. The second: that He chose them with prophethood; this was said by al-Hasan, Mujahid, and Muqatil. The third: that He chose them by preferring them in the matters with which He distinguished them over the people of their time. The intended meaning of "al-'alamin" (the worlds) is the people of their time, as we have mentioned in "al-Baqarah."

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 3, verse 34:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿offspring, one descended from another﴾. Al-Zajjaj (a grammarian) said: it is in the accusative as a substitute (badal), and the meaning is: He chose offspring, one descended from another. Ibn al-Anbari said: He said "ba'duha" (some of them) because the word dhurriyyah (offspring) is feminine; if he had said "ba'duhum" (some of them, masculine), he would have been going by the meaning of dhurriyyah (as a collective of people). Regarding the meaning of this "some of" there are two views. The first: that some of them are from others in support and religion, not in procreation; this is the meaning of the saying of Ibn Abbas and Qatadah. The second: that it refers to the lineage-chain, because all of them are the offspring of Adam, then the offspring of Noah, then the offspring of Abraham; this was mentioned by some of the people of tafsir (exegesis). Abu Bakr al-Naqqash said: the meaning of His saying ﴿offspring, one descended from another﴾ is that sons are offspring of fathers, and fathers are offspring of sons, like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿We carried their offspring in the laden ship﴾ [Ya-Sin: 41], where He made the fathers offspring of the sons. This is permissible because dhurriyyah is derived from "dhara'a Allah al-khalq" (God created the creation), so a child is called dhurriyyah to its parent because it was created from him; likewise it is permissible to say of a father that he is dhurriyyah to his son, because his son was created from him. The verb connects to him from both directions. A similar usage is His saying: ﴿They love them as they love God﴾ [al-Baqarah: 165], where the love is attributed to God, and the meaning is: as the believer's love for God. Similarly ﴿And they give food, despite their love for it﴾ [al-Insan: 8], where the love is attributed to the food.

(p-376) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿When the wife of ʿImrān said﴾. Regarding "idh" (when) there are two opinions. The first: it is superfluous (zāʾida), an opinion chosen by Abū ʿUbayda and Ibn Qutayba. The second: it is an original element of the speech, and regarding it there are three opinions. The first: the meaning is "Remember when the wife of ʿImrān said," as said by al-Mubarrad and al-Akhfash. The second: the governing element (ʿāmil) of "when she said" is the sense of "choosing" (iṣṭifāʾ), so the meaning is: He chose the family of ʿImrān when the wife of ʿImrān said, and He chose them when the angels said: "O Maryam" (Mary). This is the choice of al-Zajjāj. The third: it is connected to "All-Hearing" (samīʿ), its estimate being: "And Allah is All-Hearing when she said." This is the choice of Ibn Jarīr al-Ṭabarī. Ibn ʿAbbās said: The name of the wife of ʿImrān was Ḥinna, and she is the mother of Maryam. This ʿImrān is the son of Mātān, and not "ʿImrān the father of Mūsā," and this Maryam is not the sister of Mūsā. Between ʿĪsā and Mūsā there were one thousand eight hundred years. And "al-muḥarrar" means "al-ʿatīq" (the freed one, dedicated). Ibn Qutayba said: It is said "aʿtaqtu al-ghulām" and "ḥarrartuhu," which are synonymous. She meant: I vowed to make what is in my womb freed from servitude to the world, so that it may worship You. Al-Zajjāj said: It was obligatory upon their children that they obey them regarding their vows, so a man would vow concerning his child that he would serve in their place of worship. Ibn Isḥāq said: The cause of her vow was that He withheld offspring from her until she grew old. She saw a bird feeding its chick, so she called upon Allah to grant her a child and said: "O Allah, for You is my pledge if You grant me a child, that I will dedicate him to Bayt al-Maqdis (the Holy House)." So she conceived Maryam, and ʿImrān died while she was pregnant. Qāḍī Abū Yaʿlā said: A vow of the kind you have made is valid in our law, for when a person vows to raise his young child in the worship and obedience of Allah, and to teach him the Qur'an, jurisprudence (fiqh), and the sciences of religion, the vow is valid.

Ibn al-Jawzi's commentary on Surah 3, verse 36:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And the male is not like the female﴾ is part of her excuse, and its meaning is: the female is not suited to what the male is suited to, such as serving the mosque and staying in it, because of what befalls the female of menstruation and postnatal bleeding. Al-Suddi said: she had thought that what was in her womb was a boy, so when she gave birth to a girl, she made an excuse.

"Maryam" is a non-Arabic (a'jami) name. Regarding "al-Rajim" (the accursed) there are two opinions. The first: it means the accursed, as said by Qatadah. The second: it means the one stoned with stones, just as you say "qatil" in the sense of "maqtul" (killed); this was said by Abu 'Ubaydah. According to this, he was called "rajim" because he is pelted with the stars.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 3, verse 37:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So her Lord accepted her with a goodly acceptance﴾. Mujahid read (fa-taqabbalaha) with a sukun on the lam, (rabbaha) with a fatha on the ba', and (wa-anbataha) with a kasra on the ba' and a sukun on the ta', in the sense of supplication. Al-Zajjaj said: The original form in Arabic is fa-taqabbalaha bi-taqabbulin hasanin, but "qabul" is taken as a verbal noun of qabiliha qabulan, one says: qabiltu al-shay' qabulan, and it is permissible to say qubulan when you are pleased with it. ﴿And He caused her to grow a goodly growth﴾, i.e., He made her growing a goodly growing. "Nabatan" came in a form other than the verb anbata, in the sense of: she grew a goodly growth. Ibn al-Anbari said: Since "anbata" indicates "nabata," the verb is construed according to its meaning, as if he had said: "wa-anbataha," so she grew (nabatat) a goodly growth.

Imru' al-Qays said:

fa-sirna ila al-husna wa-raqqa kalamuna
wa-radda fa-dhallat sa'batan ayya idhlali

He meant: ayya riyadatin (what taming). When "radda" indicated "adhlalta," he construed it according to its meaning.

Regarding the meaning of the goodly growth, the exegetes have two opinions. One: it is the perfection of growth. Ibn 'Abbas said: she used to grow in a day what a child grows in a year. The second: it is that she abstained from sins. Qatada said: It was related to us that she did not commit sins as the children of Adam do.

His saying, the Exalted: (wa-kafalaha). Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir read: "wa-kafalaha" with a light fa' (fatha), and "Zakariyya'" in the nominative with madd. Abu Bakr narrated from 'Asim: a shaddah on the fa', and he put "Zakariyya'" in the accusative, and he used to lengthen "Zakariyya'" throughout the Qur'an in Abu Bakr's narration. Hafs narrated from 'Asim: a shaddah on the fa' and "Zakariyya" shortened throughout the Qur'an. Hamza and al-Kisa'i would put a shaddah on "kafalaha" and shorten "Zakariyya" throughout the Qur'an. As for "Zakariyya," al-Farra' said: In it there are three dialects. The people of the Hijaz say: "hadha Zakariyya qad ja'a," shortened, and Zakariyya', lengthened; and the people of Najd say: Zakari, so they inflect it and drop the alif. I read to our shaykh Abu Mansur al-Lughawi, from Ibn Durayd, who said: Zakariyya is a non-Arabic name; it is said: Zakariyy, and Zakariyya' with madd, and Zakariyya with qasr. Others said: and Zakari with a light ya'. Whoever says Zakariyya' with madd says in the dual Zakariyyawan, and in the plural Zakariyyawun; whoever says Zakariyya with qasr says in the dual Zakariyyan, as you say Madaniyyan; and whoever says Zakari with a light ya' says in the dual Zakariyan with a light ya', and in the plural Zakarun with the ya' dropped.

The Indication to Zakariyya's Guardianship of Maryam

Al-Suddi said: Her mother set out with her in her swaddling clothes, and they used to draw lots among those who brought their children. Zakariyya, who was their prophet on that day, said: "I am the most entitled of you to her, for her aunt is with me." They refused and went out to the river Jordan, and they cast their pens with which they wrote; the pens flowed, but Zakariyya's pen stood still, so he became her guardian. Ibn 'Abbas said: They were twenty-seven men, and they said: "We will cast our pens; whoever makes his pen rise against the current is the most entitled to her." Zakariyya's pen rose, so according to this view Zakariyya's victory was by the rising of his pen, and according to al-Suddi's view by its standing still in the flow of the water. Muqatil said: He would lock the door on her, keeping the key, and would not trust anyone with it; and when she menstruated, he would take her out to his house to be with her sister Umm Yahya, and when she became pure, he would return her to Bayt al-Maqdis. Most of them hold that he became her guardian from when she was a little girl, by lot. Some people held that he became her guardian in her childhood without a lot, because her mother had died and her maternal aunt was with him; when she reached maturity, they took her into the synagogue in fulfilment of her mother's vow, and the drawing of lots came later, after a period, because of a year of drought that struck them. Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: Zakariyya guardianship of her lasted until a year of drought struck the people, and Zakariyya complained to the Children of Israel of the narrowness of his means; they said: "We too are in the same state," so they began to pass her among themselves until they drew lots, and the lot fell on Jurayj the carpenter, who was poor, and he used to bring her small amounts which would increase. Zakariyya entered and said: "What is this? Is it according to the expenditure of Jurayj? From where is this?" She said: "It is from Allah." The sound view is what most of them hold: that the people competed for her guardianship because she was the daughter of their chief and imam, 'Imran; so said Qatada and others, and that Zakariyya prevailed over them by lot from her childhood.

As for the mihrab, Abu 'Ubayda said: (p-380) the mihrab is the chief of assemblies, its foremost and noblest part, and likewise it is of the mosque. Al-Asma'i said: The mihrab here means the upper chamber. Al-Zajjaj said: The mihrab in the language is the lofty, noble place.

The poet said:

rabbatu mihrabin idha ji'taha *** lam alqaha aw artaqi sullaman

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿He found with her provision﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: fruits of Paradise, summer fruit in winter and winter fruit in summer; this is the saying of the majority.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Whence is this to you?﴾, i.e., from where? Al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: Whenever Zakariyya went out, he would lock seven doors upon her, and when he entered he would find provision with her. Al-Hasan said: She never suckled a breast at all; her provision came to her from Paradise, and Zakariyya would say: "Whence is this to you?" and she would say: "It is from Allah"; and she spoke while still young. Muqatil claimed that Zakariyya hired a wet-nurse for her; and according to what we mentioned from Ibn Ishaq, his saying to her "Whence is this to you?" is for his amazement at what he saw with her. What the majority hold is more sound. And reckoning (al-hisab) in the language means restriction and constriction.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 3, verse 38:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿There Zakariyya called upon his Lord﴾. The exegetes (al-mufassirun) said: When Zakariyya witnessed this wondrous provision of God Most High to Maryam, fruit out of its season, he longed for a child in his old age. And ﴿from Yourself﴾ means: from Your presence. The word dhurriyya (offspring) is used for both the singular and the plural, and what is meant here is the singular. Al-Farra' said: He said ṭayyiba (good) because dhurriyya is feminine in form, and what is meant by ṭayyiba is pure and righteous. And al-Samiʿ (the All-Hearing) means al-sami' (the one who hears). It was also said: he meant the One who answers supplication (mujib al-du'a').

[p-381] His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then the angels called to him﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Asim, Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir read *fa-nadat-hu* (فَنادَتْهُ) with a *ta'* (ت). Hamza and al-Kisa'i read *fa-nadahu* (فَناداهُ) with an *alif* and *imalah* (a vowel-raising of the *alif* toward *ya'*). Abu 'Ali said: this is like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And women said﴾ [Yusuf: 30]. Ali, Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Abbas read *fa-nadahu* (فَناداهُ) with an *alif*.

There are two views concerning "the angels." The first is that it was Jibril alone. This was said by al-Suddi and Muqatil. Its justification is that the Arabs use a plural form to refer to one person: "I rode in the ships," and "I heard this from the people." The second is that they were a group of angels. This is the view of a group of scholars, including Ibn Jarir al-Tabari.

There are two views concerning "the *mihrab*." The first is that it is the mosque. The second is that it is the direction of the mosque (its *qiblah* wall).

Concerning naming the prayer-niche a *mihrab*, there are three views. The first is that it is because the imam stands alone in it and is distant from the people. From this comes their saying: "So-and-so is a *harb* (enemy) to so-and-so," when there is mutual hatred and estrangement. This was mentioned by Ibn al-Anbari from his father, from Ahmad ibn 'Ubayd. The second is that the *mihrab* in the language means the most noble places, and the most noble part of the mosque is the place where the imam stands. The third is that it derives from *harb* (war), since the one who prays is fighting against Satan.

His saying, Exalted is He: (That God gives you good news of a son) . Most readers read *inna* (أنَّ) with an open *alif*, meaning: the angels called to him "that God..." When the preposition was removed, the verb reached it and governed it in the accusative. Ibn 'Amir and Hamza read *inna* (إنْ) with a *kasrah*, implying the verb of saying: the meaning is "he called to him, and said: Indeed God gives you good news." Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read *yubashshiruka* (يُبَشِّرُكِ) with a *damm* on the *ya'* and a *fath* on the *ba'*, with a doubled *shin* throughout the Qur'an except in *Ha Mim 'Ayn Sin Qaf* (Ash-Shura). In that surah, ﴿God gives good news to His servants﴾ [Ash-Shura: 23] is read with an open *ya'*, a *damm* on the *shin*, and a single *shin*. As for Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and Asim, they doubled the *shin* in the whole Qur'an. Hamza read *yubashshiru* (يُبَشِّرُ) lightly (single *shin*) throughout the Qur'an, except His saying: ﴿So with what do you give good news?﴾ [Al-Hijr: 54]. Al-Kisa'i read *yubshiru* (يُبْشِرُ) with a single *shin* in five places: in Al 'Imran concerning the story of Zakariyya, in the story of Maryam, in Bani Isra'il, in Al-Kahf, and in *Ha Mim 'Ayn Sin Qaf*.

Al-Zajjaj said: In *yubashshiruka* (يُبَشِّرُكَ) there are three dialects. The first is *yubashshiruki* (يُبَشِّرُكِ), with an open *ba'* and a doubled *shin*. The second is *yabshuruka* (يَبْشُرُكَ), with a sukun on the *ba'* and a *damm* on the *shin*. The third is *yubshiruki* (يُبْشِرُكِ), with a *damm* on the *ya'* and a sukun on the *ba'*. The meaning of *yubashshiru* (يُبَشِّرُ) with doubling and *yubshiru* (يُبْشِرُ) with a *damm* on the *ya'* is: giving good news. The meaning of *yabshuru* (يَبْشُرُ) with a *fath* on the *ya'* is: it delights you and makes you happy. It is said: "I gave the man good news (*bashshartu al-rajul*), I give him good news: when I made him happy," and "the man was given good news (*bushshira*), he is given good news: when he became happy."

Al-Akhfash and al-Kisa'i recited:

"And when you meet those who boast of high rank, their palms dust-covered in a barren land,
Then help them, and rejoice in what they rejoice in, and when they descend into hardship, descend with them."

This is according to *bashara* (بَشَرَ), *yabsharu* (يَبْشَرُ): when he became happy. The origin of all this is that a person's skin (*bashrah*) spreads out when he is happy. From it comes their saying: "He meets me with *bishr*," meaning with a face that is open and cheerful.

Concerning the meaning of his being named "Yahya," there are five views. The first is that God gave life through him to his mother's barren womb, said by Ibn 'Abbas. The second is that God gave life to his heart with faith, said by Qatadah. The third is that He gave him life between an old man and an old woman, said by Muqatil. The fourth is that he was *hayiyy* (modest, alive) through the knowledge and wisdom he was given, said by al-Zajjaj. The fifth is that God gave him life through obedience, so he did not disobey and did not intend (sin), said by al-Hasan ibn al-Fadl.

Concerning "the word" (*kalimah*), there are two views. The first is that it refers to 'Isa, and he was called "a word" because he came into being through the word, which is "Be" (*kun*). This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Mujahid, Qatadah, al-Suddi and Muqatil. It is also said that Yahya was six months older than 'Isa, and Yahya was killed before 'Isa was raised. The second is that the "word" is the Book of God and His signs. This is the view of Abu 'Ubaydah and others. Its justification is that the Arabs say: "So-and-so recited to me a *kalimah*," meaning a *qasidah* (poem).

Concerning the meaning of *sayyid* (leader, lord), there are eight views. The first is that he is honoured before his Lord, said by Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid. The second is that he is forbearing and God-fearing, also reported from Ibn 'Abbas, and said by al-Dahhak. The third is that he is wise, said by al-Hasan, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, 'Ikrimah, 'Ata', Abu al-Sha'tha', al-Rabi' and Muqatil. The fourth is that he is a jurist and learned scholar, said by Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib. The fifth is that he is God-fearing, related by Salim from Ibn Jubayr. The sixth is that he has good character, related by Abu Rawq from al-Dahhak. The seventh is that he is noble, said by Ibn Zayd. The eighth is that he surpasses his people in goodness, said by al-Zajjaj. Ibn al-Anbari said: *sayyid* here means the chief and the leader in goodness.

As for *hasur* (chaste, one who abstains), Ibn Qutaybah said: it is the one who does not approach women. It is on the pattern *fa'ul* in the sense of *maf'ul* (passive), as if he were *mahsur* (restrained) from them, that is, held back from them. The root of *hasr* is confinement. Among what came on the pattern *fa'ul* in the sense of *maf'ul* are *rukub* (meaning *markub*, ridden), *halub* (meaning *mahlub*, milked), and *hayub* (meaning *mahib*, feared).

The commentators differed as to why he did not approach women, in four views. The first is that he did not have the capacity to approach women. 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As related from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "Every son of Adam will come on the Day of Resurrection carrying a sin, except Yahya ibn Zakariyya." He said: Then the Messenger of God ﷺ lowered his hand to the ground, took a small twig, and said: "That is because he did not have what men have, except like this twig. For this reason God called him *sayyid* and *hasur*." Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib said: he had something like a date-stone. The second is that he did not experience erection, said by Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak. The third is that he had no desire for women, said by al-Hasan, Qatadah and al-Suddi. The fourth is that he restrained himself from their desires, mentioned by al-Mawardi.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And a prophet from among the righteous﴾. Ibn al-Anbari said: its meaning is: among those righteous in state (*al-salihin al-hal*) before God.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 3, verse 40:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿He said, "My Lord, how can I have a boy?"﴾ That is: how can it be?!

Al-Kumayt said:

"How, and from where, did the longing [ṭarab] stir you?"

The scholars, among them al-Hasan, Ibn al-Anbari and Ibn Kaysan, said: It is as if he said, "In what manner will a child be born to me? Will it come by removing the barrenness from my wife and restoring my youth, or will it come while we remain in our present state?" This was a question seeking information, not an expression of doubt. Al-Zajjaj said: It is said, "ghulam" (boy), "bayn al-ghulumiyya" (between the state of boyhood), "bayn al-ghulamiyya," and "bayn al-ghulumah." Our shaykh Abu Mansur al-Lughawi said: "al-ghulam" is of the pattern fu'al, from al-ghulma (ghulma), which is the intensity of sexual desire for marriage. It is also said of an older man: "ghulam."

Layla al-Akhyaliyya, praising al-Hajjaj, said:

"A boy, when he shakes the spear, gives it to drink."

It is as though their saying of an older man, "ghulam," means that he was once a boy. And their saying of a small child, "ghulam," is in the sense of optimism, that is, he will become a boy. He said: It has also been said: "al-ghulam" is one whose beard has just begun to grow (al-tarr al-shārib). It is said of a girl: "ghulama." The poet said:

"The girl-boy (al-ghulama) and the boy are humbled for her."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And indeed old age has reached me﴾ That is: and indeed you have reached old age. Al-Zajjaj said: Everything you have reached, has reached you. There are six sayings regarding his age at that time. The first: he was one hundred and twenty years old, and his wife was ninety-eight years old; this was said by Ibn Abbas. The second: he was in his early seventies (ibn bid' wa-sab'īn), said by Qatada. The third: he was seventy-five, said by Muqatil. The fourth: he was seventy, related by Fudayl ibn Ghazwan. The fifth: he was sixty-five. The sixth: he was sixty, related by al-Zajjaj. The linguists said: "al-'aqir" among men and women is the one who does not have children. He said "'aqiran" and did not say "'aqirah," because the original use of this description is for the feminine, and the masculine form of it is as if borrowed, so it was treated like "ṭāliq" and "ḥā'iḍ." This is the saying of al-Farra'.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 3, verse 41:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And glorify [Him]﴾. Muqatil said: "Pray." Al-Zajjaj said: It is said, "I finished my subha (tasbih)," meaning: "from my prayer." Prayer was called tasbih because tasbih is the magnifying of God and declaring Him free from imperfection, and in prayer one describes Him with everything that declares Him free from imperfection.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿in the evening﴾. Al-ʿashiyy: from the time the sun declines until the end of the day. ﴿And in the morning﴾ (al-ibkar): what lies between the break of dawn and the time of forenoon (al-duha). The poet said:

"Neither does the shade in the cool of the forenoon reach it, nor does the shadow from the cool of the evening taste [it]."

Al-Zajjaj said: It is said, "abkara al-rajul yubkiru ibkaran," and "bakara yabkuru tabkiran," and "bakkara yubakkiru" (p-387) in everything in which one has gone early.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 3, verse 42:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And [mention] when the angels said, "O Mary, indeed Allah has chosen you and purified you and chosen you above the women of the worlds."﴾ A group of the exegetes said: the word "angels" here refers to Jibril (Gabriel) alone. The meaning of ischifa' (choosing, selection) has already been explained. Regarding the intended meaning of "purification" here, there are four opinions. The first: it is purification from menstruation (hayd), reported from Ibn 'Abbas. As-Suddi said: Mary did not menstruate. Some people said: it is from menstruation and postnatal bleeding (nifas). The second: purification from the touch of men, also reported from Ibn 'Abbas. The third: from disbelief (kufr), said by al-Hasan and Mujahid. The fourth: from indecency and sin, said by Muqatil. Regarding this second "choosing," there are four opinions. The first: it is an emphasis of the first. The second: the first is for worship, and the second is for the birth of 'Isa (Jesus), peace be upon him. The third: the first choosing is a vague selection and a general matter that includes righteous women, so the choosing was repeated to show her superiority over the women of the worlds. The fourth: when the first choosing was stated without qualification, the second clarified that she was chosen above women but not above men. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, and Ibn Jurayj said: He chose her above the people of her time. Ibn al-Anbari said: this is the view of the majority.

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿O Mary, be devoutly obedient to your Lord﴾. The explanation of qunut (devout obedience) has already been given in Al-Baqarah. Regarding its meaning here, there are four views. The first is that it means worship; this was said by al-Hasan. The second is prolonged standing in prayer; this was said by Mujahid (p-388). The third is obedience; this was said by Qatadah, al-Suddi, and Ibn Zayd. The fourth is sincerity; this was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

Regarding the placement of prostration before bowing, there are four views. The first is that the particle waw does not require sequence but only indicates combination, so bowing is mentioned first; this was said by al-Zajjaj and others. The second is that the meaning is: perform prostration at one time and bowing at another, not that both are combined in a single rak'ah, so that she is urged to do good. The third is that the verse contains inversion (taqdim and ta'khir), and the meaning is: bow and prostrate, like His saying: ﴿Indeed, I will cause you to die and raise you to Myself﴾ (Al 'Imran: 55). Ibn al-Anbari mentioned these two views. The fourth is that in their law prostration was indeed placed before bowing; this was mentioned by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi.

Muqatil said: its meaning is: bow along with those who pray among the readers of Bayt al-Maqdis. Mujahid said: "I prostrated until I got sores (on my forehead)."

**(p-389)** His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿That is of the tidings of the Unseen﴾. "That" refers to what preceded of the story of Zakariyya, Yahya, 'Isa and Maryam. *Al-anba'* means the reports, and *al-ghayb* means what is hidden from you. *Al-wahy* (revelation, inspiration) is everything by which you indicate something through speech, a book, a sign, or a message, as Ibn Qutayba said. The meanings of *al-wahy* in the Qur'an are many, and you will see them in our book titled *al-Wujuh wa al-Naza'ir* (The Facets and the Parallels), which is excellent.

Regarding *al-aqlam* (the arrows, or pens), there are three opinions. The first is that they are the instruments with which one writes, as said by Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr and al-Suddi. The second is that they are sticks, as said by al-Rabi' ibn Anas. The third is that they are arrow-shafts, which is the choice of Ibn Qutayba. Al-Zajjaj likewise said: they are arrow-shafts upon which they placed marks by which they could identify them, by way of drawing lots. The arrow was called *al-qalam* (the pen) because it is *yuqallam*, that is, it is trimmed and shaped. Whatever you cut from something piece by piece, you have *qallamtahu*, and from this comes *al-qalam* with which one writes, because it is trimmed time after time. From the same root: *qallamtu adhari* (I trimmed my nails).

He said: the meaning of ﴿Which of them would take charge of Maryam?﴾ is that they were looking to see which of them was obligated to undertake the guardianship of Maryam, which is the responsibility for attending to her affairs. The meaning of ﴿with them﴾ is "in their presence," and the explanation of their guardianship of her has already been given a moment ago.

Regarding what is meant by "the Word" here, there are three opinions. The first is that it is God's saying to him, "Be!" and so he was, as said by Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada. The second is that it is the angels' good tidings to Maryam about 'Isa, related by Abu Sulayman. The third is that "the Word" is a name for 'Isa, and he was called a Word because he came about through the Word. Abu Ya'la al-Qadi said: because he is guided by him just as one is guided by the Word from God, Exalted is He.

Regarding his being named *al-Masih* (the Messiah), there are six opinions. The first is that he had no hollow in his foot; *al-ukhmus* is the part of the sole of the foot that does not touch the ground. This was narrated by 'Ata' from Ibn 'Abbas. The second is that he would not pass his hand over anyone afflicted with an ailment without that person being healed; this was narrated by al-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas. The third is that he passed his hand over things for blessing, as said by al-Hasan and Sa'id. The fourth is that the meaning of *al-Masih* is "the truthful" (al-siddiq), as said by Mujahid and Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, and mentioned by al-Yazidi. Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi said: the meaning of this is that God wiped him and purified him of sins. The fifth is that he used to traverse (*yamsah*) the earth, that is, he would cross it, as mentioned by Tha'lab, and its explanation is that he was much given to wandering. The sixth is that he came forth from his mother's womb anointed with oil, as said by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi, and related by Ibn al-Qasim. Abu 'Ubayd said: *al-Masih* in the speech of the Arabs has two meanings. One is *al-Masih al-Dajjal* (the false Messiah, the Antichrist), and its original sense is *al-mamsuh* (the wiped), because he is wiped in one of his eyes. The other is 'Isa, and its origin in Hebrew is *Mushiha* with a *shin*; when the Arabs arabicized it, they changed its *shin* into a *sin*, just as they said *Musa* (Moses), whose origin in Hebrew is *Mosha*. Ibn al-Anbari said: he began with his title, saying "al-Masih 'Isa son of Maryam," because *al-Masih* is more famous than 'Isa, since it is rare for it to apply to a namesake who could be confused with him, whereas 'Isa may apply to a large number of people. So he placed it first for its fame. Do you not see that the titles of the caliphs are more famous than their names? As for his saying "'Isa son of Maryam," he attributed him to his mother in order to negate what the heretics among the Christians said about him, since they ascribed him to God, Exalted is He.

**(p-390)** His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Honoured﴾. Ibn Zayd said: *al-tawjih* in the speech of the Arabs means the beloved and the accepted. Ibn Qutayba said: *al-wajih* is one who possesses rank (*al-jah*). Al-Zajjaj said: he is one who holds an elevated station in the sight of those of standing and knowledge. It is said: "The man has become *wajih*, he attains *wajaha*, and so-and-so has *jah* among the people," that is, an elevated station.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And among those brought near﴾. Qatada said: near to God on the Day of Resurrection. *Al-mahd* is the cradle where the infant lies while nursing, and it is derived from *al-tamhid*, which is preparation and smoothing. Regarding his speaking to people in that state, there are two opinions. The first is that it was to clear his mother of what she had been accused of. The second is that it was to confirm his miracles, which indicate his prophethood. Ibn 'Abbas said: he spoke for a while in his cradle, then did not speak again until he reached the age of speech. ﴿And in maturity﴾: he said: [he was] thirty years old when God sent him, and he remained in his mission for thirty months, then God raised him up. Wahb ibn Munabbih said: revelation came to him at the age of thirty, and he remained in his prophethood for three years, then God raised him up. Ibn al-Anbari said: peace be upon him had already passed thirty, and whoever exceeds thirty has entered maturity (*al-kuhula*). The *kahl* (mature man), in the view of the Arabs, is one who has passed thirty. He was called *kahl* because his strength has gathered and his youth is complete, and it comes from their saying: "the plant has *iktahala*" (reached full growth). Ibn Faris said: the *kahl* is the man when grey hair has appeared in him.

If it is asked: he already knew that a mature man speaks, so what is the answer? There are three answers. The first is that this statement came as good tidings of his long life, that is, that he would reach maturity. It has been narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: ("and in maturity") he said: that was after his descent from heaven. The second is that he informed them that time affects him, and that days move him from one state to another, and that if he were a god this change would not have befallen him; this was mentioned by Ibn Jarir al-Tabari. The third is that what is meant by *kahl* is *halim* (forbearing), as said by Mujahid.

Abu 'Ubayd said: *al-Masih* in the speech of the Arabs has two meanings. One is *al-Masih al-Dajjal* (the false Messiah, the Antichrist), and its original sense is *al-mamsuh* (the wiped), because he is wiped in one of his eyes. The other is 'Isa, and its origin in Hebrew is *Mushiha* with a *shin*; when the Arabs arabicized it, they changed its *shin* into a *sin*, just as they said *Musa* (Moses), whose origin in Hebrew is *Mosha*. Ibn al-Anbari said: he began with his title, saying "al-Masih 'Isa son of Maryam," because *al-Masih* is more famous than 'Isa, since it is rare for it to apply to a namesake who could be confused with him, whereas 'Isa may apply to a large number of people. So he placed it first for its fame. Do you not see that the titles of the caliphs are more famous than their names? As for his saying "'Isa son of Maryam," he attributed him to his mother in order to negate what the heretics among the Christians said about him, since they ascribed him to God, Exalted is He.

**(p-390)** His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Honoured﴾. Ibn Zayd said: *al-tawjih* in the speech of the Arabs means the beloved and the accepted. Ibn Qutayba said: *al-wajih* is one who possesses rank (*al-jah*). Al-Zajjaj said: he is one who holds an elevated station in the sight of those of standing and knowledge. It is said: "The man has become *wajih*, he attains *wajaha*, and so-and-so has *jah* among the people," that is, an elevated station.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And among those brought near﴾. Qatada said: near to God on the Day of Resurrection. *Al-mahd* is the cradle where the infant lies while nursing, and it is derived from *al-tamhid*, which is preparation and smoothing. Regarding his speaking to people in that state, there are two opinions. The first is that it was to clear his mother of what she had been accused of. The second is that it was to confirm his miracles, which indicate his prophethood. Ibn 'Abbas said: he spoke for a while in his cradle, then did not speak again until he reached the age of speech. ﴿And in maturity﴾: he said: [he was] thirty years old when God sent him, and he remained in his mission for thirty months, then God raised him up. Wahb ibn Munabbih said: revelation came to him at the age of thirty, and he remained in his prophethood for three years, then God raised him up. Ibn al-Anbari said: peace be upon him had already passed thirty, and whoever exceeds thirty has entered maturity (*al-kuhula*). The *kahl* (mature man), in the view of the Arabs, is one who has passed thirty. He was called *kahl* because his strength has gathered and his youth is complete, and it comes from their saying: "the plant has *iktahala*" (reached full growth). Ibn Faris said: the *kahl* is the man when grey hair has appeared in him.

If it is asked: he already knew that a mature man speaks, so what is the answer? There are three answers. The first is that this statement came as good tidings of his long life, that is, that he would reach maturity. It has been narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: ("and in maturity") he said: that was after his descent from heaven. The second is that he informed them that time affects him, and that days move him from one state to another, and that if he were a god this change would not have befallen him; this was mentioned by Ibn Jarir al-Tabari. The third is that what is meant by *kahl* is *halim* (forbearing), as said by Mujahid.

**(p-389)** His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿That is of the tidings of the Unseen﴾. "That" refers to what preceded of the story of Zakariyya, Yahya, 'Isa and Maryam. *Al-anba'* means the reports, and *al-ghayb* means what is hidden from you. *Al-wahy* (revelation, inspiration) is everything by which you indicate something through speech, a book, a sign, or a message, as Ibn Qutayba said. The meanings of *al-wahy* in the Qur'an are many, and you will see them in our book titled *al-Wujuh wa al-Naza'ir* (The Facets and the Parallels), which is excellent.

Regarding *al-aqlam* (the arrows, or pens), there are three opinions. The first is that they are the instruments with which one writes, as said by Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr and al-Suddi. The second is that they are sticks, as said by al-Rabi' ibn Anas. The third is that they are arrow-shafts, which is the choice of Ibn Qutayba. Al-Zajjaj likewise said: they are arrow-shafts upon which they placed marks by which they could identify them, by way of drawing lots. The arrow was called *al-qalam* (the pen) because it is *yuqallam*, that is, it is trimmed and shaped. Whatever you cut from something piece by piece, you have *qallamtahu*, and from this comes *al-qalam* with which one writes, because it is trimmed time after time. From the same root: *qallamtu adhari* (I trimmed my nails).

He said: the meaning of ﴿Which of them would take charge of Maryam?﴾ is that they were looking to see which of them was obligated to undertake the guardianship of Maryam, which is the responsibility for attending to her affairs. The meaning of ﴿with them﴾ is "in their presence," and the explanation of their guardianship of her has already been given a moment ago.

Regarding what is meant by "the Word" here, there are three opinions. The first is that it is God's saying to him, "Be!" and so he was, as said by Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada. The second is that it is the angels' good tidings to Maryam about 'Isa, related by Abu Sulayman. The third is that "the Word" is a name for 'Isa, and he was called a Word because he came about through the Word. Abu Ya'la al-Qadi said: because he is guided by him just as one is guided by the Word from God, Exalted is He.

Regarding his being named *al-Masih* (the Messiah), there are six opinions. The first is that he had no hollow in his foot; *al-ukhmus* is the part of the sole of the foot that does not touch the ground. This was narrated by 'Ata' from Ibn 'Abbas. The second is that he would not pass his hand over anyone afflicted with an ailment without that person being healed; this was narrated by al-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas. The third is that he passed his hand over things for blessing, as said by al-Hasan and Sa'id. The fourth is that the meaning of *al-Masih* is "the truthful" (al-siddiq), as said by Mujahid and Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, and mentioned by al-Yazidi. Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi said: the meaning of this is that God wiped him and purified him of sins. The fifth is that he used to traverse (*yamsah*) the earth, that is, he would cross it, as mentioned by Tha'lab, and its explanation is that he was much given to wandering. The sixth is that he came forth from his mother's womb anointed with oil, as said by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi, and related by Ibn al-Qasim. Abu 'Ubayd said: *al-Masih* in the speech of the Arabs has two meanings. One is *al-Masih al-Dajjal* (the false Messiah, the Antichrist), and its original sense is *al-mamsuh* (the wiped), because he is wiped in one of his eyes. The other is 'Isa, and its origin in Hebrew is *Mushiha* with a *shin*; when the Arabs arabicized it, they changed its *shin* into a *sin*, just as they said *Musa* (Moses), whose origin in Hebrew is *Mosha*. So he placed it first for its fame. Do you not see that the titles of the caliphs are more famous than their names? As for his saying "'Isa son of Maryam," he attributed him to his mother in order to negate what the heretics among the Christians said about him, since they ascribed him to God, Exalted is He.

**(p-390)** His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Honoured﴾. Ibn Zayd said: *al-tawjih* in the speech of the Arabs means the beloved and the accepted. Ibn Qutayba said: *al-wajih* is one who possesses rank (*al-jah*). Al-Zajjaj said: he is one who holds an elevated station in the sight of those of standing and knowledge. It is said: "The man has become *wajih*, he attains *wajaha*, and so-and-so has *jah* among the people," that is, an elevated station.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And among those brought near﴾. Qatada said: near to God on the Day of Resurrection. *Al-mahd* is the cradle where the infant lies while nursing, and it is derived from *al-tamhid*, which is preparation and smoothing. The second is that it was to confirm his miracles, which indicate his prophethood. Ibn 'Abbas said: he spoke for a while in his cradle, then did not speak again until he reached the age of speech. ﴿And in maturity﴾: he said: [he was] thirty years old when God sent him, and he remained in his mission for thirty months, then God raised him up. Wahb ibn Munabbih said: revelation came to him at the age of thirty, and he remained in his prophethood for three years, then God raised him up. The *kahl* (mature man), in the view of the Arabs, is one who has passed thirty. He was called *kahl* because his strength has gathered and his youth is complete, and it comes from their saying: "the plant has *iktahala*" (reached full growth). Ibn Faris said: the *kahl* is the man when grey hair has appeared in him.
