The first is that this statement came as good tidings of his long life, that is, that he would reach maturity. It has been narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: ("and in maturity") he said: that was after his descent from heaven. The second is that he informed them that time affects him, and that days move him from one state to another, and that if he were a god this change would not have befallen him; this was mentioned by Ibn Jarir al-Tabari. The third is that what is meant by *kahl* is *halim* (forbearing), as said by Mujahid.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿She said, "My Lord, how can I have a son?"﴾ There are two views on the reason for her saying this.

The first is that she said this in amazement and as a question, not out of doubt or denial, as we indicated in the story of Zakariyya. The majority of scholars hold this view.

The second is that the one who addressed her was Jibril, and she thought he was a human being who intended her harm. This is why she said, ﴿I seek refuge in the Most Merciful from you, if you are God-fearing﴾ [Maryam: 18]. When he gave her the good news, she was not certain of the truth of his words, because she did not know that he was an angel. Therefore she said, ﴿How can I have a son?﴾ This was stated by Ibn al-Anbari.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and no man has touched me﴾, meaning, no husband has come near me. The word "mass" (touch) means intercourse, as stated by Ibn Faris. Human beings are called "bashar" (human) because of their outward appearance. "Bashara" means the outer surface of a person's skin. "Abshara al-ard" means the earth brought forth its plants. "Bashsharat al-adim" means she peeled its surface. "Tabashir al-subh" means its first appearances.

He said, meaning Jibril: ﴿Thus God creates what He wills﴾, meaning, with a cause and without a cause. The rest of the verse is explained in al-Baqarah.

[p. 391]

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 3, verse 48:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And He will teach him the Book﴾. Most readers recited "wa-nu'allimuhu" with the nun. Nafi' and Asim recited it with the ya', thereby coordinating it with His saying "yubashshiruka" (He will give you good news). Regarding the Book (al-Kitab) there are two views. The first: that it is the books of the prophets and their knowledge; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas. The second: writing (al-kitabah); this was said by Ibn Jurayj and Muqatil. Ibn 'Abbas said: wisdom (al-hikmah) is understanding (al-fiqh) and the judgments (qada') of the prophets.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 3, verse 49:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And a messenger﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: It is in the accusative on two grounds. One of them: "and We make him a messenger." The preferred reading in my view is: "and he speaks to the people as a messenger."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿That I create﴾. Most readers read "annī" with a fatḥa (anna), making it a substitute (badal) for "āyah" (sign), so that it is as if he said: "I have come to you with a sign, that I create for you..." Nāfiʿ read it with a kasra (inna), and Abū ʿAlī said: it allows two possibilities. One: that it is a new independent clause (mustaʾnafan). The second: that he explained the sign by his saying "innī akhluq," i.e., I form and I determine.

(p-392) Ibn ʿAbbās said: He took clay and fashioned from it a bat (khuffāsh), and he blew into it, and behold, it flew. It is said that he made nothing but the bat, and it is said that the Children of Israel described him by this because the bat is wondrous in its creation. It is narrated from Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī that he said to them: "What do you want?" They said: "The bat." So they asked him for the most perfect of birds in its creation, because it flies without feathers. Wahb said: The one he made would fly as long as the people were looking at it, and when it disappeared from their eyes, it fell dead, so as to distinguish the act of creation from the act of the Creator. Most readers read (fa-yakūnu ṭayran, "so it becomes a bird"), and Nāfiʿ read here and in (al-Māʾidah) "ṭāʾiran" (a flying one). Abū ʿAlī said: The argument of the majority is His saying, Exalted is He: (like the form of a bird), and He did not say "like the form of a flying one." The rationale of Nāfiʿ's reading is that he meant: what I blow into, or what I create, will be a flying one.

Regarding "al-akmah" (the one born blind), there are four opinions. The first: it is the one born blind; this was narrated by al-Ḍaḥḥāk from Ibn ʿAbbās, and Saʿīd from Qatādah, and this was the view of al-Yazīdī, Ibn Qutaybah, and al-Zajjāj. The second: it is the blind, mentioned by Ibn Jurayj from Ibn ʿAbbās, and Maʿmar from Qatādah, and this was the view of al-Ḥasan and al-Suddī. Al-Zajjāj related from al-Khalīl that al-akmah is the one who is born blind, and also the one who becomes blind, even if he was sighted. The third: it is the one with cataracts (al-aʿmash), said by ʿIkrimah. The fourth: it is the one who sees by day and does not see by night, said by Mujāhid and al-Ḍaḥḥāk. And al-abraṣ is the one who has leprosy (wadaḥ, white patches). In the time of ʿĪsā (peace be upon him), the dominant field was the science of medicine (ʿilm al-ṭibb), so he showed them a miracle of the same kind, except that in medicine there is no healing of the akmah and the abraṣ, and that was a proof of his truthfulness. Wahb said: Sometimes fifty thousand of the sick gathered around ʿĪsā in a single day, and he would only treat them by supplication. The exegetes mentioned that he raised four souls from death. It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās that all four lived until they had children, except Sām ibn Nūḥ.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And I inform you of what you eat﴾. Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said: When ʿĪsā was in the school (maktab), he would tell them what they ate, and say to the boy: "O boy, your family has prepared for you such and such food; will you feed me some of it?" Mujāhid said: "What you ate last night, and what you hid of it." This is the view of the exegetes, except that (p-393) Qatādah used to say: "And I inform you of what you eat from the table (māʾidah) that is sent down upon you, and what you store of it." He had taken a covenant from them that they would eat from it and not store it, and when they betrayed, they were transformed into swine.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 3, verse 50–51:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And confirming what was before me﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: "muṣaddiqan" (confirming) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl), meaning: "and I have come to you confirming [what was before me]." ﴿And to make lawful for you some of what was forbidden to you﴾. Qatadah said: Moses had forbidden them camels, the fat of the kidneys (thurūb), and some kinds of birds, and Jesus made them lawful.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And I have come to you with a sign﴾. That is: with signs (āyāt) by which you will know my truthfulness. He used the singular because all of them are of one kind (jins wāḥid). ﴿From your Lord﴾: that is, from the presence of your Lord.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 3, verse 50–51:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And confirming what was before me﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: "muṣaddiqan" (confirming) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl), meaning: "and I have come to you confirming [what was before me]." ﴿And to make lawful for you some of what was forbidden to you﴾. Qatadah said: Moses had forbidden them camels, the fat of the kidneys (thurūb), and some kinds of birds, and Jesus made them lawful.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And I have come to you with a sign﴾. That is: with signs (āyāt) by which you will know my truthfulness. He used the singular because all of them are of one kind (jins wāḥid). ﴿From your Lord﴾: that is, from the presence of your Lord.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 3, verse 52:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then when Jesus sensed disbelief from them﴾, meaning: he knew. Our shaykh Abu Mansur al-Lughawi said: It is said "ahastu bi-al-shay'" and "hasistu bihi," and the people's saying about known things, "mahsusat," is an error; the correct form is "al-mahassat." As for "al-mahsusat," they are the killed ones, as it is said: "hassahu," meaning he killed him. "Al-ansar" means the helpers. "Ila" is in the sense of "ma'a" (with) according to the consensus of the scholars. Al-Zajjaj said: It is good in the place of "ma'a" because "ila" denotes a limit, whereas "ma'a" joins one thing with another. Ibn al-Anbari said: It is also possible that the meaning is: "Who are my helpers toward (in the cause of) making clear the command of Allah." They differed about the reason for his seeking help from the disciples. Mujahid said: when his people disbelieved in him and intended to kill him, he sought help from the disciples. Others said: when they disbelieved in him and expelled him from their town, he sought help from the disciples. It was said: he sought their help to establish the truth and to manifest the proof.

The majority read the "ya'" of "al-hawariyyin" with a shadda. Al-Jawni, al-Jahdari, and Abu Haywa read "al-hawariyyun" with the ya' lightened. There are six sayings concerning the meaning of "al-hawariyyin." The first: they are the chosen intimates. Ibn Abbas said: "al-hawariyyun are the chosen ones of Jesus." Al-Farra' said: they were the special companions of Jesus. Al-Zajjaj said: "al-hawariyyun" in the language are those who were purified, cleansed of every fault; and likewise fine flour is "al-hawari," it is named so because it is sifted from the essence and the pure part of the wheat. The skilled linguists said: "al-hawariyyun" are the elite of the prophets, those who were pure and sincere in their affirmation and support of them. It is said: "a'in hawra'" when its whiteness is intense and its blackness is pure and intense; and one does not say "imra'a hawra'" except when, along with the intensity of the whiteness of her eyes, she is white.

The second: they are those in white garments. Sa'id ibn Jubayr related from Ibn Abbas that they were named so for the whiteness of their garments. The third: they are the launderers, named so because they used to whiten (hawwara) garments, i.e., they made them white. Al-Dahhak and Muqatil said: "al-hawariyyun" are the launderers. Al-Yazidi said: It is said that launderers are called "al-hawariyyun" because they whiten garments, and from this comes the name of fine flour "al-huwwara," and a "hawra" eye is one with clear eye-sockets.

The fourth: "al-hawariyyun" are the fighters (mujahidun).

They recited:

"We are people whom the white swords fill with their heads, and we are the hawariyyun when we advance in battle.
Our skulls on the day of meeting are our shields, walking toward death with no one among us turning back."

The fifth: "al-hawariyyun" are the fishermen. The sixth: "al-hawariyyun" are the kings. Ibn al-Anbari related these three sayings. Ibn Abbas said: the number of the hawariyyun was twelve men. Concerning their occupation there are two sayings. One: they used to catch fish, related by Sa'id ibn Jubayr from Ibn Abbas. The other: they used to wash garments, said by al-Dahhak and Abu Artah.

"His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Our Lord, we have believed in what You have sent down﴾. This is the statement of the disciples (al-Hawariyyun). What was sent down is the Injil (Gospel), and the Messenger is ʿIsa (Jesus). Regarding the meaning of "the witnesses" (al-Shahidin), there are five opinions.

The first: they are Muhammad (ﷺ) and his community, because they bear witness to the messengers that they conveyed (the message). This was narrated by ʿIkrima from Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: they are those among the believers who came before them. This was narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn ʿAbbas.

The third: they are the prophets, because every prophet is a witness over his community. This was said by ʿAta.

The fourth: the witnesses are the truthful ones (al-Sadiqun). This was said by Muqatil.

The fifth: they are those who testified to the prophets with confirmation (al-tasdiq). So the meaning of the verse is: we confirmed, and we acknowledged, so write us down along with those who did as we did. This is the statement of al-Zajjaj."

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 3, verse 54:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And they schemed, and Allah schemed﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: Scheming (al-makr) from the creatures is malice and deception, and from Allah, mighty and majestic is He, it is requital (al-mujazah). It is named by the same name because it is a requital for it, as in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Allah mocks them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 15], and ﴿And Allah is the best of schemers﴾ [Al 'Imran: 54], because His scheming is a requital and a victory for the believers. Ibn 'Abbas said: As for their scheming, the Jews wanted to kill Jesus, so he entered a khawkhah (a small window or opening in a wall), and a man from among them entered, and Allah cast upon him the likeness of Jesus, and Jesus was raised up to the heaven. When the man came out to them, they thought he was Jesus, so they killed him.

(p-٣٩٦) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿When Allah said, "O Jesus, I am going to take you and raise you to Me"﴾. Ibn Qutaybah said: *al-tawaffi* (taking in full) comes from *istifa' al-'adad* (completing the number). It is said *tawaffaytu* and *istawfaytu*, just as it is said *tayaqqantu al-khabar* and *istayqantuhu*. Then death was called *wafat* and *tawaffin*. Abu 'Ubaydah recited:

؎ Indeed the sons of al-Adrad are not of any tribe; they are not with Qays, nor are they of Asad.

؎ And Quraysh did not count them as part of their number.

That is, it did not make them complete in its count. *Al-wafa'* means completeness. Regarding this *tawaffi* there are two views. The first is that it means raising him up to the heavens. The second is that it means death. On the first view, the structure of the sentence is straightforward, without any inversion, and the meaning of "مُتَوَفِّيكَ" (*mutawaffika*) is: "I will take you from the earth, complete and whole, without the Jews being able to harm you in any way." This is the view of al-Hasan, Ibn Jurayj and Ibn Qutaybah, and al-Farra' chose it. Among the things that support this view is the saying of Allah, may He be exalted: ﴿So when You took me up, You were the Watcher over them﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 117], that is (p-٣٩٧) "You raised me to the heavens without death, for they only changed after His raising, not after His death." On the second view, there is an inversion in the verse, its meaning being: "I will raise you to Me, purify you from those who disbelieved, and take you in death afterwards." This is the view of al-Farra', al-Zajjaj and others. The benefit of informing him of the *tawaffi* on this view is to make him know that his being raised to the heavens does not prevent his death. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab said: Jesus was raised when he was thirty-three years old. Muqatil said: He was raised from Bayt al-Maqdis on the Night of Qadr in Ramadan. It was said: His mother Maryam lived six years after his raising. It is also said: She died before his raising.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And purify you from those who disbelieved﴾. There are two views concerning this. The first is that He raised him from among them. The second is that He protected him from them before that. Regarding ﴿those who followed him﴾ there are two views. The first is that they are the Muslims of the community of Muhammad (ﷺ), because they affirmed his prophethood and that he was the Spirit of Allah and His word. This is the view of Qatadah, al-Rabi' and Ibn al-Sa'ib. The second is that they are the Christians, who are above the Jews, and the Jews are humiliated and subjugated. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿concerning that about which you used to differ﴾, meaning the religion.

Allah's words: ﴿As for those who disbelieve﴾. It has been said: they are the Jews and the Christians. Their punishment in this world is by the sword and the jizya (the poll-tax levied on non-Muslim subjects under Islamic rule), and in the Hereafter, by the Fire.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 3, verse 57:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So He will give them their rewards in full﴾. The majority read it with the nun (fa-nuwaffihim). Al-Hasan, Qatadah, and Hafs from ʿAsim read it with the ya (fa-yuwaffihim), coordinated with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿When Allah said, "O ʿIsa…"﴾.

(p-398) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿That We recite to you﴾ means: the stories that have passed. ﴿Of the signs﴾ means: the indications of the truth of your prophethood, since they are reports that no unlettered person (ummi) could know. ﴿And the Wise Reminder﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: it is the Qur'an. Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is: possessing wisdom in its composition and its arrangement, and in making its benefits clear.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 3, verse 59:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, the likeness of Jesus to Allah is like the likeness of Adam﴾. The people of tafsir (exegesis) said: The occasion of the revelation of this verse was the dispute of the delegation of Najran from among the Christians with the Prophet ﷺ concerning the matter of Jesus, and we have mentioned it at the beginning of the surah. As for the comparison of Jesus with Adam, it is because they were both without a father.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He created him from dust﴾, meaning Adam. Tha'lab said: This is an explanation of the matter of Adam, and it is not a状态 (condition). [Note: the source text here reads "ولَيْسَ بِحالٍ", which means "and it is not a [valid] state/case" in the sense of "this is not a correct reading of the situation"; rendered faithfully:] And it is not the case.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then He said to him﴾, meaning to Adam, and it was said to Jesus, ﴿Be, and he is﴾, i.e., so he was. The future is here used for the past, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and they followed what the devils recited﴾, i.e., what the devils had recited.

"His saying, the Exalted: ﴿The truth is from your Lord﴾. Al-Zajjaj (Abu Ishaq al-Zajjaj, d. 311 AH) said: "Al-Haqq" (the truth) is in the nominative case as the predicate of an omitted subject (mubtada'), the meaning being: "The matter I have informed you of concerning the story of ʿIsa is the truth from your Lord." ﴿So do not be of those who doubt﴾. That is, of those who are skeptical. The address is directed to the Prophet, but it is in fact an address to mankind, because he did not doubt.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 3, verse 61:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So say: "Come"﴾. Ibn Qutayba said: *Ta'ala* is *tafa'ala* from *'alawtu* (I ascended). It is said to two men, whether men or women, *ta'alayā*; to women, *ta'alayna*. Al-Farra' said: Its origin is from *al-'uluww* (height). Then, because the Arabs used it so frequently, it became for them like *halumma* (come), to the point that they permitted saying to a man who is above a high place, "*Ta'ala*," meaning "descend." Its original meaning is ascent.

The exegetes (*mufassirun*) said: By "our sons" he meant Fatima, al-Hasan and al-Husayn.

Muslim related in his *Sahih*, from the hadith of Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, who said: "When this verse was revealed, ﴿Come, let us call our sons and your sons﴾, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) called Ali, Fatima, Hasan and Husayn, and said: 'O Allah, these are my family.'"

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and our selves﴾. In this there are five opinions.
First: He meant Ali ibn Abi Talib. This was said by al-Sha'bi. The Arabs describe a paternal cousin as being the "self" of his cousin.
Second: He meant brothers. This was said by Ibn Qutayba.
Third: He meant the people of his religion. This was said by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi.
Fourth: He meant wives.
Fifth: He meant close relatives. Ali ibn Ahmad al-Naysaburi mentioned these last two.

As for *al-ibtihal* (mutual invocation of a curse, i.e., *mubahala*), Ibn Qutayba said: It is the mutual calling down of curses. It is said: "Allah has cursed him" (*bahalahu Allah*), and "I cursed him" (*bahaltahu*), meaning "I cursed him."

Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning of *al-ibtihal* in the language is exaggeration in supplication. Its origin is *al-li'an* (mutual cursing). It is said: *bahalahu Allah*, meaning, "Allah cursed him." He commanded *al-mubahala* after the establishment of the proof.

Jabir ibn Abd Allah said: "The delegation of Najran came, among them al-Sayyid and al-Aqib," and he mentioned the hadith, until he said: "He invited them to the *mula'ana* (mutual cursing), but they agreed with him that they would ransom themselves. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) went out and took the hand of Ali, Fatima, Hasan and Husayn. Then he sent for them, but they refused to answer him, so they acknowledged to him the tribute. He said: (p-400) 'By Him who sent me with the truth, if they had done it, He would have rained fire upon the valley over them.'"
Allah's words: ﴿And there is no god except Allah﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: "min" entered here for emphasis and as an indication of the negation of all the gods that the polytheists claimed.

Allah's words: ﴿But if they turn away﴾ There are three opinions about this. The first: they turn away from the mutual invocation of curses (mubahalah), as Muqatil said. The second: they turn away from the clear proof (al-bayan) that the Prophet (ﷺ) brought, as al-Zajjaj said. The third: they turn away from acknowledging the Oneness of Allah and declaring Him free of having a consort or a son, as Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi said.

Regarding the word "corruption" (al-fasad) here, there are two opinions. The first: it is acting upon sins, as Muqatil said. The second: it is disbelief (kufr), as al-Dimashqi mentioned.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 3, verse 64:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Say, "O People of the Scripture"﴾ — there are three opinions concerning it. The first: they are the Jews; this was said by Qatadah, Ibn Jurayj, and al-Rabi' ibn Anas. The second: the delegation of Najran who disputed concerning Jesus; this was said by al-Suddi and Muqatil. The third: the People of the Two Scriptures together; this was said by al-Hasan. Ibn 'Abbas said: it was revealed concerning the qissisin (priests) and the monks, and the Prophet (ﷺ) sent it with [a copy of] it to Ja'far and his companions in Abyssinia, and Ja'far recited it while the Negus was seated, and the notables of Abyssinia [were present]. As for "the word" (al-kalimah), the exegetes said it is: "There is no god but Allah." If it is said: "These are words (kalimat), so why did He say kalimah?" — there are two answers concerning this. The first: the kalimah expresses utterances and words. The philologists said: the meaning of kalimah is a speech containing the explanation of a story, however long it may be; the Arabs say: "Zuhayr said in his kalimah," meaning in his qasidah (ode).

Al-Khansa' said:

> A rhyme (qafiyah) like the edge of the sword's blade, it remains while the one who uttered it passes away.
>
> The forelock of Yadhbul is cut off, [yet] it refused to abandon its stronghold.
>
> You spoke, Ibn 'Amr, and made it easy, while people had not spoken its like.

So the qafiyah was applied to the entire qasidah, and the usual thing about the qafiyah is that it is at the end of a word in the verse. It was called qafiyah because the word follows the verse and falls at its end, so it was named qafiyah from the Arabic saying: "qafawtu fulanan," meaning: when you follow him. To this answer al-Zajjaj and others incline. The second: the intended meaning of kalimah is kalimat (words), and He sufficed with the singular kalimah for the plural kalimat, as 'Alqamah ibn 'Abdah said:

> Therein are the carcasses of the spent (camels); as for their bones, they are white, and as for their hide, it is hard.

He meant: "as for their hides (jududuha)," and sufficed with the singular for the plural. This was mentioned by Ibn al-Anbari, and the one preceding it.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿a word equal between us and you﴾ — al-Zajjaj said: by sawa' ("equal") he means justice, and it derives from the evenness (istiwa') of a thing; it is said that for justice there is sawa', siwa', and suwa'. Zuhayr ibn Abi Sulma said:

> Show me a plot of oppression in which the equal (al-sawa') makes us equal in it.
>
> If you call for the equal, then there is no survival between me and you, [sons of] Banu Hisn.

He said: the position of "an" (that) in His saying, Exalted is He: (that you worship none but Allah) is in the genitive by way of apposition to "kalimah," meaning: come to [a word of] that we worship none but Allah. It is also permissible that "an" is in the nominative position, as if a questioner asked: "What is the kalimah?" and the answer was given: it is that we worship none but Allah.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and that some of us do not take some others as lords besides Allah﴾ — there are three opinions concerning it. The first: it is some of them prostrating to others; this was said by 'Ikrimah. The second: that some of us do not obey others in disobedience to Allah; this was said by Ibn Jurayj. The third: that we make other than Allah a lord, as the Christians said about the Messiah; this was said by Muqatil and al-Zajjaj.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 3, verse 65:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O People of the Scripture, why do you argue about Abraham?﴾ Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Hasan, and al-Suddi said: "The Christians of Najran and the rabbis of the Jews gathered before the Prophet (ﷺ). These said, 'Abraham was none other than a Jew,' and those said, 'He was none other than a Christian.' So this verse was revealed."

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 3, verse 66:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿of which you have knowledge﴾ — there are two opinions regarding it. The first: it refers to what they saw and witnessed; this was said by Qatadah. The second: it refers to what they were commanded and forbidden; this was said by al-Suddi. As for that of which they have no knowledge, it is the matter of Ibrahim (peace be upon him). Abu Salih narrated from Ibn Abbas that between Ibrahim and Musa there were five hundred and seventy-five years, and between Musa and Isa there were one thousand six hundred and thirty-two years. Ibn Ishaq said: between Ibrahim and Musa there were five hundred and sixty-five years, and between Musa and Isa there were one thousand nine hundred and twenty-five years. The meaning of al-hanif (the upright one, one who turns away from falsehood to the true religion) has already been discussed in (al-Baqarah).

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, the people most worthy of Abraham are those who followed him﴾. There are two accounts regarding the occasion of its revelation.

The first: the leaders of the Jews said to the Prophet (ﷺ), "You know well that we are more entitled to the religion of Abraham than you. He was a Jew, and nothing drives you but envy." So this verse was revealed. Its meaning: the people most entitled to the religion of Abraham are those who followed him in his religion, and this Prophet (ﷺ) is upon his religion. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: 'Amr ibn al-'As wanted to anger the Negus (al-Najashi) against the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ). So he said to the Negus, "They revile 'Isa." The Negus said, "What does your companion say about 'Isa?" They said, "He says that he is the servant of Allah, His spirit, and His word which He cast to Maryam." The Negus took from his siwak (tooth-stick) an amount that irritates the eye, and said, "By Allah, your companion has said nothing beyond this, and this speck does not weigh as much." Then he said, "Rejoice! There shall be no dahwara (harassment, injustice) today against the party of Abraham."

'Amr ibn al-'As said, "And who is the party of Abraham?" He said, "These men and their companion." So Allah revealed this verse on the day of their dispute, upon the Prophet (ﷺ). This is the saying of 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Ghanm.

(p-404)

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, the people most worthy of Abraham are those who followed him﴾. There are two accounts regarding the occasion of its revelation.

The first: the leaders of the Jews said to the Prophet (ﷺ), "You know well that we are more entitled to the religion of Abraham than you. He was a Jew, and nothing drives you but envy." So this verse was revealed. Its meaning: the people most entitled to the religion of Abraham are those who followed him in his religion, and this Prophet (ﷺ) is upon his religion. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: 'Amr ibn al-'As wanted to anger the Negus (al-Najashi) against the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ). So he said to the Negus, "They revile 'Isa." The Negus said, "What does your companion say about 'Isa?" They said, "He says that he is the servant of Allah, His spirit, and His word which He cast to Maryam." (p-404)

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 3, verse 69:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿A group of the People of the Book wish they could mislead you﴾. The occasion of its revelation: the Jews said to Mu'adh ibn Jabal and Ammar ibn Yasir, "You have abandoned your religion and followed the religion of Muhammad (ﷺ)." So this verse was revealed. This is related by Ibn Abbas. The ṭā'ifah (group) is a term for a body of people gathered around what they have gathered upon of religion, opinion, creed, and other things. Regarding this ṭā'ifah there are two views. The first: they are the Jews, as related by Ibn Abbas. The second: they are the Jews and the Christians, as related by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi. The ḍalāl (misguidance) means bewilderment. Regarding it here there are two views. The first: it is the enticing away from the truth toward falsehood, which is the view of Ibn Abbas and Muqatil. The second: it is destruction, and from it is ﴿When we are lost in the earth?﴾ [as-Sajdah: 10]. This is related by Ibn Jarir and al-Dimashqi. Regarding His saying ﴿and they do not perceive﴾ there are two views. The first: and they do not perceive that Allah guides the believers to their condition. The second: and they do not perceive that they are misguiding themselves.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Why do you disbelieve in the signs of Allah﴾. Qatadah said: that is, in Muhammad and Islam. ﴿While you bear witness﴾ that the sending of Muhammad is in your scripture, yet then you disbelieve in him.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 3, verse 71:

Allah's words: ﴿Why do you mix the truth with falsehood﴾. Al-Yazidi said: its meaning is: why do you mix the truth with falsehood? Ibn Faris said: al-labs (confusion, mixing) is the mixing of a matter, and there is a labsah (ambiguity) in the matter, i.e., it is not clear.

Regarding "the truth" and "falsehood" there are four opinions. The first: the truth is their acknowledgement of some of the Prophet's (ﷺ) affair, and the falsehood is their concealing some of his affair. The second: the truth is their belief in the Prophet (ﷺ) at the beginning of the day, and the falsehood is their disbelief in him at its end; this was related from Ibn Abbas. The third: the truth is the Torah, and the falsehood is what they wrote in it with their own hands; this was said by al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd. The fourth: the truth is Islam, and the falsehood is Judaism and Christianity; this was said by Qatadah.

Allah's words: ﴿and conceal the truth﴾. Qatadah said: they concealed Islam, and they concealed Muhammad (ﷺ).

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 3, verse 72:**

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And a group of the People of the Book said﴾. Regarding the occasion of its revelation (*sabab al-nuzul*), there are two reports.

The first: a group of the Jews said, "When you meet the companions of Muhammad at the beginning of the day, believe, and when it is the end of the day, pray your prayer, perhaps they will say, 'These are the People of the Book, and they know more than us,' and they will turn back from their religion." This was related by ʿAṭiyyah from Ibn ʿAbbās.

al-Ḥasan and al-Suddī said: Twelve rabbis of the Jews conspired together, and some of them said to others, "Enter the religion of Muhammad with your tongues at the beginning of the day, and disbelieve at its end, and say, 'We looked into our books, and consulted our scholars, and we found that Muhammad is not that one.' Thus his companions will doubt their religion, and they will say, 'They are the People of the Book, and they know more than us,' and they will return to your religion." So this verse was revealed. To this meaning the majority of scholars went.

The second: "Allah, the Exalted, turned His Prophet toward the Kaʿbah at the time of the noon prayer. A group of the scholars of the Jews said: ﴿Believe in what has been revealed to those who believe at the beginning of the day﴾, meaning, 'Believe in the qiblah toward which they prayed at dawn, and disbelieve in the one toward which they prayed at the end of the day, perhaps they will return to your qiblah.'" This was related by Abū Ṣāliḥ from Ibn ʿAbbās.

Mujāhid, Qatādah, al-Zajjāj and others said: *wajh al-nahār* (the face of the day) means its beginning (*awwaluhu*).

Al-Zajjāj recited:

*Whoever is pleased by the killing of Mālik, let him come to our women at the face of the day;*
*He will find the women bareheaded, wailing over him, having risen before the break of the dawns.*

(p-406)

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 3, verse 73:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And do not believe except one who follows your religion.﴾ The scholars differed in the interpretation of this verse, into four opinions. The first: its meaning is: "Do not believe except one who follows your religion, and do not believe that anyone can be given what you have been given of knowledge, the splitting of the sea, the manna and the quails, and other than that, and do not believe that they can argue with you before your Lord, because you are more correct in religion than them." So all of this is part of the speech of the Jews among themselves, the lam in "liman" is extra (ṣila), and His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Say: Indeed, guidance is the guidance of Allah﴾ is an interjected statement between two statements. This is the meaning of the saying of Mujahid and al-Akhfash. The second: the speech of the Jews is complete at His saying: ﴿to one who follows your religion﴾, and the remainder is from the saying of Allah, the Exalted, and nothing of their speech intervenes in it. Its implied sense is: "Say, O Muhammad: Indeed, the guidance is the guidance of Allah, that anyone may be given the like of what you have been given, O community of Muhammad, except that the Jews argue with you falsely, so they say: 'We are better than you.'" This is the meaning of the saying of al-Hasan and Sa'id ibn Jubayr. al-Farra' said: (p-407) the meaning of "an yu'ta" is: "an la yu'ta" (that it not be given). The third: there is inversion and displacement in the speech; its implied sense is: "And do not believe that anyone may be given the like of what you have been given, except one who follows your religion," so "an" has been placed later though it is previous in intention, according to the Arab manner of inversion and displacement, and the lam entered for emphasis, as in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿It may be that some of what you seek to hasten has drawn near to you﴾ [al-Naml: 72], meaning: radfukum (what follows you).

The poet said:

"I was not one to deceive a friend with friendship until the friend became a deceiver to me."

He intended: "I was not one to deceive the friend."

Another said:

"They blame the world while they milk it, the udders, until the milk does not flow for them, the teat."

He intended: "They blame the world." This was mentioned by Ibn al-Anbari. The fourth: the lam is not extra, and the meaning is: "Do not make your affirmation of the Prophet in anything that he brought except for the Jews, for if you say that to the polytheists, it would be a help to them against his affirmation." This was said by al-Zajjaj. Ibn al-Anbari said: "Do not believe that Muhammad and his companions are upon the truth except for one who follows your religion, lest the truth be discovered in your obstinacy and they argue with it against you before your Lord." According to this, the meaning of the speech is: "Do not acknowledge that anyone may be given the like of what you have been given except for one who follows your religion." This meaning was also mentioned by Makki ibn Abi Talib al-Nahwi. Ibn Kathir recited: "a-an yu'ta" with two hamzas, the first lightened and the second softened, as an interrogative, like: "a-antum a'lamu" (are you more knowing?). Abu 'Ali said: its basis is that "an" is in the position of a nominative with the inceptive, and its predicate is: "yusaddiquna bihi" (they affirm it), or "ya'taruhuna bihi" (they acknowledge it), or "yudhakkiruhu li-ghayrikum" (they mention it to others). It is also permissible that the position of "anna" be accusative, so the meaning becomes: "Do you spread the word, or do you mention, that anyone may be given...?" and similar in meaning is: ﴿Do you inform them of what Allah has opened to you?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 76]. al-A'mash and Talha ibn Musarrif recited: "an yu'ta" with a kasra on the hamza, meaning: "ma yu'ta" (what is given). And in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿or they argue with you before your Lord﴾ there are two views. The first: its meaning is: "Do not believe that they will argue with you before your Lord, because they have no proof," as said by Qatada. The second: its meaning is: "until they argue with you before your Lord by way of worship," as in the saying "he will not meet him until the Hour comes," said by al-Kisa'i.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, the bounty is in the hand of Allah﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: it means prophethood, the Book, and guidance, ﴿He gives it to whom He wills﴾, not what you, O assembly of Jews, wish for, that no one be given the like of what you have been given.

Ibn al-Jawzi, Zad al-Masir, on surah 3, verse 74:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿He singles out for His mercy whom He wills﴾. Regarding "mercy" there are three opinions. The first: it is Islam; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas and Muqatil. The second: it is prophethood; this was said by Mujahid. The third: it is the Qur'an and Islam; this was said by Ibn Jurayj.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 3, verse 75:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And among the People of the Book is one who, if you entrust him with a qintar﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: A man deposited a thousand and two hundred ounces of gold with ʿAbdullah ibn Salam, and he returned them to him, so Allah praised him with this verse. And a man deposited a dinar with Huhas ibn ʿAzura, and he betrayed him. "The People of the Book" refers to the Jews. The discussion of the qintar has already preceded. It has also been said that the "bāʾ" in His saying "with a qintar" carries the meaning of "ʿalā" (upon/over). As for the dinar, I read to our shaykh Abu Mansur al-Lughawi (the linguist), who said: The dinar is a Persian word that has been Arabized, and its origin is dinnār. Although it has been Arabized, the Arabs know no name for it other than dinar, so it has become like an Arabic word, and that is why Allah Exalted mentioned it in His Book, because He addressed them with what they knew. They also derived a verb from it, so they said: a man is mudannar, meaning one with many dinars; and a horse is mudannar, meaning a white horse with a round pattern of black and white. If it is asked: why were the People of the Book singled out as having among them a traitor and a trustworthy one, while creation is in that state generally? The answer: they betray the Muslims, considering it permissible to do so, and He clarified this in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿There is no blame upon us regarding the unlettered﴾, and so He warned against them. Muqatil said: The trustworthiness refers to those among them who embraced Islam, and the betrayal refers to those who did not embrace Islam. It has also been said: those who render back the trust are the Christians, and those who do not render it are the Jews.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿except while you remain standing over him﴾. Al-Farra' said: The people of the Hijaz say: dumtu and dumtum, and mutu and mutum. And Tamim say: mitu and dimtu with kasra, and they agree on yafʿalu: yadumu and yamutu. Regarding this standing there are two opinions. The first: it is insistence on demanding repayment; this was said by Mujahid, Qatada, al-Farra', Ibn Qutayba, and al-Zajjaj. Ibn Qutayba said: the meaning is: as long as you persistently press him for it and demand it. The origin of this is that one who demands a thing stands over it and acts upon it, while one who abandons it sits back from it. [al-Aʿsha said:

"He stands over his people in spite of their resentment, and then he pardons when he wills, or takes revenge."

That is: he demands the blood-debt and does not sit back from it.] Exalted is He said: ﴿They are not alike. Among the People of the Book is a standing community﴾ [Al ʿImran: 113], that is: upright, not abandoning it. And He, Exalted, said: ﴿Is He who stands over every soul in what it has earned [equal to others]?﴾ [al-Raʿd: 33], that is: taking account of it for what it has earned. The second: it is standing in its literal sense, so the meaning is: except while you remain standing over his head; for then he acknowledges his trust, but when you leave and then return, he denies you. This was said by al-Suddi.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿That﴾ refers to the betrayal. The "sabil" (way/blame) is sin and fault, and its parallel is ﴿There is no way (blame) against the good-doers﴾ [al-Tawba: 91]. Qatada said: The Jews only considered the wealth of the Muslims lawful because, in their view, they are not People of the Book.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and they speak against Allah a lie﴾. Al-Suddi said: They say: Allah has made the wealth of the Arabs lawful for us.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿while they know﴾. There are two opinions. The first: they know that Allah has revealed in the Torah the fulfilment of covenants and the rendering back of trusts. The second: they speak the lie while knowing that it is a lie.

"His saying: ﴿Yes⁠﴾. Allah, mighty and majestic, refuted their statement ﴿There is no blame upon us concerning the unlettered⁠﴾ with His saying ﴿Yes⁠﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: "In my view this is a complete pause (waqf al-tamam), after which He begins anew, saying ﴿Whoever fulfills his covenant⁠﴾." It is also permissible that He began the whole statement with His saying ﴿Yes, whoever fulfills⁠﴾. The covenant (al-ʿahd) is what Allah, mighty and majestic, had covenanted with them about in the Torah. Regarding the pronoun in ﴿his covenant⁠﴾ there are two opinions. One is that it refers back to Allah, exalted. The second is that it refers to the one who fulfills (the covenant)."

**Ibn al-Jawzi's commentary (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 3, verse 77:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who exchange the covenant of Allah and their oaths for a small price﴾. There are three reports concerning the occasion of its revelation.

The first: "Al-Ash'ath ibn Qays disputed with a Jew over a piece of land. The Jew denied it, so he brought him before the Prophet (ﷺ). The Prophet said to him [to al-Ash'ath]: 'Do you have proof?' He said: 'No.' He said to the Jew: 'Will you swear an oath?' Al-Ash'ath said: 'If he swears, he will take my property.' So this verse was revealed." Narrated by al-Bukhari and Muslim.

The second: that it was revealed concerning the Jews. Allah had made a covenant with them in the Torah to make clear the description of the Prophet (ﷺ), but they denied it and went against it in exchange for what they obtained from their lowly ones of worldly gain. This is the saying of Ikrimah and Muqatil.

The third: a man displayed his merchandise in the market at the beginning of the day. When it was late in the day, a man came to bargain with him, and he swore: "He had prevented it from [being sold for] such-and-such at the beginning of the day, and had it not been for the evening, he would not have sold it for that price." So this verse was revealed. This is the saying of al-Sha'bi and Mujahid.

According to the first and third reports, the "covenant" (ʿahd) means: adherence to obedience and abandoning disobedience. According to the second, it means what was covenanted to the Jews in the Torah. The "oath" (yamin) means swearing.

If we say it concerns the Jews and the disbelievers, then Allah will not speak to them on the Day of Resurrection at all. If we say it concerns the sinners, then it is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: "Allah will not speak to them with any word of goodness."

The meaning of ﴿and will not look at them﴾ is: He will not show them any kindness, as a sign of His hatred towards them. Al-Zajjaj said: You say, "So-and-so does not look at so-and-so and does not speak to him," meaning: he is angry with him.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and will not purify them﴾, that is: He will not cleanse them from the defilement of their disbelief and their sins.

Ibn al-Jawzi's commentary on Surah 3, verse 78:

His words, may He be exalted: ﴿And indeed among them is a group﴾. The scholars differed over whom it was revealed about, on two views. The first: it was revealed about the Jews, narrated by ʿAṭiyya from Ibn ʿAbbas. The second: it was revealed about the Jews and the Christians, narrated by al-Ḍaḥḥāk from Ibn ʿAbbas.

(p-412) His words, may He be exalted: ﴿And indeed﴾ is an emphatic particle (inna), and the lām in His words "a group" (la-farīqan) adds emphasis beyond the emphasis of inna.

Ibn Qutayba said: The meaning of ﴿they twist their tongues﴾ is that they turn them around with distortion and addition. Al-alsina (tongues) is the plural of lisān (tongue). Abū ʿAmr said: lisān may be masculine or feminine. Whoever treats it as masculine plurals it as alsina, and whoever treats it as feminine plurals it as alsun. Al-Farrāʾ said: We have not heard the word lisān itself from the Arabs except as masculine. The Arabs say: "A lisān came from so-and-so," meaning speech, and they treat it as masculine.

Ibn al-Aʿrābī recited:

"Your tongue is sweet-spoken, and your self is stingy, and near the Pleiades, of your friend, is a king."

Thaʿlab recited:

"I regret a tongue that came from me, so would that it were in a saddlebag ('ikm)."

Al-ʿIkm is al-ʿadl (a pair of saddlebags/a bundle). By his words "that came from me," he indicated that lisān means speech.

Thaʿlab also recited:

"The tongue of the Banū ʿĀmir came to me, its reports after an unpleasant saying."

Here he made lisān feminine, because he meant the word and the message.

**The commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 3, verse 79:**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿But rather, be﴾, meaning: "But rather, He says to them: 'Be,'" so the verb "say" is omitted because the context indicates it.

As for *al-rabbaniyyun* (the godly scholars, those devoted to their Lord), it is narrated from ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib (may Allah be pleased with him) that he said: "They are those who nourish (*yughadhdhūna*) people with wisdom and raise them upon it." Ibn ʿAbbās and Ibn Jubayr said: "They are the jurists who teach." Qatādah and ʿAṭāʾ said: "They are the jurists, the scholars, and the wise." Ibn Qutaybah said: "Its singular is *rabbānī*, and they are the scholars who teach." Abū ʿUbayd said: "I think the word is not Arabic; it is Hebrew or Syriac. That is because Abū ʿUbayda claimed that the Arabs do not know *al-rabbāniyyīn*." Abū ʿUbayd said: "Only the jurists and the people of knowledge have known it." He said: "I heard a man learned in the books say: 'They are the scholars of what is lawful and unlawful, and of commanding and forbidding.'" Ibn al-Anbārī related from some of the linguists: "*Rabbānī* is a relative noun ascribed to *Rabb* (the Lord), because knowledge is that by which Allah is obeyed. So the *alif* and *nūn* were added to the relative form for emphasis, just as they said: *rajulun liḥyānī* (a man with a very large beard) when they exaggerated in describing him as having a large beard."

(p-414) His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿by what you have been teaching of the Book﴾. Ibn Kathīr, Nāfiʿ, and Abū ʿAmr read *taʿlamūna*, with a sukūn on the ʿayn and a fatḥah on the lām. ʿĀṣim, Ibn ʿĀmir, Ḥamzah, and al-Kisāʾī read *tuʿallimūna* with the *tashdīd* (doubled letter) on the ʿayn. All of them read *tadrusūna* lightly (without *tashdīd*). Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿAbbās, Abū Razīn, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, Ṭalḥah ibn Muṣarrif, and Abū Ḥaywah read *tadrusūna* with a ḍammah on the tāʾ and *tashdīd*. *Al-dirāsah* means recitation (*al-qirāʾah*). Al-Zajjāj said: "The meaning of the speech is: let your guidance and your intention in teaching be the guidance of the scholars and the wise, because the scholar only deserves this title when he acts upon his knowledge."

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 3, verse 80:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And He would not order you to take﴾ Ibn ʿĀmir, Ḥamzah, Khalaf, Yaʿqūb, ʿĀṣim in some of the transmissions from him, ʿAbd al-Wārith from Abū ʿAmr, and al-Yazīdī in his own choice, read it with a fatḥah on the rāʾ (naṣb). The rest read it with a ḍammah on the rāʾ (rafʿ). According to the one who reads with naṣb, the meaning is: "It is not for a human being that He would order you..." and according to the one who reads with rafʿ, it is a new sentence separated from what precedes it. Ibn Jurayj said: "And Muhammad would not order you..."

The Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 3, Verse 81:

(p-415) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when Allah took the covenant (mithaq) of the Prophets﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: The position of "idh" (when) is in the accusative. The meaning is: Mention, in your narratives, when Allah took (the covenant). Ibn 'Abbas said: The mithaq is the 'ahd (pact). Regarding what they were bound to by this covenant, there are two opinions. The first: it is the affirmation of Muhammad ﷺ, reported from 'Ali, Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah and al-Suddi. The second: Allah took the covenant of the earlier (prophets) that they would certainly believe in what the later of them would bring. This was said by Tawus. Mujahid and al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: This verse is an error in the Book, and in the recitation (qira'ah) of Ibn Mas'ud it reads: (And when Allah took the covenant of those who were given the Book). Al-Rabi' argued with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then there came to you a messenger﴾. Some scholars said: The covenant was taken from the Prophets and their nations, and the mention of the Prophets was sufficient without mentioning the nations, because taking the covenant from the one who is followed indicates that it was taken from the follower. This is the meaning of the statement of Ibn 'Abbas and al-Zajjaj.

The scholars differed concerning the lam in "lima" (for what). Most readers read "lima" with a fatha on the lam and without shaddah (tashdid). Hamzah read it similarly, except that he put a kasra on the lam. Sa'id ibn Jubayr read "lamma" with a shaddah on the mim. So the reading of Ibn Jubayr means: when I have given you. Al-Farra' said regarding Hamzah's reading: He means the taking of the covenant for what He has given them, then His saying, ﴿you shall surely believe in it﴾ was made part of the taking. Al-Farra' said: Whoever put a fatha on the lam made it an extra (za'idah) particle. And "ma" here carries the meaning of a condition and a response: the meaning is, "If I give you, and whatever I give you of a Book and wisdom." Ibn al-Anbari said: The lam in His saying, exalted is He, (lima ataytukum), according to the reading of the one who doubled the mim or put a kasra, is an answer to the taking of the covenant; he said: because taking the covenant is an oath (yamin). And according to the reading of the one who lightened it, its meaning is the oath, and the answer to the oath is the lam in His saying, ﴿you shall surely believe in it﴾. He addressed them, saying "ataytukum" (I gave you), after mentioning the Prophets in the third person, because the speech carries the sense of saying and narration; so he addressed them, saying: "lima ataytukum". Nafi' read "ataynakum" with a nun and an alif.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then there came to you a messenger﴾. 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, said: Allah did not send any prophet without taking from him the pledge that, if Muhammad were sent while he was alive, he would surely believe in him and surely support him. Others said: The taking of the covenant from the Prophets means that some of them would affirm one another. The "isr" here means the 'ahd (pact), according to the consensus of the scholars. Ibn Qutaybah said: The original meaning of "isr" is burden, so the pact was named isr because it prevents one from the matter for which it was taken, and it is a burden and a restriction. All of them read the alif of "isri" with a kasra. Abu Bakr narrated from 'Isam that he read it with a damma. Abu 'Ali said: It seems that the damma is a dialectal usage (lughah).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He said: Then bear witness﴾. Ibn Faris said: Shahadah (testimony) is reporting what has been witnessed. Regarding those addressed by this, there are two opinions. The first: it is addressed to the Prophets, and then there are two views on it. The first: its meaning is: bear witness against your nations, said by 'Ali ibn Abi Talib. The second: bear witness against yourselves, said by Muqatil. The second opinion: it is addressed to the angels, said by Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab. According to this, it is a kinaya (indirect reference) to something not mentioned.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 3, verses 82–83:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Do they seek other than the religion of Allah?﴾ Abu 'Amr recited "yabghūna" with a fathah on the ya' and "turja'ūna" with a dammah on the ta', while the rest recited both with the ya'. Hafs related from 'Asim: "yabghūna" and "yarji'ūna" with the ya' in both. Ya'qub, according to his own method (aṣl), recited with a fathah on the ya' and a kasrah on the jim. Ibn 'Abbas said: "The People of the Two Books disputed, and each group claimed that it was more entitled to the religion of Ibrahim. The Prophet ﷺ said: 'Both groups are free of the religion of Ibrahim.' They became angry and said: 'By Allah, we will not accept your judgement, nor will we follow your religion,' and so this verse was revealed." The intended meaning of "the religion of Allah" is the religion of Muhammad ﷺ. ﴿And to Him has submitted﴾ meaning has yielded and humbled itself, ﴿willingly and unwillingly﴾. "Ṭawʿ" (willingness) is submission with ease, and "kurh" (unwillingness) is submission with hardship and reluctance from the self.

(p-417) Regarding the meaning of willingly and unwillingly there are six opinions. The first: that the submission of all of them took place on the Day of the Covenant, willingly and unwillingly; this was related by Mujahid from Ibn 'Abbas, and by al-A'mash from Mujahid, and al-Suddi said likewise. The second: that the believer prostrates willingly, while the disbeliever's shadow prostrates while he is unwilling; this was reported from Ibn 'Abbas, and related by Ibn Abi Najih and Layth from Mujahid. The third: that all of them acknowledged Him as the Creator, and even if some of them associated partners, their acknowledgement of this is a proof against them in their association; this is the saying of Abu al-'Aliyah, and Mansur related it from Mujahid. The fourth: that the believer submitted willingly, and the disbeliever submitted out of fear of the sword; this is the saying of al-Hasan. The fifth: that the believer submitted willingly, and the disbeliever submitted when he saw the might of Allah, but it did not benefit him at that time; this is the saying of Qatadah. The sixth: that the submission of all of them is their subjection to the execution of His command in their natures; no one can refrain from a nature with which He has created them, nor change it; this is the saying of al-Zajjaj, and it is the meaning of the saying of al-Sha'bi: "All of them submitted to Him."

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 3, verses 82–83:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Do they seek other than the religion of Allah?﴾ Abu 'Amr recited "yabghūna" with a fathah on the ya' and "turja'ūna" with a dammah on the ta', while the rest recited both with the ya'. Hafs related from 'Asim: "yabghūna" and "yarji'ūna" with the ya' in both. Ya'qub, according to his own method (aṣl), recited with a fathah on the ya' and a kasrah on the jim. The third: that all of them acknowledged Him as the Creator, and even if some of them associated partners, their acknowledgement of this is a proof against them in their association; this is the saying of Abu al-'Aliyah, and Mansur related it from Mujahid. The fourth: that the believer submitted willingly, and the disbeliever submitted out of fear of the sword; this is the saying of al-Hasan. The Almighty's saying: ﴿How will Allah guide a people who disbelieved after their belief?﴾ There are three opinions regarding its occasion of revelation.

The first: "A man from the Ansar apostatized and joined the polytheists, so this verse was revealed, up to His saying: ﴿except those who repent﴾. His people wrote it to him, and he returned repentant, [so the Prophet (ﷺ) accepted that from him and left him alone]." (p-٤١٨) This was narrated by Ikrimah from Ibn 'Abbas. Mujahid and al-Suddi mentioned that the name of that man was al-Harith ibn Suwayd.

The second: it was revealed concerning ten men who apostatized, among them al-Harith ibn Suwayd, who then regretted and returned. This was narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas, and Muqatil also said this.

The third: it concerns the People of the Book, who recognized the Prophet (ﷺ) and then disbelieved in him. This was narrated by 'Atiyyah from Ibn 'Abbas. Al-Hasan said: they are the Jews and the Christians.

It has also been said that "kayfa" (كَيْفَ, "how") here is in form an interrogative, but in meaning a negation, i.e., Allah does not guide these people.

"Abiding therein" (khalidina fiha): al-Zajjaj said: that is, in the punishment of the curse. "Nor shall they be reprieved" (wa la hum yunzarun): that is, they will not be delayed from the time [of punishment].

He said: The meaning of "they amended" (aslahu) is: they showed that they had been in error, and they amended what they had corrupted, and deceived by it those who followed them among those who have no knowledge.

Section

This verse makes an exception for those who repent from among those who did not repent. Some people have claimed that it abrogated (naskh) what the verses before it contained of threat, but it is not an abrogation.
