Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 3, verse 90:

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve after their belief and then increase in disbelief—their repentance will never be accepted. And those are the astray.﴾ (p-419) His statement, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve after their belief﴾ — the scholars differed about who it was revealed concerning, in three opinions.

The first: that it was revealed concerning those among the companions of al-Harith ibn Suwayd who did not repent. They said: "We will remain in Makkah and await for Muhammad the vicissitudes of fate (rayb al-manun)." This was said by Ibn Abbas and Muqatil.

The second: that it was revealed concerning the Jews who disbelieved in Jesus and the Injil, and then increased in disbelief by disbelieving in Muhammad and the Qur'an. This was said by al-Hasan, Qatadah, and Ata al-Khurasani.

The third: that it was revealed concerning the Jews and the Christians who disbelieved in Muhammad after their belief in his description, and then increased in disbelief by persisting in their disbelief. This was said by Abu al-Aliyah. Al-Hasan said: "Every time a verse was revealed, they disbelieved in it, and so they increased in disbelief."

As for the reason why their repentance is not accepted, there are four opinions.

The first: that they apostatized and resolved to show repentance in order to conceal their conditions, while disbelief was in their hearts. This was said by Ibn Abbas.

The second: that they are a people who repented from sins while in polytheism, but did not repent from polytheism. This was said by Abu al-Aliyah.

The third: that its meaning is: their repentance will not be accepted when death comes upon them. This is the statement of al-Hasan, Qatadah, Ata al-Khurasani, and al-Suddi.

The fourth: their repentance will not be accepted after death if they die upon disbelief. This was said by Mujahid.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 3, verse 91:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and die while they are disbelievers﴾ Abu Salih narrated from Ibn Abbas that "when the Prophet (ﷺ) conquered Makkah, those who had been companions of al-Harith ibn Suwayd and were alive in Islam entered [Islam], and this verse was revealed concerning those among them who died as disbelievers."

Al-Zajjaj said: The "mil'" (filling) of a thing is the amount that fills it. Sibawayh and al-Khalil said: "al-malu'" with a fatha on the mim is the verbal action; you say "malaʼtu al-shay'a amla'uhu mal'an," the verbal noun being with the fatha only. "Al-mala'ah" is that which is worn extended. "Al-milawah" of time is a long stretch of it (p-420); they say, "Abil jadidan, wa tamalla habiban," meaning: live with him a long time. And "dhahaban" is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz). Ibn Faris said: sometimes "al-dhahab" is made feminine, so it is said "dhahabah," and it is pluralized as "al-adhab."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and even if he offers it in ransom﴾ Al-Farra' said: The waw here may sometimes be dispensed with, and if it were omitted it would be correct, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and that he may be among the certain﴾ [al-An'am: 75]. Al-Zajjaj said: This is an error, because the function of the waw is clear, so it is not among what is dropped. Al-Nahhas said: The grammarians among the people of analysis said concerning this verse: the waw is not superfluous, and its implied sense is: "So there will not be accepted from any one of them the filling of the earth with gold, given voluntarily, and even if he offers it [as ransom]."

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 3, verse 92:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿You will never attain al-birr (righteousness)﴾. Regarding al-birr there are four opinions. The first is that it is Paradise. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, al-Suddi, and others. Ibn Jarir said: the meaning then is, "You will never attain the reward of God toward you, which you seek through your obedience." The second is taqwa (God-consciousness). This was said by ʿAta' and Muqatil. The third is obedience. This was said by ʿAtiyya. The fourth is the good for which one deserves reward. This was said by Abu Rawq. Al-Qadi Abu Yaʿla said: the verse does not intend the negation of the essence, but the negation of the existence of perfection. It is as if He said: "You will never attain the complete righteousness."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿until you spend of what you love﴾. Concerning this there are two opinions. The first is that it refers to "a servant's spending from his wealth while he is healthy and stingy," narrated by Ibn ʿUmar from the Prophet (ﷺ). The second is that it refers to spending from the wealth one loves, said by Qatada and al-Dahhak. Regarding what is meant by this spending, there are three opinions. The first is that it is the obligatory charity (sadaqa mafrusa). This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Hasan, and al-Dahhak. The second is that it is all voluntary charities. This was said by Ibn ʿUmar. The third is that it is all expenditures by which the Face of God, the Exalted, is sought, whether they are charity or not. This was reported from al-Hasan, and al-Qadi Abu Yaʿla chose it. Al-Bukhari and Muslim in the two Sahihs narrated from the hadith of Anas ibn Malik, who said: "Abu Talha was the richest of the Ansar in Madina in palm trees, and the property he loved most was Bayraha. It faced the mosque, and the Prophet (ﷺ) used to enter it and drink from its good water. Anas said: When this verse was revealed, ﴿You will never attain righteousness until you spend of what you love﴾, Abu Talha stood up and said: 'O Messenger of God, God says: ﴿You will never attain righteousness until you spend of what you love﴾, and the dearest of my property to me is Bayraha. It is a charity for God; I hope for its righteousness and its store with God, the Exalted. So place it where God shows you.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Bakh bakh! That is profitable property (mal rabih) or [the narrator doubted: rabih or ra'ih]. I have heard what you said, and I think you should give it to the nearest relatives.' So Abu Talha divided it among his relatives and the sons of his paternal uncle."

It is also narrated from ʿAbdullah ibn ʿUmar that he recited this verse and said: "I find nothing dearer to me than my slave-girl Rumaytha. She is free for the sake of God." Then he said: "Were it not that I would be returning to something I dedicated to God, I would have married her." So he married her to Nafiʿ, and she became the mother of his child. Abu Dharr was asked: "Which deeds are best?" He said: "Prayer is the pillar of Islam, jihad is the hump of the deed, and charity is a wondrous thing." Then the questioner said: "O Abu Dharr, you have left out something which is the most reliable deed in my view, which I do not see you mentioning." He said: "What is it?" He said: "Fasting." Abu Dharr said: "It is a means of drawing near, but it is not there," and he recited the saying of the Exalted: ﴿You will never attain righteousness until you spend of what you love﴾.

Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿for indeed God is Knowing of it﴾ is: He will reward for it.

[p. 421] [p. 422]

The occasion of revelation of this verse: "The Prophet ﷺ said, 'I follow the religion of Abraham.' The Jews said, 'How, when you eat the flesh of camels and drink their milk?' He said, 'That was lawful for Abraham.' They said, 'Everything we forbid, you forbid, for it was forbidden to Noah and Abraham until it reached us.' So this verse was revealed refuting them." This was reported by Abu Ruq and Ibn al-Sa'ib.

"Al-ta'am" (food) is a name for what is eaten. Ibn Qutaybah said: "Al-hill" means "al-halal" (the lawful), and similarly "al-hurm" and "al-haram," and "al-lubs" and "al-libas" (clothing).

Regarding what Israel forbade for himself, there are three opinions. The first is that it was the flesh and milk of camels. This is reported from the Prophet ﷺ, and was transmitted by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas. It is the view of al-Hasan, 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah, (p-423) Abu al-'Aliyah, and others. The second is that it was the veins (al-'uruq), reported by Sa'id ibn Jubayr from Ibn 'Abbas, and it is the view of Mujahid, Qatadah, al-Dahhak, al-Suddi, and others. The third is that it was the two ducts of the liver, the two kidneys, and the fat except what is on the back. This was said by Ikrimah.

Regarding the reason he forbade that, there are four opinions. The first: "He suffered a severe illness, so he vowed: if God cures him, he would forbid the food and drink most beloved to him." This is reported from the Prophet ﷺ. The second: he suffered from 'irq al-nasa (sciatica), so he forbade the veins; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas and others. The third: when sciatica afflicted him, the physicians prescribed for him avoiding what he then forbade, so he forbade it; this was reported by al-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas. The fourth: whenever he ate that food, sciatica afflicted him, and he would spend the night in pain, so he forbade it; this was said by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi.

They differed over whether he forbade that by God's permission or by his own ijtihad (independent reasoning), on two views.

They also differed over what established the prohibition of the food that he forbade for the Jews, on three views. The first: it became forbidden to them by his prohibition, and it was not forbidden in the Torah (al-Tawrah); this was said by 'Atiyyah. Ibn 'Abbas said: Ya'qub said, "If God restores my health, no child of mine shall eat it." The second: they agreed with their father Ya'qub in forbidding it, not that it was forbidden to them by the sacred law; then they attributed its prohibition to God, so God refuted them by His saying: ﴿Say: Bring the Torah and recite it, if you are truthful.﴾ This is the view of al-Dahhak. The third: God forbade it to them after the Torah, not in it. Whenever they committed a great sin, a good food was forbidden to them because of it, or a punishment was poured upon them. This is the view of Ibn al-Sa'ib. Ibn 'Abbas said: ﴿Bring the Torah and recite it﴾: do you find in it the prohibition of camel flesh and camel milk?

(p-424) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Then whoever fabricates falsehood against Allah after that﴾ — he says: he invented (ikhtalaqa). ﴿Falsehood against Allah after that﴾ — i.e., after the clarification in their books. It was also said: after your coming with the Torah and your recitation of it.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 3, verse 95:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Say: "Allah has spoken the truth."﴾ Al-sidq (truthfulness) is informing about a thing in accordance with what it actually is, and its opposite is al-kadhib (falsehood). They differed concerning which statement this verse refers to, on two views. One of them is that it refers to His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Abraham was neither a Jew nor a Christian﴾. This was said by Muqatil and Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi. The second is that it refers to His saying, the Exalted: ﴿All food was lawful to the Children of Israel﴾. This was said by Ibn al-Sa'ib.

God Most High says: ﴿Indeed, the first House established for mankind﴾. Mujahid said: The Muslims and the Jews boasted, and the Jews said: "The Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem) is superior to the Ka'bah." The Muslims said: "The Ka'bah is superior." So this verse was revealed.

Regarding the meaning of His saying "first" (awwal), there are two views.

The first: it is the first house that existed on earth. The proponents of this view differed on how it was the first house, in three views.

One: it appeared on the surface of the water when God created the earth, and God created it two thousand years before it, and spread out the earth from beneath it. Sa'id al-Maqburi related from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "The Ka'bah was a hashafah (a small raised mass) on the surface of the water, with two angels upon it glorifying God night and day, two thousand years before the earth."

Ibn Abbas said: "He placed the House on the water upon four pillars two thousand years before the world was created, and then the earth was spread out from beneath the House." This view is held also by Ibn Umar, Ibn Amr, Qatadah, Mujahid, al-Suddi, and others.

The second: Adam felt lonely when he was sent down, so God revealed to him: "Build for Me a house on the earth, and make around it something like what you saw My angels making around My Throne." So he built it. This was related by Abu Salih, from Ibn Abbas.

The third: it was sent down with Adam. When the Flood came, it was lifted up and became a frequented place (ma'mur) in the heavens, and Ibrahim built upon its traces. This was related by Shayban from Qatadah.

The second view: it is the first house established for mankind for worship, although there were houses before it. This is the view of Ali ibn Abi Talib (may God be pleased with him), al-Hasan, Ata' ibn al-Sa'ib, and others.

As for Bakkah, al-Zajjaj said: this name may be derived from al-bakk. It is said: "The people pushed one another (bakka al-nas ba'duhum ba'dan)," meaning: pushed.

They differed on why it is called Bakkah, in three views.

One: because of the crowding of people in it. This was said by Ibn Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Ikrimah, Qatadah, al-Farra', and Muqatil.

The second: because it breaks (tabukk) the necks of tyrants, meaning it crushes them; no tyrant intends it except that God breaks him. This was narrated from Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr, and al-Zajjaj mentioned it.

The third: because it lowers the arrogance of the haughty. It is said: "I bakakt the man," meaning: I humbled him and turned back his pride. This was said by Abu Abd al-Rahman al-Yazidi and Qutrub.

They agreed that Makkah is the name for the whole town. They differed about Bakkah in four views.

One: it is the name for the plot of ground in which the Ka'bah stands. This was said by Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Abu Malik, Ibrahim, and Atiyyah.

The second: it is what surrounds the House, and Makkah is what lies beyond that. This was said by Ikrimah.

The third: it is the mosque and the House, and Makkah is the name for the entire haram (sacred precinct). This was said by al-Zuhri and Damrah ibn Habib.

The fourth: Bakkah is Makkah. This was said by al-Dahhak and Ibn Qutaybah. Ibn Qutaybah argued that the letter ba' is substituted for the letter mim, as it is said: "samada ra'sahu" and "sabada ra'sahu," meaning he shaved it completely; and "sharrun lazimun" and "lazibun" (words of the same type).

God Most High says: ﴿blessed﴾ (mubarakan). Al-Zajjaj said: it is in the accusative as a hal (circumstantial state). The meaning is: the one that is established in Makkah while in a state of blessing.

God Most High says: ﴿and guidance﴾ (wa-hudan). That is: and [it is] possessed of guidance. It is also permissible for hudan to be in the nominative position, meaning: and it is guidance. As for its blessing, in it sins are forgiven, good deeds are multiplied, and whoever enters it is safe.

Ibn Umar related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Whoever circumambulates the House, does not raise a foot nor set down another, except that God records for him a good deed by it, removes from him a sin by it, and raises him a degree by it."

God Most High says: ﴿and guidance for the worlds﴾. Regarding guidance here, there are four views. One: it means the qiblah, so the meaning is: and the qiblah of the worlds. Two: it means mercy. Three: it means righteousness, because whoever intends it, his state is made righteous before his Lord. Four: it means clarification and indication toward God Most High through the signs in it that no one else can produce, where the dog and the gazelle gather in the haram: the dog does not stir up the gazelle, and the gazelle does not become frightened of it. This was said by al-Qadi Abu Ya'la.

**Qur'an 3:97**, the words ﴿فِيهِ آياتٌ بَيِّناتٌ﴾ ("In it are clear signs"). The majority read *āyātun* (plural). Ibn Abbas, as transmitted by Ata', read *fīhi āyatun bayyinatun maqāmu Ibrāhīm* ("In it is a clear sign: the station of Ibrahim"), and Mujahid also recited it this way. In that reading, the sign is the station of Ibrahim. As for those who read *āyātun* (plural), Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him) said: the signs are the station of Ibrahim and that whoever enters it is secure. On this reading the plural refers to the dual, which is permissible in the Arabic language, as in the words of Allah ﴿وَكُنّا لِحُكْمِهِمْ شاهِدِينَ﴾ ("And We were witnesses to their judgment," 21:78). Abu Raja' said: al-Hasan used to count them while I watched his fingers: the station of Ibrahim, and whoever enters it is secure, and ﴿وَلِلَّهِ عَلى النّاسِ حِجُّ البَيْتِ﴾ ("and pilgrimage to the House is a duty owed to Allah by the people"). Ibn Jarir said: there is an implied element in the sentence, its sense being: "among them is the station of Ibrahim." The exegetes (al-mufassirun) said: the signs in it are many, among them the station of Ibrahim, and that whoever enters it is secure, and the fact that birds do not fly over it, and that the sick seek healing through it, and that punishment is hastened for whoever violates its sanctity, and the destruction of the People of the Elephant when they intended to demolish it, and other things besides. Al-Qadi Abu Ya'la said: the word "House" here means the whole Sacred Precinct (al-Haram), because these signs exist in it, whereas the station of Ibrahim is not inside the House. The sign in the station of Ibrahim is that he stood upon a stone, and his feet left an impression in it, and this was evidence of Allah's power and of the truthfulness of Ibrahim.

**Qur'an 3:97**, the words ﴿وَمَن دَخَلَهُ كانَ آمِنًا﴾ ("and whoever enters it is secure"). Al-Qadi Abu Ya'la said: its wording is that of a report, but its meaning is a command, and its sense is: "and whoever enters it, then grant him security." It is general in application to one who committed a crime before entering and to one who committed a crime inside it after entering. However, there is a consensus (ijma', the agreement of the scholars) that one who commits a crime inside it is not granted security, because he has violated the sanctity of the Haram and rejected its protection. Thus the ruling of the verse remains applicable to one who committed a crime outside it and then sought refuge in the Haram. The jurists differed on this. Ahmad, in a narration of al-Marwadhi, said: if a man kills, or cuts off a hand, or commits a prescribed offence (hadd) outside the Haram and then enters it, the hadd is not carried out upon him and retaliation is not taken from him, but no one may sell to him, buy from him, or eat with him until he leaves. If he does any of these things within the Haram, retribution is exacted from him. Ahmad, in a narration of Hanbal, said: if he kills outside the Haram and then enters it, he is not to be killed. If the offence is less than killing, the hadd is carried out upon him, and this is also the view of Abu Hanifa and his companions. Malik and al-Shafi'i said: all of that is carried out upon him, both for killing and for lesser offences.

In the words of Allah ﴿وَمَن دَخَلَهُ كانَ آمِنًا﴾ there is evidence that none of these penalties is carried out upon him. This is the position of Ibn Umar, Ibn Abbas, Ata', al-Sha'bi, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, and Tawus.

**Qur'an 3:97**, the words ﴿وَلِلَّهِ عَلى النّاسِ حِجُّ البَيْتِ﴾ ("and pilgrimage to the House is a duty owed to Allah by the people"). Most readers pronounce the *ḥā'* of *al-ḥajj* with a fatḥa (*al-ḥajj*). Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and Hafs from Asim read it with a kasra (*al-ḥijj*). Mujahid said: when Allah revealed ﴿وَمَن يَبْتَغِ غَيْرَ الإسْلامِ دِينًا فَلَنْ يُقْبَلَ مِنهُ﴾ ("And whoever seeks a religion other than Islam, it will never be accepted from him," 3:85), the people of all the religions said: "We are Muslims." Then this verse was revealed, and the Muslims performed the pilgrimage while the polytheists abstained from it, and the Jews said: "We will never perform it."

**Qur'an 3:97**, the words ﴿مَنِ اسْتَطاعَ إلَيْهِ سَبِيلا﴾ ("for whoever is able to find a way to it"). The grammarians (al-nahwiyyun) said: *man istaṭā'a* ("whoever is able") is a substitute (badal) for *al-nās* ("the people"), and this is a substitution of part for whole (badal al-ba'ḍ min al-kull), as when you say: "I struck Zayd on his head." It has been narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Umar, Anas, and Aisha, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he was asked: "What is the way (sabil)?" He said: "Whoever has provisions and a mount."

**Qur'an 3:97**, the words ﴿وَمَن كَفَرَ﴾ ("And whoever disbelieves"). There are five opinions concerning this. The first is that its meaning is: whoever disbelieves in the pilgrimage by holding it to be not obligatory. This was transmitted by Miqsam from Ibn Abbas, and by Ibn Jurayj from Mujahid, and it is the view of al-Hasan, Ata', Ikrimah, al-Dahhak, and Muqatil. The second is that whoever does not hope for the reward of his pilgrimage and does not fear the punishment for abandoning it has disbelieved in it. This was transmitted by Ali ibn Abi Talha from Ibn Abbas, and by Ibn Abi Najih from Mujahid. The third is that it refers to disbelief in Allah, not in the pilgrimage, and this meaning is transmitted from Ikrimah and Mujahid. The fourth is that if a person is able to perform the pilgrimage but dies without doing so, he is branded between his eyes as a disbeliever; this is the view of Ibn Umar. The fifth is that it means disbelief in the verses revealed concerning the House, because some of the polytheists said: "We disbelieve in these verses." This is the view of Ibn Zayd.

**The Qur'anic verse 98:** ﴿Say: "O People of the Scripture, why do you disbelieve in the verses of Allah, while Allah is Witness over what you do?"﴾

Al-Hasan said: They are the Jews and the Christians. As for "the verses of Allah," Ibn ʿAbbas said: they are the Qur'an and Muhammad (ﷺ). As for "the Witness" (al-shahid), Ibn Qutayba said: it means the same as al-shahid (the witness). Al-Khattabi (a linguist and hadith scholar) said: it is the One from whom nothing is hidden, as if He were present and witnessing.

**The Qur'anic verse 99:** ﴿O People of the Scripture, why do you bar from the way of Allah those who believe, seeking to make it crooked, while you are witnesses?﴾

Muqatil said: The Jews invited Hudhayfa and ʿAmmar ibn Yasir to their religion, and this verse was revealed.

Concerning the intended meaning of "People of the Scripture" here, there are two opinions. The first is that they are the Jews and the Christians, as reported by al-Hasan. The second is that they are the Jews, as reported by Zayd ibn Aslam and Muqatil.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: "why do you bar from the way of Allah" means Islam and the Hajj. Qatada said: "why do you bar from the Prophet of Allah and from Islam." Al-Suddi said: When they were asked, "Do you find Muhammad in your books?" they would say, "No," and they would thus turn people away from him.

**The Qur'anic phrase:** ﴿tabghunaha﴾ (seeking it). The linguists said: the pronoun in *ha* refers to the way (al-sabil), and al-sabil may be treated as masculine or feminine. They recited the following verse:

*So do not be far off, for every youth of the people will surely come to travel that way.*

The meaning of *tabghunaha* is *tabghuna laha* (you seek for it). The Arabs say *ibghini khadiman* ("seek for me a servant"), meaning *ibtaghi-hu li* ("seek him for me"). When they want to say "seek with me and help me in searching for him," they say *ibghini*, with the *alif* vowelled with a fatha. They also say *wahabtuka dirhaman* ("I gave you a dirham"), just as they say *wahabtu laka*. The poet said:

*So their servant turned away, then called out: "Shall I hunt a dhabi (gazelle) for you, or a donkey?"*

The poet intended *asidu lakum* ("I hunt for you").

The meaning of the verse is that they seek for the way of Allah crookedness and distortion, and they wish to return faith and uprightness to disbelief and deviation, and they seek to turn away from the right course. This is the view of al-Farra', al-Zajjaj and the linguists. Ibn Jarir said: this speech follows a common Arabic pattern of directing the statement toward the people concerned, so the meaning is: you seek for the people of Allah's religion, and for those who are upon the path of truth, *iwajan*, that is, misguidance.

Abu ʿUbayda said: *al-ʿiwaj* with a kasra on the ʿayn (ʿ*iwaj*) is used for religion, speech and action, while *al-ʿawaj* with a fatha on the ʿayn (ʿ*awaj*) is used for walls and tree trunks. Al-Zajjaj said: *ʿiwaj* with a kasra is used for what has no visible form, and for what has a visible form one says *ʿawaj* with a fatha. You say: "In his affair and his religion there is ʿawaj, and in the staff there is ʿawaj."

Ibn al-Anbari reported from Tha'lab that he said: among the Arabs, *ʿiwaj* with a kasra refers to anything that cannot be encompassed, and *ʿawaj* with a fatha refers to anything that is perceived. So one says: "In the earth there is ʿiwaj, and in religion there is ʿiwaj," because these two are vast and cannot be fully grasped. And one says: "In the staff there is ʿawaj, and in the tooth there is ʿawaj," because these two can be encompassed and their reality can be reached.

Ibn Faris said: *al-ʿawaj* with a fatha refers to anything upright, such as a wall. And *al-ʿiwaj* refers to what is in a carpet, land, religion, or livelihood.

**The Qur'anic phrase:** ﴿wa-antum shuhada'﴾ (while you are witnesses). Concerning this there are two opinions. The first is that its meaning is: while you bear witness to the correctness of what you turn people away from, and to the falsehood of what you are upon. This meaning is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, Qatada and most scholars. The second is that the meaning of *shuhada'* here is "those who have intellect" ('uqala'), as mentioned by al-Qadi Abu Ya'la and others.

Occasion of revelation: "The Aws and the Khazraj had a war between them in the Jahiliyya (the pre-Islamic period). When the Prophet ﷺ came, he extinguished that war through Islam. Then, while two men, one from the Aws and one from the Khazraj, were talking, with a Jew present with them, the Jew began reminding them of their days and the enmity that had existed between them, until the two fought. Each of them called out to his people, and they came out with weapons. The Prophet ﷺ came and reconciled them, and then this verse was revealed." This is related by Mujahid, Ikrimah, and the majority.

The commentators said: the address in this verse is to the Aws and the Khazraj. Zayd ibn Aslam said: by "that group" is meant Shas ibn Qays, the Jew, and his companions. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning of "obeying them" is "following them blindly" (taqlid).

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 3, verse 101:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And whoever holds fast to Allah﴾

Ibn Qutaybah said: That is, "yamtani'" (he seeks protection, he holds firm), and the root of ʿiṣmah (protection, safeguard) is al-manʿ (prevention, restraint). Al-Zajjaj said: "yaʿtaṣim" is in the jussive mood because of "man" (whoever), and the response (jawab) is ﴿then he has certainly been guided﴾.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 3, verse 102:

Ikrimah said: It was revealed concerning the Aws and the Khazraj when they fought, and the Prophet (ﷺ) reconciled between them. Regarding "as He ought to be feared" (ḥaqqa tuqatihi), there are three opinions. The first: "That Allah is obeyed and not disobeyed, remembered and not forgotten, and thanked and not disbelieved." This was narrated by Ibn Mas'ud from the Prophet (ﷺ). It is also the view of Ibn Mas'ud, al-Hasan, Ikrimah, Qatadah and Muqatil. The second: that one strives for Allah with the striving due to Him, that the blame of any blamer does not deter a person in this, and that they stand firm for Him with justice, even against themselves, their fathers and their sons. This was narrated by Ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn Abbas. The third: that its meaning is: "Be mindful of Him in what is due upon you that you be mindful of Him in," as stated by al-Zajjaj.

Section

The scholars differed: is this statement muhkam (definitive, not abrogated) or mansukh (abrogated)? There are two opinions. The first: that it is mansukh (abrogated). This is the view of Ibn Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Qatadah, Ibn Zayd, al-Suddi and Muqatil. They said: when this verse was revealed, it was difficult for the Muslims, so it was abrogated by His saying, ﴿So fear Allah as much as you are able﴾ [al-Taghabun: 16]. The second: that it is muhkam, narrated by Ali ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn Abbas, and it is the view of Tawus. Our shaykh Ali ibn Abd Allah said: The disagreement over its abrogation and its being muhkam returns to the disagreement over the meaning intended by it. Whoever holds that it is abrogated views "as He ought to be feared" as meaning standing upon everything that is due to Him and deserved by Him, and all people are unable to fulfil this, so achieving it from anyone is impossible. Whoever holds that it is muhkam views "as He ought to be feared" as the performance of what is incumbent upon the servant according to his capacity, so His saying, ﴿as much as you are able﴾, explains "as He ought to be feared," and is neither an abrogation nor a specification.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 3, verse 103:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And hold fast, all of you together, to the rope of Allah﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: "I'tasimu" means "istamsiku" (hold firmly). As for "al-habl" (the rope), there are six opinions concerning it. The first: it is the Book of Allah, the Qur'an. This was narrated by Shaqiq from Ibn Mas'ud, and Qatadah, al-Dahhak and al-Suddi also said so. The second: it is the community (al-jama'ah), narrated by al-Sha'bi from Ibn Mas'ud. The third: it is the religion of Allah, said by Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Zayd, Muqatil and Ibn Qutaybah. Ibn Zayd said: it is Islam. The fourth: it is the covenant of Allah, said by Mujahid, 'Ata', Qatadah in one narration, and Abu 'Ubayd. Al-Zajjaj cited as evidence for this the verse of al-A'sha:

"And when a tribe's ropes pass her over, they take from the other ropes to you their ropes."

Ibn al-Anbari recited:

"If only a rope had reached Sulaym, it would have extended, with its rope, a sturdy rope."

The fifth: it is sincerity (al-ikhlas), said by Abu al-'Aliyah. The sixth: it is the command of Allah and His obedience, said by Muqatil ibn Hayyan. Al-Zajjaj said: "Jami'an" is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal), meaning: be gathered together in holding fast to it. The original form of "tafarraqu" is "tatafarraqu," but the letter ta' was elided because two letters of the same kind came together, and the elided one is the second, because the first indicates the future tense. It is not permissible to elide the letter that indicates the future, and this verb is in the jussive mood due to the prohibition; the original is "wa la tatafarraquna," so the nun was elided to indicate the jussive.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And remember the favour of Allah upon you﴾. They differed regarding who is intended by this address, in two opinions. One: they are the polytheist Arabs, among whom the strong would prey upon the weak; said by al-Hasan and Qatadah. The second: they are the Aws and the Khazraj, between whom there had been fierce warfare; said by Ibn Ishaq. "Al-a'da'" is the plural of "'aduww" (enemy). Ibn Faris said: it derives from "'adā," meaning to wrong.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿so you became﴾, i.e., you became. Al-Zajjaj said: The original meaning of "akh" (brother) in the language is one whose aim is the aim of his brother, and the Arabs say: "So-and-so seeks out what pleases so-and-so," i.e., what gladdens him. "Al-shafa" means the edge. Know that this is a parable which Allah struck for their being on the brink of destruction and their closeness to punishment, as if He said: You were on the edge of a pit of Fire, with nothing between you and falling into it except death in disbelief. Al-Suddi said: Muhammad (ﷺ) rescued you from it.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 3, verse 104:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And let there be [arising] from you a community﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning of the speech is: "Let all of you be a community calling to good, and enjoining what is right." However, "min" (from) here enters to particularize the addressees from among the other categories (of people), and it emphasizes that the command is directed at the addressees. Similar to it is: ﴿So avoid the abomination of idols﴾ [al-Hajj: 30], meaning: avoid the idols, for they are an abomination. Similar to it is the saying of the poet:

"He is a man of generous desires, who gives them and asks for them; the bearer of burdens (al-Zafr) refuses to suffer injustice from him, the one who gives freely (al-Nawfal al-Zafr)."

Here "al-Nawfal al-Zafr" is (used) because he described him as giving desires. Al-Nawfal means one who gives much in voluntary gifts (nawafil), and al-Zafr means one who carries heavy loads. And this indicates that all of them were commanded to enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong. His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿You are the best community brought forth for mankind, enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong﴾. He said: It is possible that He commanded a group from among them, because those who call (to good) ought to be scholars in what they call to, and not all creation are scholars, and knowledge can be substituted by some people for others, like jihad. As for "good" (al-khayr), there are two views concerning it.

One of them: that it is Islam; this was said by Muqatil.

The second: acting in obedience to God; this was said by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi. As for "what is right" (al-ma'ruf), it is what every sensible person recognizes as correct, and its opposite is "what is wrong" (al-munkar). It was also said: al-ma'ruf here is obedience to God, and al-munkar is disobedience to Him.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 3, verse 105:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And do not be like those who became divided and differed﴾. Regarding them there are two opinions.

The first: they are the Jews and the Christians. This was said by Ibn Abbas, and al-Hasan, along with others.

The second: they are the Haruriyya (the Kharijite sect). This was said by Abu Umama.

Ibn al-Jawzi's commentary (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 3, verse 106:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿On the Day when some faces turn white and some faces turn black﴾. Abu Razin al-‘Uqayli, Abu ‘Imran al-Jawni, and Abu Nahik read *tibyaddu* and *tisawwaddu* with a kasra on the *ta'* in both. Al-Hasan, al-Zuhri, Ibn Muhaysin, and Abu al-Jawza' read *tabyaddu* and *taswaddu* with an *alif* and a madda in both. Abu al-Jawza' and Ibn Ya'mur read *fa-amma alladhina iswaddat wa-ibyaddat*, with an *alif* and a madda. Al-Zajjaj said: God informed of the time of that punishment when He said, "On the day when some faces turn white."

Ibn ‘Abbas said: "The faces of the People of the Sunnah (the followers of the Prophet's way) turn white, and the faces of the People of Innovation (ahl al-bid'ah) turn black."

Regarding those whose faces turn black, there are five opinions:

The first: they are everyone who disbelieved in God after their faith on the Day of the Covenant (yawm al-mithaq). This was said by Ubayy ibn Ka'b.

The second: they are the Harurites (al-Harutiyya, an early Kharijite group). This was said by Abu Umama and Ishaq al-Hamadhani.

The third: they are the Jews. This was said by Ibn ‘Abbas.

The fourth: they are the hypocrites. This was said by al-Hasan. The fifth: they are the People of Innovation. This was said by Qatada.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Did you disbelieve?﴾ Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is: it will be said to them, "Did you disbelieve?" The verb of saying is omitted because the context indicates it, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And Isma'il [said], "Our Lord, accept from us"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 127], meaning: "and they both say, 'Our Lord, accept from us.'" A similar example is ﴿Peace be upon you from every gate﴾ [al-Ra'd: 23–24], meaning: "they say, 'Peace be upon you.'" The *alif* is in the form of a question, but its meaning is affirmation of fact and rebuke. If we say they are all the disbelievers, then they believed on the Day of the Covenant and then disbelieved. If we say they are the Harurites and the People of Innovation, then their disbelief after their faith is departing from the community (al-jama'a) in belief. If we say they are the Jews, then they believed in the Prophet before his mission and then disbelieved after his appearance. If we say they are the hypocrites, then they professed with their tongues and denied in their hearts.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So taste the punishment﴾. The original sense of *dhawq* (tasting) is through the mouth, and this is a metaphorical extension from it. It is as though they made what is perceived and recognized something "tasted," by way of comparison with what is recognized through eating. The Arabs say: "I have tasted (dhuqtu) from so-and-so's generosity what makes me desire his company," meaning, "I have come to know," and they say: "Taste (dhuq) the horse, and you will know what it has." 

[p. 437] Tamim ibn Muqbil said:

"Or like the swaying of a Rudayni spear, which the hands of merchants have tested, and they have made its shaft more pliant."

Another poet said:

"Indeed God has tasted the wisdom of Qays,
and when He saw its lightness, He rejected it."

By *dhawq* they mean knowledge. In the book of al-Khalil: whatever disagreeable thing befalls a person has been "tasted" by him.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿As for those whose faces turn white﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: they are the believers. "The mercy of Allah" is His Paradise. Ibn Qutaybah said: He called Paradise "mercy" because their entry into it was by His mercy. Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is: "in the reward of His mercy." He said: the repetition of "therein" (fiha) is for emphasis.

(p-438) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And Allah does not desire injustice for the worlds﴾. Some of them said: its meaning is that He does not punish them without a crime. Al-Zajjaj said: He has informed us that He punishes whoever He punishes out of deserving it.

The commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 3, verses 109–110:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿You are the best nation brought forth for mankind﴾. The occasion of its revelation was that Malik ibn al-Dayf and Wahb ibn Yahudha, the two Jews, said to Ibn Mas'ud and Salim, the freed slave of Abu Hudhayfa [and Ubayy ibn Ka'b, and Mu'adh ibn Jabal]: "Our religion is better than what you call us to, and we are superior to you." So this verse was revealed. This is the saying of Ikrima and Muqatil. Regarding who is meant by this verse, there are four opinions.

The first: they are the people of Badr. The second: they are the Emigrants (al-Muhajirun). The third: all the Companions. The fourth: the entire community of Muhammad ﷺ. All these opinions are transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas. Bahz ibn Hakim related from his father, from his grandfather, from the Prophet ﷺ, that he said: "Indeed you will complete seventy nations, you are the best of them and the most honoured of them before God, the Exalted." Al-Zajjaj said: The original address is to the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ, (p-439) but it encompasses the rest of his community.

Regarding His saying, the Exalted, ﴿You are﴾, there are two views.

One of them: it is on its original form, and what is meant by it is the past tense. Then there are three opinions regarding this.

The first: its meaning is "You were in the Preserved Tablet" (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz, the tablet in which the divine decree is recorded). The second: its meaning is "You were created and brought into existence." The commentators mentioned both of these. The third: the meaning is "You have been since you were," which Ibn al-Anbari mentioned. The second view: the meaning of "You were" is "You are," like His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And God has always been Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [An-Nisa: 96]. This was mentioned by al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj. Ibn Qutayba said: The verb may come in the form of the past tense while it refers to the present or the future, like His saying, the Exalted: "You were" (kuntum), meaning "you are." Similar to it is: ﴿And when God said, "O Jesus"﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 116], meaning "and when God says." Similar to it is: ﴿The command of God has come﴾ [An-Nahl: 1], meaning "it will come." Similar to it is: ﴿How can we speak to one who is in the cradle a child?﴾ [Maryam: 29], meaning "one who is in the cradle." Similar to it is: ﴿And God has always been Hearing and Seeing﴾ [An-Nisa: 134], (p-440) meaning "and God is Hearing and Seeing." Similar to it is: ﴿It stirs up clouds, and We drive them﴾ [Fatir: 9], meaning "so We drive them."

Regarding His saying, the Exalted: ﴿You are the best nation brought forth for mankind﴾, there are two views.

One of them: its meaning is "You are the best of people for people." Abu Hurayra said: They bring them in chains until they lead them into Islam.

The second: its meaning is "You are the best of the nations that have been brought forth."

Regarding His saying, the Exalted: ﴿You enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong﴾, there are two views.

One of them: this is a condition for being the best, and this meaning is transmitted from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, Mujahid, and al-Zajjaj.

The second: it is a praise from God for them, as said by al-Rabi' ibn Anas. Abu al-'Aliya said: "What is right" (al-ma'ruf) is monotheism, and "what is wrong" (al-munkar) is polytheism. Ibn 'Abbas said: "The People of the Book" are the Jews and the Christians.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Among them are believers﴾: those who embraced Islam, such as 'Abd Allah ibn Salam and his companions. ﴿But most of them are defiantly disobedient (al-fasiqun)﴾, meaning: the disbelievers, who did not embrace Islam.

Ibn al-Jawzi, *Zad al-Masir*, on Surah 3, verse 111:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They will not harm you except for a little annoyance.﴾ Muqatil said: The occasion of its revelation was that the leaders of the Jews targeted ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam and his companions and harmed them because they had embraced Islam, so this verse was revealed. Ibn ʿAbbas said: The "annoyance" is their saying: ﴿Ezra is the son of Allah﴾ [At-Tawbah: 30], and ﴿The Messiah is the son of Allah﴾ [At-Tawbah: 30], and ﴿Allah is the third of three﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 73]. Al-Hasan said: (p-441) It is lying against Allah, and their calling the Muslims to misguidance. Al-Zajjaj said: It is *al-buhtu* (slander, false accusation) and *al-tahrif* (distortion of the text). The purpose of the verse is to inform the Muslims that the harm they will receive from them will be only verbal harm, through the Jews calling them to error and making them hear disbelief. Then Allah promised them victory over the Jews in His saying: ﴿And if they fight you, they will turn their backs to you.﴾

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 3, verse 112:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Wherever they are found﴾. Its meaning: they are overtaken and found. That is because wherever they settled, they needed a covenant (ʿahd) from the people of that place and the payment of the poll-tax (jizya). Al-Hasan said: "This community overtook them, and the Magians used to collect the jizya from them."

As for the rope (ḥabl), Ibn ʿAbbas, ʿAṭāʾ, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, Qatada, al-Suddi, and Ibn Zayd said: the rope is the covenant. Some of them said: the meaning of the statement is: ﴿except by a covenant they take from the believers, by the permission of God﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: what comes after the exception in His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿except by a rope from God﴾, is not part of the first clause; rather the meaning is: they are humiliated, except that they hold fast to a covenant when it is granted to them. The explanation of the rest of the verse has already been given in "al-Baqara."

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 3, verse 113:**

His statement, the Exalted: ﴿They are not all alike﴾. There are two opinions regarding the occasion of its revelation.

The first: "The Prophet (ﷺ) delayed the night prayer of ʿIshāʾ one night until a third of the night had passed. Then he came and gave them the good news, saying: 'None of the People of the Book pray this prayer.' So this verse was revealed." This was related by Ibn Masʿud.

The second: When Ibn Salam embraced Islam along with a group of the Jews, their rabbis said: "None believed in Muhammad except our worst people." So this verse was revealed. This was related by Ibn ʿAbbas and Muqatil.

Regarding the meaning of the verse, there are two opinions.

The first: The community of Muhammad and the Jews are not alike. This is the view of Ibn Masʿud and al-Suddi.

The second: Not all of the Jews are alike; rather, among them is one who stands upright by the command of Allah. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas and Qatada. Al-Zajjaj said: The complete pause is at ﴿They are not alike﴾, meaning: the People of the Book are not equal. Regarding the meaning of "standing" (qāʾimah), there are three opinions.

One: It means those who are steadfast in obedience to Allah. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas and Qatada.

The second: It means those who are just. This was said by al-Hasan, Mujahid, and Ibn Jurayj.

The third: It means those who are upright. This was said by Abu ʿUbayd and al-Zajjaj. Al-Farraʾ said: He mentioned one community and did not mention another after it, and the speech is structured around another one, because "alike" (sawāʾ) necessarily requires two. The Arabs may permit omitting one of two things when there is an indication of it in the speech. Abu Dhuʾayb said:

؎ I disobeyed my heart concerning her, though I am attentive to its command; so I do not know whether her pursuit is rightness?!

He did not say "or not," nor "or error," because the meaning of the speech is known.

Another said:

؎ I do not know, when I set out for a land, seeking good, which of the two will befall me:
؎ Is the good that I seek, or the evil that seeks me?

A similar example is His statement, the Exalted: ﴿Is one who worships devoutly during the hours of the night, prostrating and standing?﴾ [az-Zumar: 9], and He did not mention its opposite, because in His statement: ﴿Say: Are those who know equal to those who do not know?﴾ [az-Zumar: 9] there is an indication of what has been omitted there.

Al-Zajjaj rejected this view, saying: The People of the Book have already been mentioned in His statement, the Exalted: ﴿They disbelieved in the signs of Allah and killed the prophets without right﴾. So Allah informed that among them is a steadfast community. What need is there to say: "and a community that is not steadfast"? Rather, He began by mentioning the action of most of them, which is disbelief and opposition, and then mentioned those among them who were distinct from these. He said: "Hours of the night" (ānāʾ al-layl) means its periods, and the singular of ānāʾ is inʾ. Ibn Faris said: It is said: an inʾ of the night has passed, and inyān; the plural is ānāʾ.

The exegetes differed as to whether these ānāʾ are specific portions of the night or not, on two opinions.

The first: They are specific. Within this view there are three opinions.

One: They are the ʿIshāʾ prayer. This was said by Ibn Masʿud and Mujahid.

The second: They are the time between Maghrib and ʿIshāʾ. This was narrated by Sufyan from Mansur.

The third: They are the middle of the night. This was said by al-Suddi.

The second opinion: They are the periods of the night without specification. This was said by Qatada and others.

Regarding His statement, the Exalted: ﴿while they prostrate﴾, there are two opinions.

The first: It is a metaphor for the prayer. This was said by Muqatil, al-Farraʾ, and al-Zajjaj.

The second: It is the well-known prostration. The intended meaning is not that they recite during prostration; rather, they combined both matters: the recitation and the prostration.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 3, verse 114–115:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And whatever good they do, it will not be denied them﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, and Abu Bakr from 'Asim read "taf'alu" and "takfuruhu" with the letter ta' in both places, in the address form, due to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿You are the best nation﴾. Qatadah said: "fa-lan tukfarūhu" means: it will not be lost to you (lan yadilla 'ankum). A group, among them Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Hafs from 'Asim, and 'Abd al-Warith from Abu 'Amr, read "yaf'alu" and "yakfuru" with the letter ya' in both places, as a report about the standing community. The rest of Abu 'Amr's transmitters allow choosing between the ya' and the ta'.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 3, verse 114–115:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And whatever good they do, it will not be denied them﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, and Abu Bakr from 'Asim read "taf'alu" and "takfuruhu" with the letter ta' in both places, in the address form, due to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿You are the best nation﴾. Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 3, verses 116–117:

Allah's words: ﴿The likeness of what they spend in this worldly life﴾. The scholars differed concerning whom it was revealed about, in four opinions.

(p-445) First: it concerns the expenditures and charities of the disbelievers. This is the view of Mujahid.

Second: it concerns the expenditure of the lowly among the Jews upon their scholars. This is the view of Muqatil.

Third: it concerns the expenditure of the polytheists on the Day of Badr.

Fourth: it concerns the expenditure of the hypocrites when they went out with the Muslims to fight the polytheists. Abu al-Hasan al-Mawardi mentioned these two opinions. Al-Suddi said: "He only struck the expenditure as a likeness for their deeds in their polytheism." Regarding the word al-sirr (the cold wind, or frosty blast), there are three opinions.

First: it is the cold, the view of most scholars.

Second: it is fire, the view of Ibn Abbas. Ibn al-Anbari said: "Fire is described as sirr only because of its crackling sound when it blazes."

Third: that al-sirr means sound and movement, as with stones and pebbles, and from it comes the squeak of a sandal (sarir al-na'l). This was mentioned by Ibn al-Anbari. Al-harth means the crop. Concerning the meaning of "they wronged themselves," there are two opinions.

One: they wronged themselves by disbelief, sins, and withholding Allah's right.

The other: they wronged themselves by sowing at a time other than the time of sowing.

Allah's words: ﴿And Allah did not wrong them﴾. Ibn Abbas said: that is, it did not diminish them without a crime they had committed; rather, He sent that upon them because of their wronging themselves by withholding Allah's right from it. This is a likeness which Allah struck to nullify their deeds in the Hereafter.

Tha'lab related to us, saying: Allah began this verse with the wind, and the meaning is "upon the crop," like His words: ﴿like the likeness of one who shouts to that which hears nothing﴾. The actual meaning is "upon that to which it is shouted." Close to this is His words: ﴿And those of you who die and leave wives behind, they shall wait with themselves [for] four months and ten [days]﴾. He spoke of "the wives" and left out "those who," as if He said: "the wives of those of you who die shall wait," and He began with "those who," while His intention is "after the wives." He also recited:

Perhaps, if the wind inclines me one inclination, toward the son of Abi Dayyan he may feel remorse.

He spoke of the son of Abi Dayyan and left out himself, while he only intended: "Perhaps the son of Abi Dayyan may feel remorse if the wind inclines me one inclination." Sometimes something is mentioned first while the intended meaning is delay, like His words: ﴿And on the Day of Resurrection you will see those who lied against Allah, their faces blackened﴾ [az-Zumar 39:60]. The meaning is: you will see the faces of those who lied against Allah blackened on the Day of Resurrection.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 3, verses 116–117:

Allah's words: ﴿The likeness of what they spend in this worldly life﴾. The scholars differed concerning whom it was revealed about, in four opinions.

(p-445) First: it concerns the expenditures and charities of the disbelievers. This is the view of Mujahid.

Second: it concerns the expenditure of the lowly among the Jews upon their scholars. This is the view of Muqatil.

Third: it concerns the expenditure of the polytheists on the Day of Badr.

Fourth: it concerns the expenditure of the hypocrites when they went out with the Muslims to fight the polytheists. Abu al-Hasan al-Mawardi mentioned these two opinions. Al-Suddi said: "He only struck the expenditure as a likeness for their deeds in their polytheism." Regarding the word al-sirr (the cold wind, or frosty blast), there are three opinions.

One: they wronged themselves by disbelief, sins, and withholding Allah's right.

The other: they wronged themselves by sowing at a time other than the time of sowing.

Allah's words: ﴿And Allah did not wrong them﴾. Ibn Abbas said: that is, it did not diminish them without a crime they had committed; rather, He sent that upon them because of their wronging themselves by withholding Allah's right from it. This is a likeness which Allah struck to nullify their deeds in the Hereafter.

Tha'lab related to us, saying: Allah began this verse with the wind, and the meaning is "upon the crop," like His words: ﴿like the likeness of one who shouts to that which hears nothing﴾. The actual meaning is "upon that to which it is shouted." Close to this is His words: ﴿And those of you who die and leave wives behind, they shall wait with themselves [for] four months and ten [days]﴾. He spoke of "the wives" and left out "those who," as if He said: "the wives of those of you who die shall wait," and He began with "those who," while His intention is "after the wives." He also recited:

Perhaps, if the wind inclines me one inclination, toward the son of Abi Dayyan he may feel remorse.

He spoke of the son of Abi Dayyan and left out himself, while he only intended: "Perhaps the son of Abi Dayyan may feel remorse if the wind inclines me one inclination." Sometimes something is mentioned first while the intended meaning is delay, like His words: ﴿And on the Day of Resurrection you will see those who lied against Allah, their faces blackened﴾ [az-Zumar 39:60]. The meaning is: you will see the faces of those who lied against Allah blackened on the Day of Resurrection.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 3, verse 118:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O you who have believed, do not take as bitana (inner confidants) those other than your own,﴾ Ibn ʿAbbas and Mujahid said: It was revealed concerning a group of the believers who used to show friendliness to the hypocrites and keep close company with some of the Jews, because of the kinship, friendship, neighbourliness, fosterage, and alliance that existed between them. So they were forbidden from taking them as intimate confidants. Al-Zajjaj said: *al-bitana* means the intimates who are privy to a person's affairs and with whom he is at ease. It is said: "So-and-so is a *bitana* of so-and-so," meaning he is one who enters into his confidence and is familiar with him. The meaning of ﴿they will not spare you any effort﴾ is: they will not hold back in their utmost efforts to bring you into what harms you.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They wish that you would suffer hardship.﴾ That is, they wish for your *ʿanat*, which is whatever distress and harm befalls you. It is said: "So-and-so *yuʿannit* so-and-so," meaning he intends to inflict hardship and harm upon him. The root of this is from their saying *akamatun ʿanūt*, when a hill is long and its path is difficult to traverse. Ibn Qutayba said: The meaning of ﴿other than you﴾ is: other than the Muslims. And *al-khabal* means evil.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Hatred has already appeared from their mouths.﴾ Ibn ʿAbbas said: That is, there has already become evident to you from them (p-447) lying, insulting, and opposition to your religion. Qadi Abu Yaʿla said: In this verse there is an indication that it is not permissible to seek the assistance of *ahl al-dhimma* (protected non-Muslim subjects, *dhimmis*) in the affairs of the Muslims, such as administrative posts and scribal work. For this reason Ahmad said: The imam should not seek the assistance of *ahl al-dhimma* in fighting *ahl al-harb* (the people of war). It is related from ʿUmar that it reached him that Abu Musa had appointed a man from *ahl al-dhimma* as a scribe, so ʿUmar wrote to him rebuking him and said: Do not restore them to honour after Allah has humbled them.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 3, verse 119:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Here you are, you love them, but they do not love you⁠—﴾ Ibn ʿAbbas said: Most of the Ansar used to associate with the Jews and the Jews with them. When the Ansar embraced Islam, the Jews came to hate them, and this verse was revealed. The address in this verse is to the believers. Ibn Qutaybah said: The meaning of the speech is: "Here you are, O people," and as for "tuhibbunahum" (you love them), the hāʾ and mīm refer to those who were forbidden from befriending them. Regarding the meaning of the believers' love for them, there are four opinions.

The first is that it is inclination toward them by nature, because of kinship, fosterage, and alliance. This meaning is transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second is that it means mercy toward them, because of the sins they commit, which are met with severe punishment. This meaning is transmitted from Qatadah.

The third is that it is because of the hypocrites' display of faith. This was narrated from Abu al-ʿĀliyah.

The fourth is that it means desiring Islam for them, while they desire the Muslims to disbelieve. This is the saying of al-Mufaddal and al-Zajjaj. And "al-kitab" (the Book) is in the sense of "al-kutub" (the books), as said by al-Zajjaj.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿When they meet you, they say, "We believe," but when they are alone, they bite their fingertips at you out of rage. Say: Die in your rage. Indeed, Allah is Knowing of what is in the breasts.﴾ This is the condition of the hypocrites, and Muqatil said: They are the Jews. "Al-anamil" means the tips of the fingers. Ibn ʿAbbas said: "Al-ghayz" is intense anger against you. It was said that this is a figure of speech, presenting an image of what befell them, even though there is no actual biting of fingertips. The meaning of ﴿Die in your rage﴾ is: remain with it until you die. Their rage stemmed from seeing the unity of the Muslims gathered together. Ibn Jarir said: This is a command from Allah Exalted to His Prophet to invoke against them, that Allah destroy them through grief from rage.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 3, verse 120:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿If good touches you, it grieves them; and if evil befalls you, they rejoice at it.﴾ Qatada said: "The good" is unity (al-ulfa) and community (al-jama'a). "The evil" is division (al-furqa) and disagreement (al-ikhtilaf), and a portion of the Muslims being struck. Ibn Qutayba said: "The good" is blessing (al-ni'ma), and "the evil" is calamity (al-musība).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And if you are patient﴾ — there are two opinions on it. One: patience over their harm (adha), said by Ibn 'Abbas. The second: patience over the command of Allah, said by Muqatil.

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and fear Allah﴾, there are two opinions. One: it means shirk (association of partners with Allah), said by Ibn 'Abbas. The second: it means sins (al-ma'asi), said by Muqatil.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿will not harm you﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi' and Abu 'Amr read "yadirkum" with a kasra on the ḍād and a light (unstressed) rā'. 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "la yadurrukum" with a ḍamma on the ḍād and a shadda (doubling) on the rā'. Al-Zajjaj said: "al-Durr" and "al-Ḍayr" have one meaning. As for "al-kayd" (scheming), Ibn Qutayba said it is "al-makr" (deceit). Abu Sulayman al-Khattabi said: "al-Muhit" is the one whose power encompasses all of His creation, and whose knowledge encompasses all things.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 3, verse 121:

The first opinion: it is the Day of Uhud. This was said by ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn ʿAwf, Ibn Masʿud, Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Zuhri, Qatadah, al-Suddi, al-Rabiʿ, and Ibn Ishaq. The reason is that he (ﷺ) went out on the Day of Uhud from the house of ʿAʾishah toward Uhud, and he began arranging his companions in battle lines.

The second: it is the Day of the Confederates (al-Ahzab), said by al-Hasan, Mujahid, and Muqatil.

The third: it is the Day of Badr, also transmitted from al-Hasan. Ibn Jarir said: "The first is more sound, because of His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿When two parties among you were about to lose heart﴾, and the scholars have agreed that this was on the Day of Uhud."

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿And Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing﴾. Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi said: "He hears your consultation with them about going out, and their intention for going out, and He knows what they conceal of love for martyrdom."

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 3, verse 122:

Allah's saying: ﴿When two parties among you were about to lose heart﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: The positioning (al-tabwi'a) was at that time. Tafshala means: to become cowardly and to falter. ﴿And Allah is their Protector﴾, that is, their Helper. Jabir ibn Abd Allah said: "They are of us, Banu Salama and Banu Haritha, and we would not wish that it were not so, because of Allah's saying: ﴿And Allah is their Protector.﴾" Al-Hasan said: They are two groups of the Ansar who were moved by that intention, but Allah preserved them. It was also said: When Abd Allah ibn Ubayy returned with his companions on the day of Uhud, the two groups were about to follow him, but Allah preserved them.

(p-450)* Section

As for tawakkul (trust in God), Ibn Abbas said: It is reliance on Allah. Ibn Faris said: It is the display of incapacity [in the matter] and depending on another, and it is said: "So-and-so is a wukala tukala," meaning: incapable, who entrusts his affair to another. Others said: It is "tafa''ala" from al-wakala (delegation); it is said: "I entrusted my affair to so-and-so, so he took charge of it (tawakkala bihi)," meaning: he guaranteed it, undertook it, and I am relying on him (mutawakkil alayhi). Some of them said: It is committing the matter to Allah, with confidence in His good management.

His words, may God Most High say: ﴿And God had already helped you at Badr﴾. There are two views regarding the naming of Badr.

The first: it is a well belonging to a man named Badr. This was said by al-Sha'bi.

The second: it is the name of the place where they met. This was mentioned by al-Waqidi, citing his shaykhs.

His words, may God Most High say: ﴿while you were humiliated﴾, meaning, due to the fewness of numbers and equipment. ﴿so that you may be grateful﴾, meaning, so that you may be among the grateful.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 3, verse 124:

The Most High said: ﴿When you said to the believers, "Is it not enough for you that your Lord should reinforce you with three thousand angels sent down?"﴾ Al-Sha'bi said: Karaz ibn Jabir said to the polytheists of Makkah, "I will reinforce you with my people," and this weighed heavily upon the Muslims, so this verse was revealed. On which day did that happen? There are two opinions concerning this.

One of them: it was the Day of Badr. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrimah, Mujahid, and Qatadah (p. 451). The second: it was the Day of Uhud, when He promised them reinforcement if they remained patient; but when they did not remain patient, they were not reinforced. This was narrated from 'Ikrimah, al-Dahhak, and Muqatil. The first opinion is more sound. Al-kafiyah (what suffices) is the measure that fills a need. Al-iktifa' (being sufficed) is restricting oneself to that. Al-imdad (reinforcement) is giving one thing after another.

The Most High said: ﴿sent down﴾ (munzalin). Most readers recited it with a light (unshaddated) zay, but Ibn 'Amir recited it with a doubled (shaddah) zay.

﴿And they come at you from their immediate fury﴾ [the Qur'an, 3:125]. On this there are two opinions.

The first is that its meaning is: from their direction and this journey of theirs. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Qatada, Muqatil, and al-Zajjaj.

The second is: from their anger at this moment. This was said by 'Ikrima, Mujahid, al-Dahhak, and others. Ibn Jarir said: whoever says "from their direction" means the beginning of their departure on the day of Badr, and whoever says "from their anger" means the beginning of their anger over their dead on the day of Badr. The root of al-fawr (immediacy) is the beginning of a matter as it is undertaken. It is said: فارت القدر (the pot boiled) when what is in it begins to bubble, and then it continues. Ibn Faris said: al-fawr is boiling. It is said: فارت القدر تفور (the pot boils and bubbles), and فار غضبه (his anger surged) when it swelled up. People also say: فعله من فوره (he did it at once), meaning before it had calmed down.

Regarding "the day of their fawr," there are two opinions. The first is that it is the day of Badr, said by Qatada. The second is the day of Uhud, said by Mujahid and al-Dahhak: they had become angry on the day of Uhud over what they had suffered on the day of Badr.

Allah's words: (مسوِّمين) (marked/distinguished). Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, and 'Asim read مُسَوِّمِينَ with a kasra on the waw, while the rest read it with a fatha. Whoever reads it with a fatha means that Allah marked them. Whoever reads it with a kasra means that the angels marked themselves. Al-Akhfash said: they marked their horses. A hadith from the Prophet (ﷺ) says that on the day of Badr he said: "Mark yourselves, for the angels have marked themselves," attributing the action to them, and this is the evidence for the kasra reading. Ibn Qutayba said: the meaning of مسوِّمين is "marked with the sign of war," and it derives from السيماء (sign/mark). The سومة is the mark by which a horseman identifies himself. 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, said: the mark of the angels' horses on the day of Badr was white wool on their tails and forelocks. Abu Hurayra said: it was red wool (al-'ihn al-ahmar). Mujahid said: the tails of their horses were cut short, and there was wool on them. Hisham ibn 'Urwa said: the angels were on piebald horses, and they wore yellow turbans. Ibn 'Abbas related from a man of Banu Ghifar who said: "My cousin and I attended Badr while we were still polytheists. A cloud approached, and when it came near the horses we heard the neighing of horses in it, and we heard a rider saying: 'Advance, Hayzum!' As for my companion, he died on the spot, and as for me, I almost perished, then I recovered."

Abu Dawud al-Mazini said: "On the day of Badr I pursued a polytheist to strike him, but his head fell before my sword reached him, so I knew that someone else had killed him."

On the number of angels on the day of Badr there are five opinions.

The first is five thousand, said by al-Hasan. Jubayr ibn Mut'im related from 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "While I was drawing water from the well of Badr, a strong wind came that I had never seen stronger. Then another strong wind came, which I had never seen stronger except the one before it. Then another strong wind came that I had never seen stronger. The first wind was Jibril, who descended with two thousand angels and was with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). The second wind was Mika'il, who descended with two thousand angels on the right of the Messenger of Allah. The third wind was Israfil, who descended with a thousand angels on the left of the Messenger of Allah, and I was on his left. Allah defeated His enemies."

The second is four thousand, said by al-Sha'bi. The third is a thousand, said by Mujahid.

The fourth is nine thousand, mentioned by al-Zajjaj.

The fifth is eight thousand, mentioned by some of the exegetes (mufassirin).

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 3, verse 126:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah did not make it﴾, meaning the reinforcement, ﴿except as good news﴾, i.e., except as glad tidings that comfort your souls, ﴿and that your hearts may be assured thereby﴾, so that they would be calm in the battle and not waver. Most scholars hold that this reinforcement was on the Day of Badr. Mujahid said: it was on the Day of Uhud. And it is related from him what indicates that Allah reinforced them on both days with the angels together, except that the angels did not fight except on the Day of Badr.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And victory is not except from Allah﴾, i.e., it is not by the abundance of numbers or the quantity of equipment.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 3, verse 127:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿That He might cut off a part﴾. Its meaning: He helped you at Badr so that He might cut off a part. Al-Zajjaj said: that is, so that He might kill a portion of them. As to which day this happened, there are two views.

The first: it was on the day of Badr. This was said by al-Hasan, Qatadah, and the majority.

The second: the day of Uhud, when twenty-eight of them were killed. This was said by al-Suddi.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Or He might overthrow them﴾. Concerning this there are seven views.

The first: its meaning is "He defeats them." This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and al-Zajjaj.

The second: "He humiliates them." This was said by Qatadah and Muqatil.

The third: "He throws them down." This was said by Abu 'Ubayd and al-Yazidi. Al-Khalil said: it is the throwing down upon the face.

The fourth: "He destroys them." This was said by Abu 'Ubaydah. The fifth: "He curses them." This was said by al-Suddi.

The sixth: "He gives victory over them." This was said by al-Mubarrad. (p-455) The seventh: "He enrages them." This was said by al-Nadr ibn Shumayl, and Ibn Qutaybah chose it. Ibn Qutaybah said: the people of analysis hold that the ta' in it is a transformation from a dal, as if the original were: yukabbidahum, meaning: He strikes them in their livers (akbad) with grief, rage, and intense enmity. From this one says: "So-and-so has had grief burn his liver (kabid)," and "enmity has burned his liver." The Arabs say: "The enemy has a black liver." Al-A'sha said:

"I did not endure the trouble of coming to a people who are enemies, and whose livers are black."

It is as if the livers, when burned by intense enmity, turned black. From this the enemy is called kashih, because he hides enmity in his kashh (flank). The kashh is the side, but they mean the liver, because the liver is there. The poet said:

"He concealed resentments over their flanks."

The ta' and the dal are close in articulation point, and the Arabs assimilate one into the other and substitute one for the other, as in their saying: "harata al-thawb wa-harada-hu" when he tore the garment; and likewise: "kubita al-'aduww" and "kabbada-hu." Similar examples are numerous.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So that they return disappointed﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: the khaʼib (disappointed) is the one who has not attained what he hoped for. Others said: the difference between khaybah (disappointment) and yaʼs (despair) is that khaybah occurs only after hope, whereas yaʼs may occur without hope.

[p-456] His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿You have no part in the affair﴾. There are five reports concerning the occasion of its revelation.

The first: "The Prophet ﷺ had his rubā'iyyah (one of his front teeth) broken on the day of Uhud, and he was wounded on his forehead until the blood flowed over his face. He said: 'How can a people prosper who have done this to their Prophet, while he calls them to their Lord, the Mighty and Majestic?' Then this verse was revealed." Muslim related it in his al-Afrad (a collection of narrations he alone transmitted) from the hadith of Anas. This is also the view of Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Qatadah, and al-Rabi'.

The second: "The Prophet ﷺ cursed some of the hypocrites, and then this verse was revealed." This was said by Ibn 'Umar.

The third: "The Prophet ﷺ intended to curse those who fled on the day of Uhud, and then this verse was revealed, so he refrained from that." This is reported from Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Abbas.

The fourth: "Seventy men from the Ahl al-Suffah (the companions who lived in the shaded area of the Prophet's mosque, the poor emigrants) went out to two tribes of Banu Sulaym, 'Usayyah and Dhakwan, and they were all killed. So the Prophet ﷺ invoked curses upon them for forty days, and then this verse was revealed." This was said by Muqatil ibn Sulayman.

(p-457) The fifth: "When the Prophet ﷺ saw Hamzah mutilated, he said: 'I will mutilate so-and-so of them,' and then this verse was revealed." This was said by al-Waqidi.

Regarding the meaning of the verse, there are two views.

One: You have no part in their guidance or their punishment.

The other: You have no part in victory or defeat. It has also been said that the lam in "lak" (for you) means "ilayka" (toward you).

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿or He turns to them in forgiveness﴾. Al-Farra' said: regarding its accusative case there are two possibilities. If you wish, you may take it as conjoined to His saying ﴿that He may cut off a portion﴾. If you wish, you may take its accusative as in the manner of "ḥattā" (until), as you say: "I will not cease to be with you until (ḥattā) you give me." Since He negated the affair from His Prophet, He affirmed that all matters belong to Him by His saying: ﴿And to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth.﴾

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, do not consume riba﴾. The people of tafsir (exegesis) said: this verse was revealed concerning the riba (usury) of the jahiliyyah (the Age of Ignorance). Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: A man would be owed wealth by another man, and when the term came due, he would say, "Defer it for me, and I will increase your debt on your wealth." That is the multiplied, manifold increase (al-adaf al-mudaafah).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, do not consume riba﴾. The people of tafsir (exegesis) said: this verse was revealed concerning the riba (usury) of the jahiliyyah (the Age of Ignorance). Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: A man would be owed wealth by another man, and when the term came due, he would say, "Defer it for me, and I will increase your debt on your wealth." That is the multiplied, manifold increase (al-adaf al-mudaafah).

(p-459) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And fear the Fire which has been prepared for the disbelievers﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: This is a warning to the believers, lest they consider usury (riba) lawful. Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning is: Beware of making lawful what Allah has forbidden, for you would then become disbelievers.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 3, verses 132–133:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And hasten to forgiveness from your Lord﴾. All of them (the readers) affirmed the waw in "wa-sari'u" (وَسارِعُوا) except Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir, for they did not include it. Abu 'Ali said: Likewise it is in the codices (maṣāḥif) of the people of Madina and Syria. So whoever reads with the waw conjoins "wa-sari'u" to "wa-atī'ū" (وَأطِيعُوا). And whoever omits it, that is because the second sentence is closely linked to the first, so it dispenses with the conjunction (ʿaṭf). The meaning of the verse: hasten to that which necessitates forgiveness. Regarding what is meant by the necessitator of forgiveness here, there are ten sayings.

The first: it is sincerity (al-ikhlas), as said by 'Uthman ibn 'Affan, may Allah be pleased with him.

The second: performing the obligatory duties (al-fara'id), as said by 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him.

The third: Islam, as said by Ibn 'Abbas.

(p-460). The fourth: the first takbir of the prayer, as said by Anas ibn Malik.

The fifth: obedience (al-ta'a), as said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr. The sixth: repentance (al-tawba), as said by Ikrima.

The seventh: emigration (al-hijra), as said by Abu al-'Aliya. The eighth: jihad, as said by al-Dahhak.

The ninth: the five daily prayers, as said by Yaman. The tenth: righteous deeds, as said by Muqatil.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and a Garden whose breadth is the heavens and the earth﴾. Ibn Qutayba said: By "'arḍ" (breadth) he meant vastness (al-si'a), not the breadth that is opposite to length. The Arabs say: "bilad 'arida" (wide lands), meaning spacious. The Prophet ﷺ said to those who fled on the day of Uhud: "Indeed you went off into it 'arida (in wide flight)."

The poet said:

As if the lands of Allah, though they are wide, upon the fearful one who is sought are the palm of a fowler (a narrow snare).

He said: The origin of this is from 'arḍ, which is the opposite of length; when a thing is broad it is vast, and when it is not broad it becomes narrow and thin. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: If some of them were joined to others, the Garden would be in their breadth.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 3, verses 132–133:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And hasten to forgiveness from your Lord﴾. All of them (the readers) affirmed the waw in "wa-sari'u" (وَسارِعُوا) except Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir, for they did not include it. Abu 'Ali said: Likewise it is in the codices (maṣāḥif) of the people of Madina and Syria. So whoever reads with the waw conjoins "wa-sari'u" to "wa-atī'ū" (وَأطِيعُوا). And whoever omits it, that is because the second sentence is closely linked to the first, so it dispenses with the conjunction (ʿaṭf). The meaning of the verse: hasten to that which necessitates forgiveness. Regarding what is meant by the necessitator of forgiveness here, there are ten sayings.

The first: it is sincerity (al-ikhlas), as said by 'Uthman ibn 'Affan, may Allah be pleased with him.

The second: performing the obligatory duties (al-fara'id), as said by 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him.

The third: Islam, as said by Ibn 'Abbas.

(p-460). The fourth: the first takbir of the prayer, as said by Anas ibn Malik.

The fifth: obedience (al-ta'a), as said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr. The sixth: repentance (al-tawba), as said by Ikrima.

The seventh: emigration (al-hijra), as said by Abu al-'Aliya. The eighth: jihad, as said by al-Dahhak.

The ninth: the five daily prayers, as said by Yaman. The tenth: righteous deeds, as said by Muqatil.
