Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 3, verse 134:

Allah's statement: ﴿Those who spend in ease and in hardship﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: "In hardship and in ease." The meaning of the verse is that they desired to deal with Allah, so prosperity did not make them arrogant and cause them to forget, and adversity did not prevent them so that they became stingy.

Allah's statement: ﴿And those who restrain anger﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: One says, "I restrained (kazamtu) the anger" when you hold back what is within yourself of it, and "the camel restrained (kazama) over its cud" when it swallows it back into its throat. Ibn al-Anbari said: The original meaning of kazm is holding back in the face of anger and distress. Ibn 'Umar related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "No servant swallows a gulp more excellent in the sight of Allah than a gulp of anger that he restrains seeking the face of Allah, the Blessed and Exalted."

Allah's statement: ﴿And those who pardon people﴾. There are two opinions regarding this:

The first: that it refers to pardoning the slaves (mamalik), said by Ibn 'Abbas and al-Rabi'.

The second: that it is on its general sense, so they pardon whoever wrongs them, said by Zayd ibn Aslam and Muqatil.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 3, verses 135–136:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And those who, when they commit an act of immorality﴾. Concerning the occasion of its revelation there are three opinions.

The first: "A woman came to Nabhan the date-seller to buy dates from him, and he embraced her and kissed her. Then he regretted it and went to the Prophet (ﷺ) and mentioned that, and this verse was revealed." This was related by ʿAtaʾ from Ibn ʿAbbas.

(p-462) The second: "An Ansari man and a man from Thaqif were made brothers by the Prophet (ﷺ). The Thaqafi went out with the Prophet (ﷺ) on some of his campaigns, and the Ansari would look after the Thaqafi's family. One day he came and saw the woman, who had washed and was letting her hair down. He entered without asking permission, and went to kiss her. She placed her palm over her face, and he kissed it. Then he regretted it and turned back, and she said: 'Glory be to God! You have betrayed your trust and disobeyed your Lord, and you have not achieved your aim.' He went out wandering in the mountains, repenting to God for his sin. When the Thaqafi returned, the woman informed him of what had been done. So he set out searching for him until he was guided to him, and found him in prostration, saying: 'My sin, my sin, I have betrayed my brother.' He said to him: 'O so-and-so, go to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and ask him about your sin; perhaps God will make a way out for you.' So he returned to Madinah, and this verse was revealed concerning his repentance." This was related by Abu Salih from Ibn ʿAbbas, and Muqatil mentioned it.

The third: "The Muslims said to the Prophet (ﷺ): 'The Children of Israel are more honoured by God than us! When one of them sinned, the expiation of his sins would be written on the threshold of his door.' So this verse was revealed, and the Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Shall I not inform you of something better than that?' and he recited this verse and the one before it." This is the saying of ʿAtaʾ.

They differed as to whether this verse describes the spenders in ease and hardship, or whether it refers to another group, on two views.

One of them: that it is a description of them; this was said by al-Hasan.

The second: that it refers to a different category; this was said by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi.

Al-fahisha (immorality) is that which is ugly, and everything that exceeds its measure is fahish. Concerning what is meant by it here there are two views.

One of them: that it is fornication (al-zina). This was said by Jabir ibn Zayd, al-Suddi, and Muqatil.

The second: that it is every major sin; this was said by a group of exegetes.

They differed concerning the "wrongdoing" (zulm) mentioned after it. Some did not distinguish between it and immorality, and said: wronging oneself is also immorality. Others distinguished, and said: it refers to minor sins. Concerning His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿they remember God﴾ there are two views.

One of them: that it is remembrance by the tongue, which is seeking forgiveness; this was said by Ibn Masʿud and ʿAtaʾ, among others.

The second: that it is remembrance of the heart. Within this there are five views.

The first: that it is remembrance of being presented before God; this was said by al-Dahhak.

The second: that it is remembrance of being questioned about it on the Day of Resurrection; this was said by al-Waqidi.

The third: remembrance of God's threat against them for what they committed; this was said by Ibn Jarir.

The fourth: remembrance of God's prohibition of it to them.

The fifth: remembrance of God's forgiveness; Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi mentioned both views.

As for persistence (al-islar), al-Zajjaj said: it is persisting in a thing. Ibn Faris said: it is resolve upon a thing and steadfastness in it. Concerning what is meant by persistence, the exegetes have three views.

One of them: that it is committing the sin while being preoccupied with it. This is the view of Mujahid.

The second: that it is remaining upon it without seeking forgiveness; this is the view of Qatadah and Ibn Ishaq.

(p-464) The third: that it is abandoning seeking forgiveness for it; this is the view of al-Suddi. Concerning the meaning of ﴿while they know﴾ there are three views.

One of them: while they know that persistence harms, and that abandoning it is better than continuing; this was said by Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Hasan.

The second: they know that God accepts the repentance of whoever repents; this was said by Mujahid and Abu ʿImarah.

The third: they know that they have sinned; this was said by al-Suddi and Muqatil.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And those who, when they commit an act of immorality﴾. Concerning the occasion of its revelation there are three opinions.

(p-464) The third: that it is abandoning seeking forgiveness for it; this is the view of al-Suddi. Concerning the meaning of ﴿while they know﴾ there are three views.

One of them: while they know that persistence harms, and that abandoning it is better than continuing; this was said by Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Hasan.

The second: they know that God accepts the repentance of whoever repents; this was said by Mujahid and Abu ʿImarah.

The third: they know that they have sinned; this was said by al-Suddi and Muqatil.

The first view: "Peoples of customs and laws (sunan wa-shara'i') have passed before you, so look at what We did to those among them who denied." This is the saying of Ibn 'Abbas.

The second view: "The customs of God (sunan Allah) in destroying the nations that denied have passed before you, so take heed from them." This is the saying of Mujahid. Regarding the meaning of ﴿So travel through the earth﴾ there are two views.

The first: it is travel by journeying, as said by al-Zajjaj: "When you journey on your travels, you will come to know the reports of those who perished by their denial." The second: it is reflection (tafakkur). The meaning of "look" (fa-nzurū) is "take heed" (i'tabirū), and "the end" (al-'aqibah) is the final outcome of the matter.

"His saying, the Exalted: ﴿This is an exposition for mankind﴾. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: This verse is the first to be revealed from "Al 'Imran". Concerning what is referred to by "this" there are two opinions.

One of them: that it is the Qur'an. This was said by al-Hasan, Qatadah, and Muqatil.

The second: that it explains the news of the earlier nations. This was said by Ibn Ishaq. And al-Bayan (exposition): the uncovering of a thing. Bana al-shay' (the thing became clear): it became evident. And so-and-so is abyan (clearer/more eloquent) than so-and-so, meaning: more eloquent. Al-Sha'bi said: "This is an exposition for mankind" means a clarification from blindness, a guidance from misguidance, and an admonition from ignorance."

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 3, verse 139:

Allah's words: ﴿Do not be weak, nor grieve﴾. The occasion of its revelation was that when the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) were routed at the Battle of Uhud, Khalid ibn al-Walid came toward them with the cavalry of the polytheists, wanting to overcome them on the mountain. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "O Allah, let them not overcome us. O Allah, we have no strength except through You." Then these verses were revealed. This was related by Ibn Abbas. Ibn Abbas and Mujahid said: ﴿Do not be weak﴾ means: do not be feeble. As for what they were forbidden to grieve over, there are four views.

The first: that it was the killing of their Muslim brothers. This was said by Ibn Abbas.

The second: that it was their defeat at Uhud and their being killed. This was said by Muqatil.

The third: that it was what befell the Prophet (ﷺ) of wounds to his head and the breaking of his front tooth. This was mentioned by al-Mawardi.

The fourth: that it was what escaped them of the spoils of war. This was mentioned by Ali ibn Ahmad al-Nisaburi.

Allah's words: ﴿And you will be the superior ones﴾. Ibn Abbas said: it means, you will be the victors, and the final outcome is yours.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 3, verse 140:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿If a wound (qarh) touches you﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: "On the day of Uhud they were struck by a wound, so they complained to the Prophet ﷺ about what they had suffered, and this verse was revealed." As for al-massu (المَسّ), it means al-isabah (الإصابة), i.e. reaching or striking.

Ibn Kathir, Abu ʿAmr, Ibn ʿAmir and Nafiʿ read "qarhun" (قَرْحٌ) with a fatha on the qaf. Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Abu Bakr, on the authority of ʿAsim, read "quruhun" (قُرْحٌ) with a damma on the qaf.

The scholars differed over whether the two readings have the same meaning or not. Abu ʿUbayd said: "al-qarh" with a fatha means wounds and killing, while "al-quruh" with a damma means the pain of wounds. Al-Zajjaj said: "In the language, both have one meaning, which is wounds and the pain of them." He said: "The meaning of ﴿We alternate them﴾ (nudawiluha) is that We make the turn of fortune (al-dawlah) fall, at times, to the disbelievers over the believers when the believers disobey. As for when they obey, they are victorious." (p. 467) And the meaning of ﴿that Allah may know﴾ is: that He may know it as having actually occurred from them, because He already knows it beforehand, and He only requites what has occurred. Ibn ʿAbbas said: the meaning of "knowledge" here is "seeing."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and that He may take from among you martyrs (shuhada')﴾. Abu al-Duha said: it was revealed concerning those killed at Uhud. Ibn Jurayj said: the Muslims used to say, "Our Lord, show us a day like the day of Badr, in which we may seek martyrdom," so He took martyrs from among them on the day of Uhud. Ibn ʿAbbas said: "al-zalimun" (الظالمون) here refers to the hypocrites. Others said: they are those who turned back on the day of Uhud along with Ibn Ubayy the hypocrite.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 3, verse 141:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And that Allah may purify those who believe﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning of the speech is: Allah made the days alternate among the people, so that He might purify the believers and destroy the disbelievers. Regarding al-tamhis (purification/refinement), there are two views.

The first is that it means trial and testing, and they recited:

"I saw Fadil as something wrapped up, then tamhis uncovered it until it appeared clearly twisted."

This is the view of al-Hasan, Mujahid, al-Suddi, Muqatil, Ibn Qutaybah and others.

The second is that it means cleansing and purifying, and this is the view of al-Zajjaj. It is related from al-Mubarrad, who said: It is said "mahhasa al-habl mahsan" when the down is removed from the rope until it becomes clean, and the meaning of their saying "[O Allah,] purify (mahhis) our sins from us" is: remove them from us. Al-Zajjaj related from al-Khalil that al-tamhis is al-takhlis (sifting out), as it is said: "mahhastu al-shay' umahhisuhu mahsan" when I purified the thing. So according to the first view, al-tamhis is the testing of the believers with what befalls them, and according to the second, it is their cleansing from sins through that. Al-Farra' said: The meaning of the verse is: and that Allah may purify from sins those who believe.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and destroy the disbelievers﴾. Concerning this there are four views.

The first: He destroys them, said by Ibn Abbas. The second: He removes their call (da'wah), said by Muqatil. The third: He diminishes them and reduces their numbers, said by al-Farra'. The fourth: He nullifies their deeds, mentioned by al-Zajjaj.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 3, verse 142–143:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And you used to wish for death﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: When Allah the Exalted informed them, through His Prophet ﷺ, of the honor He bestowed upon the martyrs of the Day of Badr, they desired that, so they wished for a battle in which they might be martyred and thereby join their brothers. Then Allah showed them the Day of Uhud, and they did not remain long before they fled, except for those whom Allah willed among them. So this was revealed concerning them: ﴿And you used to wish for death﴾, meaning war, ﴿before you encountered it﴾, that is, before you looked upon it on the Day of Uhud, ﴿and you have certainly seen it﴾ on that day. Al-Farra' and Ibn Qutaybah said: that is, you saw its causes, which are the sword and similar weapons. Regarding the meaning of ﴿while you were looking on﴾ there are three opinions.

The first: "You were looking at the swords." This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: that it was mentioned for emphasis. This was said by al-Akhfash. Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is: "You have certainly seen it while you were sighted, just as you say: I saw such-and-such, and there is no defect in your eye," that is, you saw it with true sight.

(p-469). The third: that its meaning is "while you were looking at what you had wished for." There is an implied element in the verse [i.e., "you have certainly seen it while you were looking on"]. So why did you flee?!

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 3, verse 144:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Muhammad is nothing but a messenger﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: Satan cried out on the day of Uhud: "Muhammad has been killed." So a people said: "If Muhammad has been killed, we will give ourselves over to them (i.e., to the enemy), for they are our clansmen and our brothers. And if Muhammad were alive, we would not have been defeated." So they permitted themselves to flee, and this verse was revealed. Al-Dahhak said: A group of the hypocrites said: "Muhammad has been killed, so return to your former religion." Then this verse was revealed. Qatadah said: Some people said: "If he were a prophet, he would not have been killed." And some people, among whom were the Companions of the Messenger of Allah, said: "Fight for what your Prophet fought for, until you join him." Then this verse was revealed. The meaning of the verse: He will die just as the messengers before him died. So if he dies in his bed, or is killed like those prophets who were killed before him, will you turn back on your heels? That is, will you return to what you were upon of disbelief? This is by way of example. It is said of everyone who turns back from what he was upon: "He has turned back on his heels." Its origin is the act of retreating backwards (rajʿat al-qahqarā), and the ʿaqib (heel) is the back part of the foot.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But they will not harm Allah at all﴾. That is: they will not diminish anything of Allah by their turning back; rather, they harm only themselves. ﴿And Allah will reward﴾, that is, He will reward ﴿the grateful﴾, and concerning them there are three opinions.

One: they are those who remain steadfast upon their religion. This was said by ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him, and he said: "Abu Bakr was the leader of the grateful."

The second: they are those who are grateful for guidance and success (al-tawfiq wa-l-hidayah). The third: they are those grateful for the religion.

(p-470) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And it is not for a soul to die except by permission of Allah﴾. Regarding "permission" there are two opinions.

The first: that it means the command. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas. The second: that it is the permission itself. This is the view of Muqatil.

Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning of the verse is: "No soul would die except by the permission of Allah."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿a decree with a specified term﴾. This is an emphasis, and the meaning is: Allah has decreed that as a decree with a specified term, i.e., a decree having a fixed term. The term (ajal) is the known time. A similar emphatic usage is ﴿the decree of Allah upon you﴾ [al-Nisa', 24], because when He said ﴿Forbidden to you are your mothers﴾ [al-Nisa', 22], it indicated that it was obligatory, so He emphasized it with ﴿the decree of Allah upon you﴾ [al-Nisa', 24]. Likewise His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿the handiwork of Allah﴾ [al-Naml, 88], because when He said ﴿and you see the mountains, you think them fixed﴾ [al-Naml, 88], it indicated that it was the creation of Allah, so He emphasized it with ﴿the handiwork of Allah﴾.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And whoever desires the reward of this world, We will give him of it﴾. That is: whoever directs his deed toward the world, he is given from it, whether little or much; and whoever directs his deed toward the Hereafter, he is given from it. Muqatil said: the verse refers to those who stood firm on the Day of Uhud, and those who sought the spoils of war.

Section

Most scholars hold that this statement is muhkam (clear, not abrogated). A group held that it was abrogated by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿We hasten for him therein what We will, to whom We intend﴾ [al-Isra', 18]. The correct view is that it is muhkam, because no one is given anything except by the power and will of Allah.

The meaning of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿We will give him of it﴾ is: what We will and what We have decreed for him; and He did not say "what he wills."

(p-471) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And how many a prophet﴾. The majority read "wa-ka'ayyin" with the pattern of "ka-'ayn." Ibn Kathir read "wa-ka'in" with the pattern of "ka-'in." Al-Farra' said: The people of the Hijaz say "ka'ayn," like "ka'ayn" (ka-ʿayn), making the hamza fatha and doubling the yaʾ. But the Tamim say "wa-ka'in," as if it were a fa'il (active participle) from "ki'tu" (ki'tu). Al-Kisa'i recited to me:

"And many a one you see striving among the people, eager against a son from whom there came a brave man and a scorpion."

Another said:

"And many a believer has been struck by a calamity, whose outcome is upon Allah, and from Him is its reward."

Ibn Qutayba said: "ka'in" means "kam" (how many), like His saying: ﴿And how many a town rebelled against the command of its Lord﴾ [al-Talaq: 8]. It has two forms: "ka'ayn" with a hamza and a doubled yaʾ, and "ka'in" on the pattern of "qa'il" [and ba'i'] and both have been read [all in the Qur'an]. The more common and more eloquent is the lightened form. The poet said:

"And many a one has made us see death from a person of greeting, when he disdains us or persists in sin."

Another said:

"And many a silent person you see who pleases you, whose increase or deficiency lies in his speech."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Fought along with him many devoted ones (ribbiyyun)﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Aban, and al-Mufaddal (p-472), both from 'Asim, read "qutila" with a damma on the qaf and a kasra on the ta', without an alif. The rest read "qatala" with an alif. Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Razin, Abu Raja', al-Hasan, Ibn Ya'mur, Ibn Jubayr, Qatada, 'Ikrima, and Ayyub read "ribbiyyun" with a damma on the ra'. Ibn 'Abbas, Anas, Abu Mijlaz, Abu al-'Aliya, and al-Jahdari read it with a fatha. On the omission of the alif, two possibilities arise.

One: that the killing was of the prophet alone, and the meaning is: "And how many a prophet was killed, and with him were ribbiyyun, so they did not weaken after his killing."

Two: that the killing was of the ribbiyyun, and "so they did not weaken" refers to those of them who remained. On the affirmation of the alif, the meaning is: the people fought, so they did not weaken. As for the meaning of ribbiyyun, there are five sayings.

One: that they are the multitudes (al-uluf). This was said by Ibn Mas'ud and, in one narration, Ibn 'Abbas, and al-Farra' chose it.

The second: large groups. Al-'Awfi narrated it from Ibn 'Abbas, and Mujahid, 'Ikrima, al-Dahhak, Qatada, al-Suddi, and al-Rabi' also said it, and Ibn Qutayba chose it.

The third: that they are the jurists and scholars. Sa'id ibn Jubayr narrated it from Ibn 'Abbas, and al-Hasan said it, and al-Yazidi and al-Zajjaj chose it.

The fourth: that they are the followers, said by Ibn Zayd.

The fifth: that they are the God-fearing devotees who know Allah, exalted is He, said by Ibn Faris.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So they did not weaken﴾. Regarding it there are two sayings.

One: it is weakness, said by Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Qutayba. The second: it is incapacity, said by Qatada.

Ibn Qutayba said: "al-istikana" is humility, submission, and abasement, and from it comes "miskin" (the poor). Regarding the meaning of the statement there are two sayings.

One: "so they did not weaken" through fear, nor did they grow feeble through loss of strength, nor did they submit through humbling themselves.

(p-473) The second: "so they did not weaken" at the killing of their prophet, nor did they become feeble before their enemy, nor did they submit to what had befallen them.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 3, verse 147:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And their saying was not﴾ meaning: the Rabbiyyun (the companions of the prophets who fought alongside them). ﴿except that they said, "Our Lord, forgive us our sins﴾, that is: their saying was nothing other than seeking forgiveness. Al-israf (excess) is transgressing the limit. It has been said that by "sins" minor sins are meant, and by "excess" major sins.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And make firm our feet﴾. Ibn Abbas said: "in fighting." Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is: "Make us firm upon Your religion, for the one who is firm upon his religion is firm in his war."

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 3, verse 148:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So Allah gave them the reward of this world﴾. Concerning it there are two opinions.

One of them: it is victory. This was said by Qatadah. The second: it is spoils of war (ghanimah). This was said by Ibn Jurayj. It is also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: victory and spoils of war.

Concerning the goodness of the reward of the Hereafter there are two opinions. One of them is that it is Paradise.

The second: it is the reward and forgiveness. This is an instruction from Allah, the Exalted, to the believers as to what they should do and say when meeting the enemy.

The first opinion: they are the hypocrites, according to Ibn 'Abbas and Muqatil.

The second: they are the Jews and the Christians; this was said by Ibn Jurayj.

The third: they are the worshippers of idols; this was said by al-Suddi. They said: they had commanded the Muslims to return from their religion. And the meaning of ﴿They will turn you back on your heels﴾ is: they will turn you toward polytheism, ﴿and you will turn back as losers﴾ by way of punishment.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 3, verse 150:

﴿Nay, Allah is your Protector, and He is the best of helpers.﴾ His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Nay, Allah is your Protector﴾, meaning: your Guardian (waliyy), who will give you victory over them. So be free of any need for alliance with the disbelievers.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 3, verse 151:

Allah's words: ﴿We shall cast terror into the hearts of those who disbelieved﴾. Al-Suddi said: When the polytheists set out from Uhud toward Makkah, they regretted it part of the way and said: "You killed them until only a remnant was left, and you left them?! Turn back and wipe them out." So Allah cast terror into their hearts, and this verse was revealed. Al-Qadhf (casting) means al-qadhf (throwing). Al-Ru'b (terror) means al-khawf (fear).

Ibn Kathir, Nafi', 'Asim, Abu 'Amr and Hamzah read "al-Ru'b" with a silent ('ayn) and light (unstressed) pronunciation. Ibn 'Amir, al-Kisa'i, Ya'qub and Abu Ja'far read it with the 'ayn vowelled with a damma and stressed (emphatic), wherever it occurs.

Al-Sultan (authority/proof) here means al-hujjah (proof) according to the consensus of the scholars. Al-Ma'wa (abode) means the place to which one retreats. Al-Mathwa (dwelling) means the station, and al-Thawa means residence.

Ibn 'Abbas said: "al-Zalimun" (the wrongdoers) here means the disbelievers.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 3, verse 152:

Allah's statement: ﴿And Allah had certainly fulfilled His promise to you﴾. Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi said: When the Prophet (ﷺ) and his Companions returned from Uhud, some of them said: "How did this befall us, when Allah had promised us victory?" So this verse was revealed. The commentators (mufassirun) said: Allah the Exalted had promised the believers victory at Uhud, and He gave them victory, but when they disobeyed and sought the spoils, they were defeated. Ibn 'Abbas said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was never given victory in any battle as he was at Uhud. This was denied to him, and he said: "Between me and you is the Book of Allah. Indeed Allah says: ﴿And Allah had certainly fulfilled His promise to you when you were killing them by His permission﴾." As for al-hiss (killing), it is what Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Mujahid, al-Suddi and the majority said. Ibn Qutaybah said: "tahussunahum" means you annihilate them by killing; it is said "sanatun hasus" when a year destroys everything, and "jarad mahsus" when the cold has killed it.

Regarding His statement ﴿by His permission﴾ there are three views. The first: by His command, said by Ibn 'Abbas. The second: by His knowledge, said by al-Zajjaj. The third: by His decree, said by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi.

Allah's statement: ﴿until when you lost courage﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: That is, you became cowardly. ﴿and disputed about the matter﴾, that is, you differed, ﴿after He had shown you what you love﴾, meaning victory. Al-Farra' said: there is inversion (taqdim and ta'khir) in it; its meaning is: "until when you disputed about the matter, you lost courage and disobeyed," and this waw is extra, like His statement: ﴿So when they had both submitted and he laid him down upon his forehead﴾ [al-Saffat: 103], ﴿and We called him﴾, meaning: We called him. As for their dispute, some of the archers said: "The polytheists have been routed, so what prevents us from taking the spoils?" Others said: "Rather, we will stand firm in our place as the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) commanded us." So some of them left their post and sought the spoils, and they abandoned their place; that was their disobedience. The Prophet (ﷺ) had instructed them: "Even if you see birds snatching us, do not leave your place."

Allah's statement: ﴿Among you are those who desire this world﴾. The commentators said: They are the ones who sought the spoils and abandoned their place. ﴿And among you are those who desire the Hereafter﴾, and they are the ones who stood firm. Ibn Mas'ud said: "I did not think that any of the Companions of Muhammad desired this world until this verse was revealed."

Allah's statement: ﴿Then He turned you away from them﴾, that is, He repelled you from the polytheists through your killing and your defeat. ﴿to test you﴾, that is, to try you, so that the patient is distinguished from the anxious.

Allah's statement: ﴿And certainly He pardoned you﴾. There are two views concerning it. The first: He pardoned you from punishment, said by Ibn 'Abbas. The second: He pardoned you from being completely destroyed, said by al-Hasan. He used to say: "These were with the Messenger of Allah in the way of Allah, angry for the sake of Allah, fighting in the way of Allah; they were forbidden from something and they neglected it, and they did not stop until they were overcome with this grief. And the wicked person today commits every major sin, and engages in every calamity, and claims there is no harm upon him, but he will soon know."

Allah's statement: ﴿And Allah is full of bounty toward the believers﴾. There are two views concerning it. The first: in that He pardoned them, said by Ibn 'Abbas. The second: in that they were not all killed, said by Muqatil.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 3, verse 153:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿When you were climbing [away] and not turning back for anyone﴾. The exegetes said: "idh" (when) is connected to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah had already pardoned you﴾. Most of the readers read "tus‘idūna" with a dammah on the tā' and a kasrah on the ‘ayn, from "tus‘idūna," which is from al-ism‘ād (ascending, i.e., going away from a place and departing). Abān narrated from Tha‘lab, from ‘Āṣim, that it was read with a fatḥah, and this is the reading of al-Ḥasan and Mujāhid, and it is from al-ṣu‘ūd (climbing). Al-Farrā' said: al-ismā‘ād is used at the beginning of journeys and departures; you say: "We set out (ascended) from Baghdad toward Khurasan." But when you climb a ladder or a step, you say: "ṣa‘idtu" (I climbed), and you do not say "uṣ‘idtu." Al-Zajjāj said: whoever begins a journey from a place has "uṣ‘id," but al-ṣu‘ūd is from below to above. Whoever reads the tā' and the ‘ayn with a fatḥah means climbing the mountain. The exegetes have two views on the meaning of the verse.

One: that it refers to their climbing the mountain. This was said by Ibn ‘Abbās and Mujāhid.

The second: that it refers to fleeing far away in defeat. This was said by Qatādah and Ibn Qutaybah. "Talwūna" means "ta‘rujūna" (ascending).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿anyone﴾ is general, and it has been narrated from Ibn ‘Abbās that the Prophet (ﷺ) was intended by it. He said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) was calling out to them from behind them: 'To the servants of Allah, I am the Messenger of Allah.'" ‘Ā'ishah, Abū Mijlaz, Abū al-Jawzā', and Ḥumayd read "‘alā aḥad" with a dammah on the alif and the ḥā', meaning the mountain.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So He rewarded you﴾, i.e., He recompensed you. Al-Farrā' said: the reward (ithābah) here carries the sense of punishment, but it is as the poet said:

I fear that Ziyād's gift may be shackles, black or hard-bound whips (muḥadrajah), reddish.

Al-muḥadrajah: the whips. And al-sūd, it is said, are the fetters.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿grief upon grief﴾. Regarding this bā' (ba') there are four views.

One: it means "ma‘a" (with). The second: it means "ba‘d" (after). The third: it means "‘alā" (upon). According to these three views, the two griefs are connected to the Companions. The exegetes have five views on what is meant by these two griefs.

One: the first grief is what befell them of defeat and killing. The second: the sighting of the polytheists' cavalry over them by Khālid ibn al-Walīd, said by Ibn ‘Abbās and Muqātil.

The second: the first is their first flight, and the second is their flight when they heard that Muhammad had been killed, said by Mujāhid.

The third: the first is what escaped them of the spoils and what befell them of killing and wounds, and the second is when they heard that the Prophet (ﷺ) had been killed, said by Qatādah.

The fourth: the first is what escaped them of the spoils and the victory, and the second is the sighting of Abū Sufyān over them, said by al-Suddī.

The fifth: the first is the sighting of Khālid ibn al-Walīd over them, and the second is the sighting of Abū Sufyān over them, mentioned by al-Tha‘labī.

The fourth view: the bā' means recompense, so its implied meaning is: "He gave you grief just as you gave grief to others." Then one of the two griefs belongs to the Companions, which is one of their sorrows that we mentioned from the exegetes, and the grief for which they were recompensed belongs to others. Regarding what is meant by "others," there are two views.

One: they are the polytheists who caused them grief on the Day of Badr, said by al-Ḥasan.

The second: it is the Prophet (ﷺ), whom they grieved by opposing him, so they were recompensed for that, by their being grieved for what befell them, said by al-Zajjāj.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿so that you would not grieve﴾. Regarding "lā" there are two views.

One: it remains on its original basis, and its meaning is negation. On this view, there are two views on the meaning of the statement.

One: "So He rewarded you with grief that made you forget the sorrow over what had escaped you and what had befallen you." It has been narrated that when they heard the Prophet had been killed, they forgot what had befallen them and what had escaped them.

The second: it is connected to His saying: ﴿And He had already pardoned you﴾, so the meaning of the statement is: He pardoned you, so that you would not grieve over what had escaped you and what had befallen you, because His pardon removes every grief.

The second view: it is a redundant particle (ṣilah), and the meaning of the statement is: so that you would grieve over what had escaped you and what had befallen you, as a punishment for you for your opposition. Among its examples is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So that the People of the Book would not know that they have no power over anything of Allah's bounty﴾ [al-Ḥadīd: 29], i.e., so that they would know. This is the saying of al-Mufaḍḍal. Ibn ‘Abbās said: what escaped them was the spoils, and what befell them was the killing and the defeat.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 3, verse 154:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then He sent down upon you, after distress, security (amanah)﴾. Ibn Qutaybah said: al-amanah is al-amn (security). It is said: "security (al-amanah) descended upon the earth." Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning of the verse is: He recompensed you for what had befallen you of terror by granting you a security in which you slept, because one who is greatly fearful can hardly sleep. And "nu'asan" (drowsiness) is in the accusative as a substitute (badal) for "amanah." It is said: "na'isa al-rajul yan'as nu'asan, fa-huwa na'is" (the man became drowsy). Some say: "nu'san." Al-Farra' said: I have heard it, but I do not favour it. The scholars said: nu'as (drowsiness) is the lightest sleep. Regarding the aspect of the favour bestowed upon them through drowsiness, there are two views.

One: that He made them secure after their fear, until they slept, so the favour lies in the removal of fear, for one who is afraid does not sleep. The second: He strengthened them by rest for the fighting.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿It overcomes a group among you﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, 'Asim and Ibn 'Amir read "yaghsha" with the ya' and with tafkhim (emphatic pronunciation), and it refers to drowsiness (nu'as). Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read "taghsha" with the ta' and with imalah (inclination), and it refers back to security (amanah). As for the group that was overcome by sleep, they are the believers; and the group whose own selves had caused them concern are the hypocrites, whose concern was the deliverance of their own selves, so sleep departed from them. Abu Talhah said: The sword would fall from my hand, then I would take it up, then it would fall, and I would take it up again, from the drowsiness. And I kept looking, and there was not one of them that day but was swaying beneath his shield from drowsiness. Al-Zubayr said: Allah sent sleep upon us, and there was not a man among us but his chin was upon his chest; by Allah, I was hearing, as in a dream, the words of Mu'attib ibn Qushayr: ﴿If we had had any say in the matter, we would not have been killed here﴾, and I memorised them from him.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They think about Allah other than the truth﴾. On this there are four views.

One: that they thought Allah would not help Muhammad and his companions; narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: that they denied the qadar (divine decree); narrated by al-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas.

The third: that they thought Muhammad had been killed; said by Muqatil.

The fourth: they thought the affair of the Prophet (ﷺ) would be extinguished; said by al-Zajjaj.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿the thought of the Jahiliyyah﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: that is, like the thought of the Jahiliyyah.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They say: "Is there anything of the affair in our hands?"﴾. Its wording is that of a question, but its meaning is negation; its estimated sense is: "There is nothing of the affair in our hands." Al-Hasan said: They said, "If the affair had been up to us, we would not have gone out; we were taken out against our will." Others said: By "the affair" is meant victory and triumph. They said: Victory belongs only to the polytheists. ﴿Say: Indeed, the affair entirely﴾, that is, victory, triumph, decree and destiny, ﴿belongs to Allah﴾. Most readers read "Inna al-amra kullahu lillahi" with the lam in the accusative (fathah), while Abu 'Amr read it with the lam in the nominative (dammah). Abu 'Ali said: The argument of the one who reads it in the accusative is that "kullahu" is equivalent to "ajma'in" in comprehensiveness and generality; had he said "inna al-amra ajma'" it would have had to be in the accusative, and "kullahu" has the same force as "ajma'in." As for the one who reads it in the nominative, it is because the sentence has begun with it, just as the verse begins with His saying: "kulluhum atihi" (all of them will come to Him).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They conceal within themselves﴾. Regarding what they concealed, there are three views.

One: that it is their saying, "If we had been in our houses, we would not have been killed here."

The second: that it is their concealing of disbelief and doubt regarding the command of Allah.

The third: regret at their presence with the Muslims at Uhud.

Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi said: The one who said, "Is there anything of the affair in our hands?" was 'Abdullah ibn Ubayy; and the one who said, "If we had had any say in the matter," was Mu'attib ibn Qushayr.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Say: Even if you had been in your houses﴾, that is, even if you had stayed behind, those for whom killing had been decreed would have gone out to their place of slaughter, and sitting at home would not have saved them. Al-mudaji' (those destined to lie down) means those who would be struck down by killing. Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning of "baraza" (they went out) is that they went out to open ground (biraz), which is the uncovered place. The meaning of ﴿and that Allah might test what is in your breasts﴾ is: that He might test it through your deeds, for He had known it in the unseen, so He would know it as witnessed.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and that He might purify what is in your hearts﴾. Qatadah said: He intended to make it manifest, from doubt and suspicion, through what He showed them of the wonders of His handiwork, namely the security, and the disclosure of the inner secrets of the hypocrites. This purification is specific to the believers. Others said: By purification is meant the making clear of what is in the hearts of belief in Allah, His Messenger and the believers; so it is addressed to the hypocrites.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And Allah is All-Knowing of what is in the breasts﴾, that is, of what is within them. Ibn al-Anbari said: its meaning is that He knows the reality of what is in the breasts of hidden things; the feminine form "dhat" carries the sense of "reality (haqiqah)", just as the Arabs say: "laqitu-hu dhata yawm" (I met him on a certain day). They use the feminine because their intention is: "I met him once in a day."

(p-483) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, those of you who turned away on the day the two armies met﴾. The address is to the believers, and their "turning away" is their fleeing from the enemy. "The two armies" (al-jam'an): the host of the believers and the host of the polytheists, and that day was the Day of Uhud.

"Istazallahum" means: he sought their slips (zallatahum). Ibn Qutaybah said: it is like when you say, "I hastened so-and-so" (istaʿjaltu fulanan), meaning I sought his haste; and "I employed him" (istaʿmaltuhu), meaning I sought his work. "And what they had earned" (wa-alladhi kasabu) he means by it the sins.

Regarding the cause of their fleeing that day, there are two opinions.

The first: they heard that the Prophet (ﷺ) had been killed, so they allowed themselves to flee. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas, along with others.

The second: Satan reminded them of their misdeeds, so they disliked meeting Allah except in a state they would be pleased with. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

(p-484) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, do not be like those who disbelieved﴾ — i.e., like the hypocrites (munafiqun) who said to their brothers in hypocrisy. It was also said: "their brothers" refers to their kin by lineage.

Al-Zajjaj (d. 311 AH) said: He said "when they travel" (idha darabu) and did not say "when they traveled" (idh darabu), because he means: their condition is this always. You say: "So-and-so, when he speaks, tells the truth; and when he is struck, he endures." "Idha" (when) is used for what is future, except that the judgment about this future is only made because of what has been reported about it in the past.

The exegetes said: the meaning of ﴿travel in the land﴾ is: journey and go about. "Ghuzzan" is the plural of ghazi (warrior on expedition). In the speech there is an omitted element, its estimate being: "when they travel in the land and die, or go out raiding and are killed."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That Allah may make that﴾ — Ibn Abbas said: That Allah may make what they assumed, that had they been with them they would have been safe, ﴿a regret in their hearts﴾, i.e., grief. Ibn Faris said: "hasrah" is the anguish over a thing that has been lost.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah gives life and causes death﴾ — i.e., a person's caution does not prevent his appointed term.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah is Seeing of what you do﴾. Ibn Kathir, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read ya'maluna with the letter ya' (yaʿmalūna, third person), while the rest read it with the letter ta' (taʿmalūna, second person). Abu Ali (al-Farisi) said: the argument of the one who reads with ya' is that it is preceded by third-person address, which is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they said to their brothers﴾. As for the one who reads with ta', his argument is ﴿do not be like those who disbelieved﴾.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 3, verse 157:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And if you are killed﴾. The lam in "la-in" is the lam of oath (lam al-qasam), its implied sense being: "By Allah, if you are killed in jihad, ﴿or you die﴾ in your residence."

Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, and Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, recited "mutt" (مُتُّ), "muttum" (مُتُّمْ) and "mutna" (مُتْنا) with a damma on the mim (مِيم) throughout the Qur'an. Hafs narrated from 'Asim: ﴿or you die﴾ and ﴿And if you die﴾ with a damma on the mim in these two places only, and the rest of the Qur'an with a kasra. Nafi', Hamza, and al-Kisa'i recited every instance in the Qur'an with a kasra.

(p-485) His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Surely forgiveness from Allah and mercy are better than what they amass﴾. That is: better than the transient goods of this world for which you abandon jihad in order to gather them. Hafs, from 'Asim, recited "yajma'un" (يَجْمَعُونَ) with a ya' (ya), meaning: better than what others gather, those whom they left jihad for the sake of gathering. Ibn 'Abbas said: "better" than what the hypocrites gather in this world.

**"And if you die or are killed"**: That is, while you are residing (at home), or in your struggle in the way of God (jihad). **"Indeed to God you will be gathered"**: This is a warning of the Resurrection. Al-hashr (gathering) means collecting together with driving.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 3, verse 159:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So by mercy from Allah, you were lenient with them﴾. Al-Farra', Ibn Qutaybah and al-Zajjaj said: "ma" (what) here is a particle of expansion (ṣila), and similar to it is ﴿So for their breaking of their covenant﴾. Ibn al-Anbari said: the insertion of "ma" here produces emphasis.

Al-Nabigha said:

The man desires to live long, and a long life is not what harms him.

He emphasized by mentioning "ma", and concerning whom this mercy is connected there are two opinions.

One: that it is connected to the Prophet (ﷺ). The second: to the believers.

Qatadah said: The meaning of ﴿you were lenient with them﴾ is: your side was gentle, your character was good, and your forbearance was great. Al-Zajjaj said: "al-fazz" (harsh) is one who is rough of side and bad of character; it is said: fazaztu, tafuzzu, fazaza, and "al-fazz" is the water of the stomach and the dung, and it was named "fazz" because of the thickness of its drink. As for "ghalīẓ al-qalb" (hard of heart), it is said: it is the one hard of heart. So the mention of harshness and roughness, though they have one meaning, is for emphasis. Ibn Abbas said: "al-fazz" refers to speech, and "ghalīẓ al-qalb" refers to action.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿they would have dispersed﴾, meaning: they would have scattered. It is said: "fadadtu 'an al-kitab khatmahu" when I separated its seal from it. ﴿So pardon them﴾, meaning: overlook their lapses, and ask Allah for forgiveness for their sins. ﴿And consult them in the matter﴾, its meaning: extract their opinions and learn what they have. It is said that it is from: "shartu al-'asal" (I extracted the honey).

They recited:

And he swore by Allah, truly, that you are ∗∗∗ sweeter than the quail-meat when its honey is extracted.

Al-Zajjaj said: It is said: "shawartu al-rajul mushawara wa shuran", and what results from that is called "al-mashura"; and some say "al-mashura". It is said: so-and-so is beautiful in form and appearance (al-shura), meaning good in bearing and clothing. The meaning of their saying "I consulted so-and-so" is that you revealed what is with him and what is with me. "Shurtu al-dabba": when you tested it, and you knew its condition in its going. "Shurtu al-'asal": when you took it from the places of the bees. And "'asal mushar" (extracted honey). Al-A'sha said:

As if the clove and ginger ∗∗∗ spent the night in its mouth and extracted honey.

And "al-aray" is honey. The scholars differed as to what purpose Allah commanded His Prophet to consult his companions, despite his being complete in judgment and perfect in management, in three opinions.

One: so that those after him would follow his example; this is the saying of al-Hasan and Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah.

The second: to comfort their hearts; this is the saying of Qatadah, al-Rabi', Ibn Ishaq and Muqatil. Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, said: a parallel to this is his (ﷺ) saying: "A virgin is consulted concerning herself", he only meant seeking her contentment; for if she disliked it, the father would have had the right to marry her; and likewise the consultation of Ibrahim (peace be upon him) with his son when he was commanded to slaughter him.

The third: to inform of the blessing of consultation; this is the saying of al-Dahhak. Among the benefits of consultation is that when the consulter's matter does not succeed, he knows that the failure of success is pure decree, so he does not blame himself; and among them is that he may resolve upon a matter, then the correct course becomes clear to him in another's words, so he knows the incapacity of himself to encompass the many aspects of benefit. Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, said: consultation is the very essence of guidance, and whoever is self-sufficient in his opinion has gambled; and planning before action secures you from regret. Some wise people said: right judgment is not derived by anything like consultation, nor are blessings guarded by anything like consolation, nor is hatred acquired by anything like arrogance. Know that he (ﷺ) was only commanded to consult his companions regarding matters on which no revelation had come to him, and he mentioned them generally, while the intended ones were those of virtue and experience among them. Concerning that in which he was commanded to consult them, there are two opinions, related by al-Qadi Abu Ya'la.

One: that it is only the matter of worldly affairs. The second: the matter of religion and the world, and this is more sound.

Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Abbas recited: "wa shawarahum fi ba'di al-amr" (and consult them in some of the matter).

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So when you have decided﴾. Ibn Faris said: "al-azm" is the binding of the heart upon a thing, and intending to do it. Abu Razin, Abu Mijlaz, Abu al-'Aliyah, 'Ikrimah, and al-Jahdari recited ("fa-idha 'azamta") with a dhamma on the ta'. As for "al-tawakkul" (reliance), its explanation has already passed.

The meaning of the speech: so when you have decided to do something, then rely upon Allah, not upon consultation.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 3, verse 160:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿If Allah helps you﴾. Ibn Faris said: an-nasr (help) is aid, and al-khudhlan (forsaking) is abandoning aid. It has been said: the pronoun in His saying ﴿after Him﴾ refers back to His forsaking (of them).

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 3, verse 161:**

His saying, ﴿It is not for a prophet to misappropriate [yaghulla]﴾: There are seven opinions concerning the occasion of its revelation.

(p-490) The first: A piece of cloth from the spoils (*maghnam*) went missing on the day of Badr, and some people said, "Perhaps the Prophet (ﷺ) took it." So this verse was revealed. It was narrated by ʿIkrimah from Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: A man misappropriated some of the spoils of Hawazin on the day of Hunayn, and so this verse was revealed. It was narrated by al-Dahhak from Ibn ʿAbbas.

The third: Some of the notables of the people asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) to give them a share of the spoils in particular, and so this verse was revealed. It is also reported from Ibn ʿAbbas.

The fourth: The Prophet (ﷺ) dispatched advance scouts (*talaʾiʿ*), and the Prophet (ﷺ) gained spoils, but he did not distribute a share to the scouts. They said, "He divided the fayʾ and did not divide it for us," and so this verse was revealed. This was said by al-Dahhak.

The fifth: Some people misappropriated on the day of Badr, and so this verse was revealed. This was said by Qatadah.

The sixth: It was revealed concerning those who abandoned their position on the day of Uhud out of desire for booty, saying, "We fear that the Prophet (ﷺ) will say: 'Whoever takes something, it is his.'" The Prophet (ﷺ) said to them: "Did I not instruct you that you should not leave? Did you suppose that we would misappropriate?" And so this verse was revealed. This was said by Ibn al-Sa'ib and Muqatil.

The seventh: It was revealed concerning the misappropriation of revelation (*ghulul al-wahy*). This was said by al-Qurazi and Ibn Ishaq.

Some of the exegetes mentioned that they disliked what the Qur'an contained of criticism of their religion and their gods, so they asked him (ﷺ) to conceal that, and so this verse was revealed.

(p-491) The readers differed concerning *yaghulla*. Ibn Kathir, ʿAsim and Abu ʿAmr read it with a *fatha* on the *yāʾ* and a *ḍamma* on the *ghayn*, and its meaning is "to betray" (*yakhūnu*). Concerning this betrayal there are two views:

One: betrayal of property, according to the majority.

The second: betrayal of revelation, according to al-Qurazi and Ibn Ishaq.

The rest of the readers read it with a *ḍamma* on the *yāʾ* and a *fatha* on the *ghayn*, and it has two possible readings.

The first: that the meaning is "he is betrayed" (*yukhān*). [It may also mean "he is found to be a betrayer" (*yulfā khāʾinan*). It is said: *aghlaltu fulānan*, meaning "I found him to be a misappropriator," just as one says *aḥmaqtuhu*, "I found him to be a fool," and *aḥmadtuhu*, "I found him praiseworthy."] This was said by al-Hasan and Ibn Qutaybah.

The second: "he betrays," said by al-Farra'. al-Zajjaj permitted it, but Ibn Qutaybah rejected it, saying: "If he meant 'he betrays,' he would have said *yaghlul*, just as one says *yafsuq*, *yakhūn* and *yafjur*."

It is also said that the *lām* in His saying *linabiyyin* is transferred (*manqūlah*), and the meaning of the verse is: "It was not the Prophet's [place] to misappropriate." A parallel to this is ﴿It is not for God to take a son﴾ [Maryam: 36], meaning: it was not for God to take a son.

This verse is among the most subtle forms of allusion (*taʿrīḍ*), since the innocence of the Prophet (ﷺ) from misappropriation had already been established, and so it indicates that misappropriation occurs in others. A parallel to this is ﴿Indeed we or you are surely upon guidance or in clear error﴾ [Saba': 25]. Something similar has been reported from al-Suddi.

His saying, ﴿And whoever misappropriates will bring what he misappropriated on the Day of Resurrection﴾: *Ghulul* is taking something from the spoils secretly. From it comes *ghilala*, which is a garment worn beneath the clothes. *Ghalal* is water flowing between the trees. *Ghill* is the resentment lodged in the breast. The root of this category is concealment. Concerning his bringing what he misappropriated there are three opinions.

(p-492) The first: that he will come bearing what he misappropriated, carrying it. This is supported by what al-Bukhari and Muslim reported in the two *Sahihs* from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) stood among us one day and mentioned misappropriation, magnifying it and magnifying its matter. Then he said: 'I will not find any one of you coming on the Day of Resurrection with a camel upon his neck that has a bellow, saying: "O Messenger of God, help me!" I will say: "I cannot do anything for you; I have already conveyed [the message] to you." I will not find any one of you coming on the Day of Resurrection with a horse upon his neck that neighs, saying: "O Messenger of God, help me!" I will say: "I cannot do anything for you; I have already conveyed [the message] to you." I will not find any one of you coming on the Day of Resurrection with a sheep upon his neck that bleats, saying: "O Messenger of God, help me!" I will say: "I cannot do anything for you; I have already conveyed [the message] to you." I will not find any one of you coming on the Day of Resurrection with a soul upon his neck that cries out, saying: "O Messenger of God, help me!" I will say: "I cannot do anything for you; I have already conveyed [the message] to you." I will not find any one of you coming on the Day of Resurrection with pieces of cloth upon his neck fluttering, saying: "O Messenger of God, help me!" I will say: "I cannot do anything for you; I have already conveyed [the message] to you." I will not find any one of you coming on the Day of Resurrection with gold or silver upon his neck, saying: "O Messenger of God, help me!" I will say: "I cannot do anything for you; I have already conveyed [the message] to you.'"'" *Rughāʾ* is the sound of a camel, *thughāʾ* is the sound of a sheep, *nafs* is what is taken as captives (*sabī*) by misappropriation, *riqāʿ* are garments, and *ṣāmit* is property.

The second opinion: that he will come bearing the sin of what he misappropriated.

The third: that he will give back the equivalent of what he misappropriated from his good deeds. The first opinion is the most sound because of the authentic report.

(p-493) His saying, ﴿Then every soul will be paid in full for what it earned﴾: that is, it will be given the recompense for what it earned.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 3, verse 162:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Is he who follows the pleasure of Allah﴾ — the scholars differed about the meaning of this verse, into two opinions.

The first: its meaning is: "Is he who follows the pleasure of Allah, by not embezzling [the spoils], like one who returns with the anger of Allah [upon him] for having embezzled?" This is the saying of Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Dahhak, and the majority (al-Jumhur).

The second: when the Prophet (ﷺ) commanded the Muslims to follow him on the Day of Uhud, the believers followed him, and a group of the hypocrites (munafiqun) stayed behind. So Allah informed about the condition of the one who followed him and the one who stayed behind from him. This is the saying of al-Zajjaj.

**The words of Allah, Exalted: ﴿They are of varying degrees﴾.** Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is, "They are possessors of degrees." Regarding the meaning of "degrees," there are two opinions.

One: they are the degrees of Paradise. This was said by al-Hasan.

The second: they are their virtues, so some of them are more virtuous than others. This was said by al-Farra' and Ibn Qutaybah.

Regarding who is meant by this statement, there are two opinions.

One: they are those who followed the pleasure of Allah, and those who earned the wrath of Allah. For those who followed the pleasure of Allah there is reward, and for those who earned His wrath there is punishment. This is the statement of Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: they are only those who followed the pleasure of Allah, for they differ in their stations. This is the statement of Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Abu Salih, and Muqatil.

(p. 494) Allah's words: ﴿Indeed, Allah conferred favor upon the believers﴾, meaning He bestowed blessings upon them. "Anfusuhum" (their own selves) means their community. It was also said to mean their lineage. Al-Dahhak and Abu al-Jawza' read (مِن أنْفَسِهِمْ) *min anfasihim*, with a fatha on the fa'.

There are four opinions on the sense of the favor in His being "from among themselves":

The first is that he was known for his lineage among them. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada.

The second is that they had been informed of his affair and knew his truthfulness. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

The third is that it would be easier for them to learn from him, since his language matched their language. This was said by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi.

The fourth is that their nobility is completed by the appearance of a prophet from among them. This was said by al-Mawardi.

Is this verse specific or general? On this there are two opinions.

One is that it is specific to the Arabs. This is related from 'Aisha and the majority.

The other is that it is general to all believers, so the meaning is that he is not an angel, nor from among other than the children of Adam. This is the view chosen by al-Zajjaj.

The explanation of the rest of the verse has already passed in (Surat al-Baqara).

(p. 495) Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Why is it that when a calamity strikes you, though you had struck (the enemy) with twice as much,﴾ ... 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "When the Day of Uhud came, they were punished for what they had done on the Day of Badr, by taking ransom. Seventy of them were killed, the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ fled, his lower incisor (rubā'iyyah) was broken, his helmet (al-bayḍah) was crushed upon his head, and blood flowed down his face. Then this verse was revealed [up to His saying: ﴿Say: It is from yourselves﴾]," he said, "because of your taking of ransom."

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Why is it that when a calamity strikes you﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: "This is the conjunctive wāw (wāw al-nasaq), to which the interrogative alif (alif al-istifhām) has been added, so it remains fatḥah in its form before the addition. Similarly, when someone says, 'So-and-so spoke such-and-such,' the one responding says: 'Is he one who says that?'" As for "al-muṣībah" (the calamity), it refers to what befell them on the Day of Uhud, while they had already inflicted twice that upon the polytheists on the Day of Badr, for seventy of them had been killed, so they had killed seventy on the Day of Badr and taken seventy captive. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, Qatadah, and the majority, except that al-Zajjaj said: "You inflicted a similar (calamity) on the Day of Uhud and a similar one on the Day of Badr," thus placing the "two-fold" across the two days.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿How is this?﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: "From where has this struck us, while we are Muslims?"

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Say: It is from yourselves﴾. Concerning this there are three views.

(p. 496) The first: its meaning is "because of your taking the ransom on the Day of Badr." This was said by 'Umar ibn al-Khattab. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Jibril came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: 'Indeed Allah has disliked what your people did in taking ransom, and He has commanded you to give them a choice between striking the necks of the captives, or accepting ransom on condition that the same number of them be killed.' He mentioned that to the people, and they said: 'Our clans and our brothers! Rather, we will take ransom from them, and the same number of us will be martyred.' So there were killed among them on the Day of Uhud seventy, equal to the number of the captives of Badr." On this view, the meaning is: "Say: It is because of your taking the ransom and your choosing death for yourselves."

The second: that this occurred due to the disobedience of the archers on the Day of Uhud and their abandoning the command of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, and Muqatil, among others.

The third: that it was due to their opposing the Messenger in going out of Madinah on the Day of Uhud, for he had commanded them to remain fortified within it, but they said: "Rather, we will go out." This was said by Qatadah and al-Rabi'. Muqatil said: "Indeed Allah is over all things capable," of victory and defeat.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 3, verses 166–167:

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And what struck you on the day the two hosts met﴾. "The two hosts" are the Prophet (ﷺ) and his companions, and Abu Sufyan and his companions. This was on the day of Uhud, and the account of what befell them has already been mentioned.

(p. 497) The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿by the permission of Allah﴾. Regarding this there are three opinions.

The first is His command. The second is His decree, related from Ibn Abbas. The third is His knowledge, as stated by al-Zajjaj.

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿and that He might know the believers﴾. That is, so that the faith of the believers would become manifest through their steadfastness in the face of what befell them, and so that the hypocrisy of the hypocrites would become manifest through their cowardice and their lack of patience. Ibn Qutayba said: "Nifaq (hypocrisy) is derived from naafaa' al-yarbu' (the escape-hole of the jerboa). The jerboa has a burrow (juhr) among its burrows, from which it emerges when the hole through which it entered is blocked." Al-Ziyadi related from al-Asmai: "The jerboa has four burrows: the naafaa' (the one from which it often exits and into which it often enters); the qaasi'a', so named because it throws out the dirt of the burrow and then packs some of it, as if sealing the mouth of the burrow with it, and from this one says: 'So-and-so was wounded and the blood has clotted (qasa'a bi-l-dam)', meaning it filled up and did not flow; the daamaa', so named because it throws the dirt out of the mouth of the burrow and then plasters the mouth of the burrow with it, as if smearing it, and from this one says: 'DaMMim qadrak bi-shahm' (smear your pot with fat), meaning coat it with it; and the raahitaa', whose derivation he did not mention, and which it makes as one of a number of burrows, so that if one of them is blocked, it exits from another." Abu Zayd said: "The hypocrite is likened to it, because he enters Islam with his words and exits from it by a hidden knot, just as the jerboa enters by one door and leaves by another." Ibn Qutayba said: "Nifaq is an Islamic term that the Arabs did not know before Islam."

Ibn Abbas said: "Those who showed hypocrisy are Abdullah ibn Ubayy and his companions." Musa ibn Uqba said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) went out on the day of Uhud with the Muslims, who numbered a thousand men, while the polytheists numbered three thousand. Ibn Ubayy turned back from him with three hundred."

As for ﴿fighting﴾ (qital), it is the direct engagement in battle. Regarding the meaning of ﴿repelling﴾ (al-daf'), there are three opinions.

The first is that it means increasing the numbers. This was related by Mujahid from Ibn Abbas, and it is the view of al-Hasan, Ikrima, al-Dahhak, al-Suddi, Ibn Jurayj, and others.

(p. 498) The second is that its meaning is: defend yourselves and your sanctities (haram). This was related by Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas, and it is the view of Muqatil.

The third is that it also means fighting, as stated by Ibn Zayd.

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿If we knew there would be fighting﴾. Regarding this there are three opinions.

The first is that its meaning is: if we knew that today there would be fighting, we would not have left you. This was mentioned by Ibn Ishaq.

The second: if we were skilled at fighting, we would have followed you.

The third: its meaning is only that there would be killing, not fighting. These two were mentioned by al-Mawardi.

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿They were nearer to disbelief that day than to faith﴾, that is, nearer to disbelief, ﴿than to faith﴾, that is, to faith. He said "that day" because before that they had not displayed what they displayed; so by their outward state before that, they had been nearer to faith.

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿They say with their mouths what is not in their hearts﴾. Regarding this there are two aspects, mentioned by al-Mawardi.

The first: they utter faith, while in their hearts there is nothing but disbelief.

The second: they say, "We are helpers," while they are enemies. Regarding what they conceal, he mentioned two aspects.

The first is that it is hypocrisy. The second is enmity.

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And what struck you on the day the two hosts met﴾. "The two hosts" are the Prophet (ﷺ) and his companions, and Abu Sufyan and his companions. This was on the day of Uhud, and the account of what befell them has already been mentioned.
